Total at output in parallel with $I_{1}$:

$$R_{out}=R_{1}\parallel R_{down}$$

Ideal $I_{1}$, $R_{1}=\infty$:

$$R_{out}=R_{down}$$

This is $\approx g_{m2}r_{o2}$ times larger than
a simple common-source $r_{o1}$.

Small signal KCL. Let $v_{x}$ at $X$.

$M_{1}$: $v_{gs1}=v_{in}$, $v_{ds1}=v_{x}$

$$i_{d1}=g_{m1}v_{in}+\frac{v_{x}}{r_{o1}}$$

into $M_{1}$ drain.

$M_{2}$: $v_{gs2}=-v_{x}$, $v_{bs2}=-v_{x}$,
$v_{ds2}=v_{out}-v_{x}$

$$i_{d2}=-(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})v_{x}+\frac{v_{out}-v_{x}}{r_{o2}}$$

into $M_{2}$ drain.

KCL at $X$: $i_{d1}=i_{d2}$.
KCL at $v_{out}$: $i_{d2}=-v_{out}/R_{1}$.

i.e.

$$g_{m1}v_{in}+\frac{v_{x}}{r_{o1}}+\frac{v_{out}}{R_{1}}=0$$

$$A_{v}=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=
-\frac{g_{m1}}{\frac{1}{R_{1}}+\frac{1}{r_{o1}}\frac{1/r_{o2}+1/R_{1}}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+1/r_{o2}}}$$

$$A_{v}=-g_{m1}R_{1}\frac{r_{o1}+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o1}r_{o2}}{R_{1}+R_{down}}$$

$$A_{v}=-g_{m1}r_{o1}\left[1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}\right]$$

Approximate:

Neglecting body effect $g_{mb2}=0$:

$$R_{out}\approx g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}$$
$$A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}$$

vs $g_{m1}r_{o1}$ for simple CS with ideal load.

Impedance at $X$ is $r_{o1}\parallel R_{in2}$,
where $R_{in2}=(R_{1}+r_{o2})/(1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2})$
looking into $M_{2}$ source. For $R_{1}=\infty$,
$v_{x}/v_{in}\approx -g_{m1}r_{o1}$.

Input resistance at gate of $M_{1}$ at low
frequency:

$$R_{in}=\infty$$

Circuit is inverting, high gain, high output
impedance, reduced output swing.

answers.question: Explain why the Miller effect is less pronounced in a cascode.

answer.text:
In a common-source the feedback capacitance
$C_{gd}$ - or $C_{\mu}$ in a BJT - bridges a large inverting gain.

$$ A_v = \frac{v_d}{v_g} \approx -g_m R_D $$

By Miller:

$$ C_{in} = C_{gd}(1-A_v) \approx C_{gd}(1+g_m R_D) $$
$$ C_{out} = C_{gd}(1-1/A_v) \approx C_{gd} $$

A small physical $C_{gd}$ looks like a huge capacitor to ground at the input, forming a low frequency input pole with $R_{sig}$. This is the Miller effect: a large opposite-phase swing on the two sides of $C_{gd}$ requires a large charging current from the input.

A cascode splits V-to-I and I-to-V:

common-source $M1$ stacked with common-gate $M2$. $M1$ gives transconductance, $M2$ gives voltage gain as a current buffer.

1. Input device has no voltage gain.

The load seen at the drain of $M1$ is not $R_D$, it is the input resistance of a common-gate looking into the source:

$$ R_{in2} = \frac{R_D+r_{o2}}{1+g_{m2}r_{o2}} \approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}} $$

So:

$$ A_{v1} = \frac{v_{d1}}{v_{in}} = -g_{m1}(r_{o1}\parallel R_{in2}) \approx -\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}} \approx -1 $$

The Miller multiplication on $M1$ is then:

$$ C_{in1} = C_{gd1}(1-A_{v1}) \approx 2 C_{gd1} $$

instead of $C_{gd1}(1+g_{m1}R_D)$ which can be 10-100x larger.

Intuitively, $M2$ holds $v_{d1}$ almost constant. If $v_{in}$ rises, $i_{d1}$ rises. $M2$ must pass that extra current, so $|v_{gs2}|$ rises a little, i.e. its source, $v_{d1}$, moves down a little. No large swing across $C_{gd1}$, no large Miller current.

2. High gain device has no Miller to the input.

All the voltage gain happens in $M2$:

$$ A_{v2} = \frac{v_{out}}{v_{s2}} \approx +g_{m2}R_D $$

But $M2$'s gate is AC ground. Its $C_{gs2}$ goes from input, the source, to ground. Its $C_{gd2}$ goes from output, the drain, to ground. Neither bridges input to output of the overall amplifier.

In particular the large output swing is isolated from the overall input. It just adds normal capacitance to ground at the output and at the intermediate node, not Miller-multiplied capacitance at the input.

So the input pole

$$\omega_{p,in} \approx 1 / R_{sig}[C_{gs1}+ (1-A_{v1})C_{gd1}]$$

is pushed to much higher frequency. The price is an extra pole at the $M1$-drain / $M2$-source node, but the impedance there is $\sim 1/g_{m2}$, so that pole is at $\sim g_{m2}/C$ and very high.

In short: low gain across the input device's feedback cap, and grounding of the high-gain device's feedback cap.

The reasoning matches the golden solution's dominant mechanism and conclusion, with no significant errors.

answers.question: Explain why the Miller effect is less pronounced in a cascode.

answer.text:
Miller multiplication needs inverting voltage gain
across a capacitor bridging input to output.

For a capacitor $C_{gd}$ from gate to drain with
$A_v = v_d/v_g$:

$$ I_{Cgd} = j\omega C_{gd}(v_g-v_d) = j\omega C_{gd}(1-A_v)v_g $$

at the input it looks like:

$$ C_{in} = C_{gd}(1-A_v) \approx C_{gd}(1+|A_v|) $$

In a single common-source the same transistor provides
both transconductance and voltage gain:

$$ A_v = -g_m (R_D \parallel r_o) $$

large, e.g. 10-100. So $C_{gd}$ appears 10-100x larger at the input, creating a large dominant input pole.

A cascode splits the two functions:

1. M1, common-source, does V-to-I,
2. M2, common-gate, does I-to-V.

M1 is loaded not by $R_D$ but by the low impedance
looking into the source of a common-gate:

$$ R_{in2} = \frac{R_D+r_{o2}}{1+g_{m2}r_{o2}} \approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}} $$

So the voltage gain of the input device itself is:

$$ A_{v1} = \frac{v_{d1}}{v_{g1}} = -g_{m1} (r_{o1} \parallel R_{in2}) \approx -\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}} \approx -1 $$

The drain of M1 is held almost constant. The swing is small.
Hence its Miller factor is:

$$ C_{in1} = C_{gd1}(1-A_{v1}) \approx 2 C_{gd1} $$

not $(1+g_mR_D)C_{gd1}$.

The large voltage gain now occurs in M2:

$$ A_{v2} = \frac{v_{d2}}{v_{s2}} \approx +g_{m2}(R_D\parallel r_{o2}) $$

but M2 has no bridging capacitor between its input, the source, and its output, the drain. Its gate is AC ground. So:

* $C_{gd2}$ goes from output to AC ground, just output load
* $C_{gs2}$ goes from input-intermediate node to AC ground, just load on that node

No $(1+|A_{v2}|)$ multiplication.

In short: the transistor with Miller bridging, M1, has $\approx$ unity gain, and the transistor with large gain, M2, has no Miller bridging.

answers.question: Explain why the Miller effect is less pronounced in a cascode.

answer.text:
In a common source / common emitter the large Miller multiplication
comes from the capacitor that directly bridges input to output.

For a bridging $C$ between input and output with voltage gain
$A_v = V_o/V_i$ Miller's theorem says:

$$ C_{in} = C\,(1-A_v) $$

In a single CS stage, $A_v = -g_m R_D$ is large and inverting:

$$ C_{in} \approx C_{gs} + (1+g_m R_D) C_{gd} $$

$C_{gd}$, resp. $C_\mu$, is multiplied by the full gain. That large
input capacitance and output-to-input feedback kills bandwidth.

A cascode splits that one large gain into two stages with no
single capacitor seeing the full gain:

$$ \text{CS input device} \rightarrow \text{CG cascode device} $$

with overall $A_v = A_{v1}\cdot A_{v2}$ still large.

1. **Input device sees only small gain.** $Q_1$ is loaded not by $R_D$ but by the low impedance looking into the source of the grounded-gate $Q_2$:

$$ R_{in2} \approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}} $$

So

$$ A_{v1} = \frac{v_{x}}{v_i} \approx -g_{m1} (r_{o1} || R_{in2}) \approx -\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}} \approx -1 $$

where $v_x$ is the intermediate drain1/source2 node.

$C_{gd1}$ now bridges input to $v_x$, not to the final
output, so it is multiplied only by $1-A_{v1} \approx 2$:

$$ C_{in} \approx C_{gs1} + 2 C_{gd1} $$

instead of $(1+g_m R_D)C_{gd1}$. Physically, the CG buffers the drain of $Q_1$ from the big output swing. $V_{d1}$ barely moves, so little feedback current flows through $C_{gd1}$.

2. **Cascode device has no Miller multiplication.** For $Q_2$, the common terminal, gate, is AC ground. Its $C_{gd2}$ goes from output to AC ground, not from output to input. It just loads the output:

$$ C_{o} \approx C_{gd2} $$

Similarly $C_{gs2}$ goes from the intermediate node to AC ground. There is no capacitor directly between its input, the source, and its output, the drain, except small $C_{ds}$.

In short: no capacitor spans the full high-gain input-to-output path. The big output swing is isolated from the input by the grounded-gate device, so reverse feedthrough is essentially eliminated and the input pole is pushed to much higher frequency.

The reasoning matches the golden solution's central mechanism and conclusion, with no significant errors or omissions.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 17.

answer.text:
This is a common-gate stage with active load.

* $M_{2}$ : CG input device. Gate ac ground by $V_{b1}$,
  source is input, drain is output.
* $M_{1}$ : PMOS current source load. Source to $V_{DD}$
  ac ground, gate ac ground by $V_{b2}$, drain to
  output.

Body is strapped to source in both devices in the
symbol, so no back gate. Put

$$g_{m}=\sqrt{2\mu C_{ox}\frac{W}{L}I_{D}}\;,\;
r_{o}= \frac{1}{\lambda I_{D}} $$

Assume both in saturation and small signal.

$M_{1}$ with $v_{g1}=v_{s1}=0$ has $v_{gs1}=0$.
It is simply $r_{o1}$ from output to ac ground.
Indeed for either NMOS or PMOS, with currents
entering the device,

$$i_{d}=g_{m}v_{gs}+g_{ds}v_{ds}$$

For $M_{1}$: $v_{s1}=0$, $v_{g1}=0$, $v_{d1}=v_{out}$,

$$i_{d1}=g_{m1}\cdot 0 +\frac{v_{out}}{r_{o1}}$$

i.e. $r_{o1}$ to ground.

For $M_{2}$: $v_{s2}=v_{in}$, $v_{g2}=0$, $v_{d2}=v_{out}$,

$$v_{gs2}=-v_{in},\quad v_{ds2}=v_{out}-v_{in}$$

$$i_{d2}=g_{m2}v_{gs2}+\frac{v_{ds2}}{r_{o2}}
 =-g_{m2}v_{in}+\frac{v_{out}-v_{in}}{r_{o2}} \tag{1}$$

If body were to GND, replace $g_{m2}$ by $g_{m2}+g_{mb2}$.

### DC

In DC, series connection forces

$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_{D}$$

$$I_{D}\approx \frac12\mu_{p}C_{ox}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_{1}
 (V_{DD}-V_{b2}-|V_{THp}|)^{2}$$

$$I_{D}\approx \frac12\mu_{n}C_{ox}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_{2}
 (V_{b1}-V_{IN}-V_{THn})^{2}$$

neglecting $\lambda$. Hence $V_{IN}$ DC is fixed by
$V_{b1}$ and $I_{D}$:

$$V_{IN}=V_{b1}-V_{THn}-\sqrt{\frac{2I_{D}}
 {\mu_{n}C_{ox}(W/L)_{2}}}$$

Saturation:

$M_{2}$ NMOS: $V_{DS2}\ge V_{GS2}-V_{THn}$

$$V_{out}-V_{IN}\ge V_{b1}-V_{IN}-V_{THn}$$

$$V_{out}\ge V_{b1}-V_{THn} \tag{2}$$

$M_{1}$ PMOS: $V_{SD1}\ge V_{SG1}-|V_{THp}|$

$$V_{DD}-V_{out}\ge V_{DD}-V_{b2}-|V_{THp}|$$

$$V_{out}\le V_{b2}+|V_{THp}| \tag{3}$$

So for both saturated

$$V_{b1}-V_{THn}\le V_{out}\le V_{b2}+|V_{THp}|$$

The output DC node is high impedance, $r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$.
Any mismatch in $I_{D1},I_{D2}$ drives $V_{out}$ to one
rail. In practice the bias must be stabilized by feedback.

### Voltage gain

KCL at output node, open output. Currents entering
the node from the two drains are $-i_{d1}$ and $-i_{d2}$:

$$i_{d1}+i_{d2}=0$$

$$\frac{v_{out}}{r_{o1}}-g_{m2}v_{in}
 +\frac{v_{out}-v_{in}}{r_{o2}}=0$$

$$v_{out}\left(\frac1{r_{o1}}+\frac1{r_{o2}}\right)
 =v_{in}\left(g_{m2}+\frac1{r_{o2}}\right)$$

$$ A_{v}=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=
 \frac{g_{m2}+g_{ds2}}{g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}} $$

$$A_{v}= \frac{1+g_{m2}r_{o2}}{1+r_{o2}/r_{o1}}
 =\frac{r_{o1}}{r_{o1}+r_{o2}}(1+g_{m2}r_{o2})$$

Since $g_{m2}r_{o2}\gg 1$,

$$A_{v}\approx g_{m2}(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})>0$$

Non-inverting, large, like a common-source with
active load. $g_{m1}$ does not appear.

With body effect to GND: $g_{m2}\to g_{m2}+g_{mb2}$.

Intuition: $\Delta V_{in}$ down increases $V_{GS2}$,
increases $M_{2}$ current, pulls more current through
high impedance $r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$, $V_{out}$ falls.
Actually $v_{gs}=-v_{in}$, drain current change is
in phase with $-v_{in}$, voltage drop across load gives
$+$ sign. CG is non-inverting.

### Input resistance

Current entering source is $i_{in}=i_{s2}=-i_{d2}$,
gate draws no current:

From (1),

$$i_{in}=g_{m2}v_{in}-\frac{v_{out}-v_{in}}{r_{o2}}
 =v_{in}\left(g_{m2}+\frac1{r_{o2}}\right)-\frac{v_{out}}{r_{o2}}$$

Using $v_{out}=A_{v}v_{in}$,

$$\frac{i_{in}}{v_{in}}=
 \left(g_{m2}+\frac1{r_{o2}}\right)
 \left[1-\frac{1/r_{o2}}{1/r_{o1}+1/r_{o2}}\right]$$

$$R_{in}=\frac{v_{in}}{i_{in}}=
 \frac{r_{o1}+r_{o2}}{1+g_{m2}r_{o2}}$$

This is the classic $R_{in}=(R_{D}+r_{o})/(1+g_{m}r_{o})$
with $R_{D}=r_{o1}$.

For $R_{D}=0$, $R_{in}=1/(g_{m2}+g_{ds2})\approx 1/g_{m2}$.
Here $R_{D}=r_{o1}$ is large, so $R_{in}$ is raised:

$$R_{in}\approx \frac1{g_{m2}}\left(1+\frac{r_{o1}}{r_{o2}}\right)$$

e.g. $r_{o1}\approx r_{o2}$ : $R_{in}\approx 2/g_{m2}$.
For ideal current source $r_{o1}\to\infty$, $R_{in}\to\infty$
at low frequency because ac $i_{d2}$ is forced to zero.

With body: $g_{m2}\to g_{m2}+g_{mb2}$.

### Output resistance

Short $v_{in}=0$ for $R_{out}$. Then $M_{2}$ source
is ac ground, gate ac ground. Impedance looking into
drain is $r_{o2}$. In parallel with $r_{o1}$:

$$R_{out}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$$

More generally with source resistance $R_{sig}$:

$$R_{out}=r_{o1}\parallel\left[r_{o2}+(1+g_{m2}r_{o2})R_{sig}\right]$$

Hence $A_{v}\approx g_{m2}R_{out}$.

In summary: high gain non-inverting amplifier,
low $\sim 1/g_{m}$ input impedance, high output
impedance.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 17.

answer.text:
Figure 17 is a single stage:

* $M_{2}$ : common-gate input device.
  source = $V_{in}$, gate = AC ground $V_{b1}$,
  drain = $V_{out}$.
* $M_{1}$ : PMOS current source load.
  source + n-well = $V_{DD}$, gate = AC ground $V_{b2}$,
  drain = $V_{out}$.

$V_{DD},V_{b1},V_{b2}$ are AC ground. $M_{1}$ supplies
the DC bias current of $M_{2}$ and presents a high
small signal impedance to the output node.

Assume both in saturation. In a normal p-sub process

* $M_{1}$ is in its own n-well, bulk to source,
  no back-gate.
* $M_{2}$ bulk is to GND, source is at $\ne 0$,
  back-gate exists unless in triple well.

Put $v_{bs1}=0$, $v_{bs2}= -v_{in}$ for AC.
Put $g_{ds1}=1/r_{o1}$, $g_{ds2}=1/r_{o2}$.

### DC operation

Let the bias current be $I_{D}$ :

$$ I_{D}=I_{D1}=I_{D2} $$

$$ I_{D1}\approx \tfrac12 \mu_{p}C_{ox}(W/L)_{1}
(V_{DD}-V_{b2}-|V_{THP}|)^{2}(1+\lambda_{p}V_{SD1}) $$
$$ I_{D2}\approx \tfrac12 \mu_{n}C_{ox}(W/L)_{2}
(V_{b1}-V_{in,DC}-V_{THN}')^{2}(1+\lambda_{n}V_{DS2}) $$

$V_{b2}$ nominally defines $I_{D}$, $V_{b1}$ and
$V_{in,DC}$ define $V_{GS2}$.

Increase $V_{in}$ decreases $V_{GS2}$, decreases
the pull-down current of $M_{2}$. The pull-up
$M_{1}$ then pulls $V_{out}$ up. It is non-inverting.

For saturation:

$M_{2}$ : $V_{DS2}\ge V_{GS2}-V_{THN}$

$$ V_{out}-V_{in}\ge V_{b1}-V_{in}-V_{THN} $$

$$ V_{out} \ge V_{b1}-V_{THN} $$

$M_{1}$ PMOS : $V_{SD1}\ge V_{SG1}-|V_{THP}|$

$$ V_{DD}-V_{out} \ge V_{DD}-V_{b2}-|V_{THP}| $$

$$ V_{out}\le V_{DD}-V_{ov1} $$

where $V_{ov1}=V_{SG1}-|V_{THP}|$.

Allowed output:

$$ V_{b1}-V_{THN} \le V_{out} \le V_{DD}-V_{ov1} $$

$M_{2}$ on requires $V_{b1}-V_{in,DC}\ge V_{THN}'$.

Note $V_{out}$ DC is a high impedance node,
$r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$ to AC ground. Like the
CS with current source load the DC value is
very sensitive to $I_{D1}-I_{D2}$ mismatch.

### Small signal model

Gate $M_{2}$ grounded, source driven by $v_{in}$,
drain to $v_{out}$ :

$$ v_{gs2} = -v_{in},\quad v_{bs2}=-v_{in},\quad
v_{ds2}=v_{out}-v_{in} $$

Drain incremental current into drain:

$$ i_{d2}=g_{m2}v_{gs2}+g_{mb2}v_{bs2}+g_{ds2}v_{ds2} $$
$$ = -(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})v_{in}+g_{ds2}(v_{out}-v_{in}) $$

$M_{1}$: $v_{sg1}=0$, $v_{bs1}=0$, so only $r_{o1}$
between $V_{DD}$ AC ground and $v_{out}$.

KCL at output, no other load:

$$ \frac{v_{out}}{r_{o1}} + i_{d2} = 0 $$

i.e.

$$ -\frac{v_{out}}{r_{o1}} = -(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})v_{in}
+ g_{ds2}(v_{out}-v_{in}) $$

$$ v_{out}\left(\frac1{r_{o1}}+g_{ds2}\right)
 = (g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2})v_{in} $$

Hence voltage gain:

$$ A_{v}=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}} =
(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2})(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}) $$

$$ \approx +(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}) $$

Positive, of the same order as a CS stage with
active load. With bulk to source, $g_{mb2}=0$:

$$ A_{v}\approx g_{m2}(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}) $$

### Input resistance

Drive source with $v_{x}$, gate grounded, drain
loaded by $R_{D}=r_{o1}$. With $v_{s}=v_{x}$,
$v_{d}$ at drain:

$$ \frac{v_{d}}{R_{D}}+i_{d}=0 $$
$$ i_{d}=-(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})v_{x}+g_{ds2}(v_{d}-v_{x}) $$

$$ v_{d} = \frac{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2}}
{1/R_{D}+g_{ds2}}v_{x} $$

Test current injected in source is $i_{x}=-i_{d}$,
since gate and bulk draw no current:

$$ i_{x}=(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2})v_{x}-g_{ds2}v_{d} $$

$$ =\frac{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2}}{1+g_{ds2}R_{D}}v_{x} $$

$$ R_{in}=\frac{v_{x}}{i_{x}}
 =\frac{1+g_{ds2}R_{D}}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2}} $$
$$ =\frac{R_{D}+r_{o2}}{1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}} $$

With $R_{D}=r_{o1}$ :

$$ R_{in}=\frac{r_{o1}+r_{o2}}
{1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}} $$

For $r_{o}\to\infty$ :

$$ R_{in}\to \frac1{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}} $$

This low value is characteristic of CG. With
finite $r_{o1}\sim r_{o2}$, $R_{in}\approx 2/(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})$.

### Output resistance

Look into drain with source resistance $R_{S}$.
Resistance into $M_{2}$ drain alone is

$$ R_{d2}=r_{o2}+R_{S}+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}R_{S} $$
$$ \approx r_{o2}[1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})R_{S}] $$

In parallel with $r_{o1}$ :

$$ R_{out}=r_{o1}\parallel R_{d2} $$

For ideal voltage drive $R_{S}=0$ :

$$ R_{out}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2} $$

high, as for active loaded CS.

In summary: non-inverting high-gain, low $R_{in}$,
high $R_{out}$ stage. No Miller multiplication of
$C_{gd2}$, hence wideband. The low $R_{in}\sim 1/g_{m}$
is useful for current input, cascode load, etc.

* $M_{2}$: input device in common gate.
  source = input $V_{in}$, gate = AC ground $V_{b1}$,
  drain = output $V_{out}$.
* $M_{1}$: PMOS current source load.
  source to $V_{DD}$, gate = DC $V_{b2}$, drain = output.

Assume both in saturation with DC current $I_{D}$:

$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_{D}$$

$M_{1}$ has $n$-well tied to source, no back gate.
$M_{2}$ is $n$-MOS in $p$-sub, body to GND.
Its source is at $V_{in,DC}\ne 0$ AC-wise, so

for $M_{1}$: $g_{m1},r_{o1}$. $g_{mb1}=0$.

In small signal $V_{DD}, V_{b1}, V_{b2}$ are AC ground.

$M_{1}$ : $V_{sg1}=0$, so only $r_{o1}$ from
$V_{out}$ to ground remains.

$M_{2}$ : gate grounded, body grounded:

$$v_{gs2} = -v_{in}$$
$$v_{bs2} = -v_{in}$$
$$v_{ds2} = v_{out}-v_{in}$$

Current from drain to source in $M_{2}$:

$$I_{d\to s}=g_{m2}v_{gs2}+g_{mb2}v_{bs2}+\frac{v_{ds2}}{r_{o2}}$$

$r_{o1}$ to ground plus $M_{2}$ branch to input:

$$\frac{v_{out}}{r_{o1}}+g_{m2}v_{gs2}+g_{mb2}v_{bs2}
+\frac{v_{out}-v_{in}}{r_{o2}}=0$$

$$\frac{v_{out}}{r_{o1}}-(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})v_{in}
+\frac{v_{out}-v_{in}}{r_{o2}}=0$$

Hence voltage gain:

$$v_{out}\left(\frac1{r_{o1}}+\frac1{r_{o2}}\right)
=v_{in}\left(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+\frac1{r_{o2}}\right)$$

$$ A_{v}=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=
\left(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+\frac1{r_{o2}}\right)(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}) $$

$$\approx (g_{m2}+g_{mb2})(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})$$

Positive, non-inverting. Increase $V_{in}$ decreases
$V_{GS2}$, decreases $I_{D2}$, the PMOS pulls $V_{out}$ up.

$r_{o}$ must be kept. With ideal loads gain $\to\infty$.

Without body effect: $g_{mb2}=0$,
$A_{v}\approx g_{m2}(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})$.

### Input resistance

Let $i_{in}$ enter the source. KCL at source:

$$i_{in}+I_{d\to s}=0$$

$$i_{in}=-g_{m2}v_{gs2}-g_{mb2}v_{bs2}-\frac{v_{out}-v_{in}}{r_{o2}}$$

$$i_{in}=(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})v_{in}-\frac{v_{out}-v_{in}}{r_{o2}}$$

$$ \frac{i_{in}}{v_{in}} = g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+\frac1{r_{o2}}-\frac{A_{v}}{r_{o2}} $$

Using $A_{v}$ above:

$$\frac1{R_{in}}=\left(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+\frac1{r_{o2}}\right)
\frac{r_{o2}}{r_{o1}+r_{o2}}$$

$$ R_{in}=\frac{1+r_{o1}/r_{o2}}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+1/r_{o2}}
=\frac{r_{o1}+r_{o2}}{1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}} $$

This is the classic
$R_{in}=(1+R_{D}/r_{o})/(g_{m}+g_{mb}+1/r_{o})$
with $R_{D}=r_{o1}$.

If $r_{o1}\ll r_{o2}$ : $R_{in}\approx 1/(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})$.
If $r_{o1}=r_{o2}=r_{o}$ : $R_{in}\approx 2/(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})$
for $(g_{m}+g_{mb})r_{o}\gg 1$.
Active load raises $R_{in}$.

### Output resistance

Put $v_{in}=0$ with source resistance $R_{S}$, apply $v_{x}$
at output. Impedance looking into drain of $M_{2}$ is

$$R_{o2}=r_{o2}+[1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}]R_{S}$$

in parallel with $r_{o1}$:

$$R_{out}=r_{o1}\parallel \left\{r_{o2}+[1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}]R_{S}\right\}$$

For ideal voltage drive $R_{S}=0$:

$$R_{out}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$$

High impedance, similar to common-source active load.

In short: low $\approx 1/g_{m}$ input impedance
current buffer with positive high gain $g_{m}(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})$
and high output impedance.

DC constraints for saturation:

$M_{2}$: $V_{DS2}\ge V_{GS2}-V_{THN}$ :

$$V_{out}\ge V_{b1}-V_{THN}$$

$M_{1}$: $V_{SD1}\ge V_{SG1}-|V_{THP}|$ :

$$V_{DD}-V_{out}\ge V_{DD}-V_{b2}-|V_{THP}|$$

$$V_{out}\le V_{b2}+|V_{THP}|$$

The DC output level is high impedance and very
sensitive to $I_{D1}-I_{D2}$ mismatch.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 19.

answer.text:
This is a common-source stage whose driver is
the series composite of $M_{1},M_{2}$.

Put $V_{X}$ for $D_{1}=S_{2}$.

$$V_{GS1}=V_{in},\;V_{DS1}=V_{X}$$
$$V_{GS2}=V_{in}-V_{X},\;V_{DS2}=V_{out}-V_{X}$$

$M_{1}$ has $V_{BS1}=0$. $M_{2}$ has $V_{BS2}=-V_{X}$.
Neglect body effect and $\lambda$ first.
$V_{TH1}=V_{TH2}=V_{TH}$,
$\beta_{i}= \mu_{n}C_{ox}W_{i}/L_{i}$.

Same $I_{D}$ must flow in $M_{1},M_{2}$.

Both cannot be saturated. Indeed saturation
currents would be

$$I_{D1}=\frac12\beta_{1}(V_{in}-V_{TH})^{2}$$
$$I_{D2}=\frac12\beta_{2}(V_{in}-V_{X}-V_{TH})^{2}$$

$I_{D1}=I_{D2}$ gives with $V_{OV1}=V_{in}-V_{TH}$,

$$\sqrt{\frac{\beta_{1}}{\beta_{2}}}V_{OV1}=V_{OV1}-V_{X}$$

$$V_{X}=V_{OV1}\left[1-\sqrt{\beta_{1}/\beta_{2}}\right]$$

$M_{1}$ saturation needs $V_{X}\ge V_{OV1}$,
impossible. In fact for equal sizes the
saturation current of $M_{2}$,
with $V_{GS2}=V_{in}-V_{X}<V_{GS1}$,
is $<I_{D1sat}$. $M_{2}$ limits the current.

Plausible active mode is:

* $M_{1}$ triode,
* $M_{2}$ saturation,

provided $V_{out}$ is high enough.

Then

$$I_{D}= \beta_{1}\left[V_{OV1}V_{X}-\frac{V_{X}^{2}}2\right] \tag{1}$$
triode $M_{1}$

$$I_{D}= \frac12\beta_{2}(V_{OV1}-V_{X})^{2} \tag{2}$$
saturation $M_{2}$.

Put $x=V_{X}/V_{OV1}$. Equating:

$$\beta_{1}\left[x-\frac{x^{2}}2\right]=\frac12\beta_{2}(1-x)^{2}$$

$$(\beta_{1}+\beta_{2})x^{2}-2(\beta_{1}+\beta_{2})x+\beta_{2}=0$$

$$x^{2}-2x+\frac{\beta_{2}}{\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}}=0$$

$x<1$:

$$x = 1-\sqrt{\frac{\beta_{1}}{\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}}} \tag{3}$$

$$V_{X}=V_{OV1}\left[1-\sqrt{\frac{\beta_{1}}{\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}}}\right]$$

$0<V_{X}<V_{OV1}$, so $M_{1}$ is indeed triode.
Insert in (2):

$$I_{D}=\frac12\beta_{2}V_{OV1}^{2}\frac{\beta_{1}}{\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}}$$

$$I_{D}=\frac12\frac{\beta_{1}\beta_{2}}{\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}}(V_{in}-V_{TH})^{2} \tag{4}$$

i.e. square-law with

$$\frac1{\beta_{eq}}=\frac1{\beta_{1}}+\frac1{\beta_{2}}$$

$$\beta_{eq}=\mu_{n}C_{ox}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_{eq}$$

$$\frac{L_{eq}}{W_{eq}}=\frac{L_{1}}{W_{1}}+\frac{L_{2}}{W_{2}}$$

In particular if $W_{1}=W_{2}=W$,

$$L_{eq}=L_{1}+L_{2}$$

The series stack behaves DC-wise as a single
long-channel transistor of summed length.
For identical devices $\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}=\beta$:

$$x=1-1/\sqrt2\approx 0.29$$
$$V_{X}\approx 0.29\,V_{OV1}$$
$$I_{D}=\frac14\beta V_{OV1}^{2}=\frac12\frac{\beta}2V_{OV1}^{2}$$

$M_{2}$ saturation condition:

$$V_{DS2}\ge V_{GS2}-V_{TH}$$
$$V_{out}-V_{X}\ge V_{in}-V_{X}-V_{TH}$$

$$V_{out}\ge V_{in}-V_{TH} \tag{5}$$

exactly as for a single device. So:

* $V_{in}<V_{TH}$: both off, $V_{out}=V_{DD}$.
* Moderate $V_{in}$: $M_{1}$ triode, $M_{2}$ sat,
  $V_{out}=V_{DD}-I_{D}R_{D}$ with $I_{D}$ in (4).
  This is the active inverting amplifier region.
* Large $V_{in}$ such that (5) fails: $M_{2}$
  enters triode too, $V_{out}$ low.

Transfer characteristic is identical to a normal CS
stage with $(W/L)_{eq}$.

Small signal. $M_{1}$ in triode:

$$g_{m1}=\beta_{1}V_{X},\quad g_{ds1}=\beta_{1}(V_{OV1}-V_{X})$$

$M_{2}$ in saturation:

$$g_{m2}=\beta_{2}(V_{OV1}-V_{X}),\quad g_{ds2}=1/r_{o2},\quad g_{mb2}$$

Let $v_{x}$ be the intermediate node.
KCL $i_{d1}=i_{d2}$ :

$$g_{m1}v_{in}+g_{ds1}v_{x}=g_{m2}(v_{in}-v_{x})-g_{mb2}v_{x}+g_{ds2}(v_{out}-v_{x})$$

KCL at output:

$$\frac{v_{out}}{R_{D}}+g_{m2}(v_{in}-v_{x})-g_{mb2}v_{x}+g_{ds2}(v_{out}-v_{x})=0$$

Solving, with $G_{x}=g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2}+g_{ds1}$,

$$A_{v}=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=-R_{D}\frac{g_{m1}(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2})+g_{m2}g_{ds1}}{G_{x}+R_{D}g_{ds1}g_{ds2}}$$

i.e.

$$A_{v}=-G_{m}(R_{D}\parallel R_{o})$$

$$G_{m}=\frac{g_{m1}(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2})+g_{m2}g_{ds1}}{G_{x}}$$

$$R_{o}=\frac{G_{x}}{g_{ds1}g_{ds2}}$$

$R_{o}$ is the impedance looking into $M_{2}$
drain with $v_{in}=0$. Indeed impedance at
$X$ is $1/g_{ds1}$ and cascode formula gives
$R_{o}=r_{o2}+[1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}]/g_{ds1}$.

Neglecting $g_{ds2},g_{mb2}$, using triode/sat
expressions above,

$$G_{m}= \frac{\beta_{1}\beta_{2}}{\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}}V_{OV1}=\beta_{eq}V_{OV1}=g_{m,eq}$$

$$R_{o}\approx \frac{g_{m2}+g_{ds1}}{g_{ds1}g_{ds2}}=\frac{1+k_{2}/k_{1}}{\lambda_{2}I_{D}}$$

For $k_{1}=k_{2}$, $R_{o}\approx 2r_{o2}$.
This is $r_{o,eq}=1/\lambda_{eq}I_{D}$ with
$\lambda_{eq}=\lambda/2$ for $L_{eq}=2L$.
Hence to first order:

$$A_{v}\approx -g_{m,eq}(R_{D}\parallel r_{o,eq})$$

Composite is a long device: smaller $g_{m}$,
larger $r_{o}$, larger intrinsic $g_{m}r_{o}$,
same saturation boundary $V_{out}\ge V_{OV}$.

Body effect of $M_{2}$, $V_{TH2}(V_{X})>V_{TH0}$,
slightly lowers current and $G_{m}$. It is
second order because $V_{X}$ is a fraction of
$V_{OV}$. With isolated body tied to source
it disappears and equivalence is exact apart from $\lambda$.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 19.

answer.text:
Two NMOS in series with a common gate form
to first order one long NMOS.

Let $X$ be $D_{1}=S_{2}$, $k=\mu_{n}C_{ox}W/L$,
$V_{ov}=V_{in}-V_{TH}$. $M_{1}$ has $V_{SB1}=0$.
$M_{2}$ has $V_{SB2}=V_{X}$. Neglect for the
moment $\lambda ,\gamma$.

$V_{GS1}=V_{in}$, $V_{DS1}=V_{X}$,
$V_{GS2}=V_{in}-V_{X}$, $V_{DS2}=V_{out}-V_{X}$.

For $V_{in}<V_{TH}$, $I_{D}=0$, $V_{out}=V_{DD}$.

Assume $I_{D}>0$. $M_{1}$ cannot be saturated.
Indeed saturation of $M_{1}$ requires

$$V_{X}\ge V_{in}-V_{TH1}$$

Then $V_{GS2}=V_{in}-V_{X}\le V_{TH1}$.
With body effect $V_{TH2}\ge V_{TH1}$, $M_{2}$
would be off. Hence for $I_{D}>0$:

* $M_{1}$ is in triode,
* $M_{2}$ can be saturated.

$M_{2}$ saturated requires

$$V_{DS2}\ge V_{GS2}-V_{TH}$$
$$V_{out}-V_{X}\ge V_{in}-V_{X}-V_{TH}$$

i.e.

$$V_{out}\ge V_{in}-V_{TH}=V_{ov} $$

same as a single common-source. This is the
normal amplifying region.

Currents, $\lambda=0$:

$$\begin{aligned}
I_{D1} &=k_{1}\left[V_{ov}V_{X}-\frac{V_{X}^{2}}{2}\right] \\
I_{D2} &=\frac{k_{2}}{2}\left(V_{ov}-V_{X}\right)^{2}
\end{aligned}$$

triode for $M_{1}$, saturation for $M_{2}$.
$I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_{D}$ gives

$$k_{1}\left[V_{ov}^{2}-(V_{ov}-V_{X})^{2}\right]
 =k_{2}(V_{ov}-V_{X})^{2}$$

$$ (V_{ov}-V_{X})^{2}=V_{ov}^{2}\frac{k_{1}}{k_{1}+k_{2}} $$

$$I_{D}=\frac{k_{2}}{2}(V_{ov}-V_{X})^{2}
 =\frac12\frac{k_{1}k_{2}}{k_{1}+k_{2}}V_{ov}^{2}$$

Hence

$$I_{D}=\frac12 k_{eq}V_{ov}^{2}$$

with

$$\frac1{k_{eq}}=\frac1{k_{1}}+\frac1{k_{2}}$$

i.e.

$$k_{eq}=\frac{\mu_{n}C_{ox}}{L_{1}/W_{1}+L_{2}/W_{2}}$$

In particular if $W_{1}=W_{2}=W$,

$$k_{eq}= \mu_{n}C_{ox}\frac{W}{L_{1}+L_{2}}$$

This is one NMOS of $W_{eq}=W$, $L_{eq}=L_{1}+L_{2}$.
That is the series = long channel equivalence.

The intermediate voltage:

$$V_{X}=V_{ov}\left[1-\sqrt{\frac{k_{1}}{k_{1}+k_{2}}}\right]$$

E.g. $k_{1}=k_{2}$, $V_{X}\approx 0.29\,V_{ov}$,
$V_{GS2}-V_{TH}\approx 0.71\,V_{ov}$.

Large signal transfer in saturation of $M_{2}$:

$$V_{out}=V_{DD}-R_{D}I_{D}$$
$$=V_{DD}-\frac{R_{D}k_{eq}}{2}(V_{in}-V_{TH})^{2}$$

until $V_{out}=V_{in}-V_{TH}$ where $M_{2}$
enters triode.

Small signal. $M_{1}$ is triode:

$$i_{d1}=g_{m1}v_{gs1}+g_{ds1}v_{ds1}$$

$$g_{m1}=k_{1}V_{X},\quad g_{ds1}=k_{1}(V_{ov}-V_{X})$$

$M_{2}$ is saturated with body:

$$i_{d2}=g_{m2}v_{gs2}+g_{mb2}v_{bs2}+g_{ds2}v_{ds2}$$

Let $v_{x}$ be small signal at $X$, $v_{gs1}=v_{in}$,
$v_{ds1}=v_{x}$, $v_{gs2}=v_{in}-v_{x}$,
$v_{bs2}=-v_{x}$, $v_{ds2}=v_{out}-v_{x}$.

$$i_{d1}=g_{m1}v_{in}+g_{ds1}v_{x}$$
$$i_{d2}=g_{m2}v_{in}-(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2})v_{x}
 +g_{ds2}v_{out}$$

KCL at $X$: $i_{d1}=i_{d2}$.
KCL at output, no load: $i_{d2}=-v_{out}/R_{D}$.

Solving,

$$A_{v}=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}
 =-\,R_{D}\frac{g_{m2}g_{ds1}+g_{m1}(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2})}
 {R_{D}g_{ds1}g_{ds2}+g_{ds1}+g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2}}$$

This is $-G_{m}(R_{D}\parallel R_{out})$ with

$$R_{out}=\frac{g_{ds1}+g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2}}
 {g_{ds1}g_{ds2}}$$

$$=\frac1{g_{ds2}}+\frac{1+g_{m2}r_{o2}+g_{mb2}r_{o2}}{g_{ds1}}$$

looking into $M_{2}$ drain with $1/g_{ds1}$ in
source, and

$$G_{m}=\frac{g_{m2}g_{ds1}+g_{m1}(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2})}
 {g_{ds1}+g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2}}$$

For $g_{ds2}=0$, $g_{mb2}=0$,

$$A_{v}=-R_{D}\,g_{m2}\frac{g_{ds1}+g_{m1}}{g_{ds1}+g_{m2}}$$

But $g_{ds1}+g_{m1}=k_{1}V_{ov}$,
$g_{ds1}+g_{m2}=(k_{1}+k_{2})(V_{ov}-V_{X})$,
so

$$G_{m,0}=k_{eq}V_{ov}=\sqrt{2k_{eq}I_{D}}$$

the $g_{m}$ of the equivalent long device.
Then $A_{v}\approx -G_{m,0}R_{D}$.

Including $\lambda$: $g_{ds2}=1/r_{o2}$,
$g_{ds1}\approx k_{1}(V_{ov}-V_{X})\gg g_{ds2}$,
$$R_{out}\approx r_{o2}\left(1+\frac{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}{g_{ds1}}\right)$$
For identical devices, $g_{m2}/g_{ds1}=1$,
$R_{out}\approx 2r_{o2}$, i.e. $r_{o}$ of a
device twice as long. Intrinsic gain
$G_{m}R_{out}$ is essentially that of the
$L_{1}+L_{2}$ device.

Body effect of $M_{2}$ makes $V_{TH2}>V_{TH1}$,
lowers current slightly, lowers $G_{m}$ and
raises $R_{out}$. To first order the circuit
is a common-source stage with lower $g_{m}$,
higher $r_{o}$, about the same $-g_{m}(R_{D}\parallel r_{o})$
as a single $W/(L_{1}+L_{2})$ device, at the
cost of larger $V_{in}$ for the same $I_{D}$
and an extra pole at node $X$.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 19.

answer.text:
This is a common source stage with resistive load
whose pull down is two NMOS in series with common
gate.

Let the top of $M_{1}$ = bottom of $M_{2}=X$,
$V_{X}$ its DC voltage.

$$V_{S1}=0,\; V_{D1}=V_{X},\; V_{G1}=V_{in}$$
$$V_{S2}=V_{X},\; V_{D2}=V_{out},\; V_{G2}=V_{in}$$

The symbols show the body tied to the source for
both devices, so no back bias. Put $V_{th1}=V_{th2}=V_{th}$.
Long channel square law, $\lambda=0$ first.

$$V_{GS1}=V_{in},\; V_{DS1}=V_{X}$$
$$V_{GS2}=V_{in}-V_{X},\; V_{DS2}=V_{out}-V_{X}$$

$M_{1}$ in saturation requires
$$V_{X} \ge V_{in}-V_{th}$$
$M_{2}$ in saturation requires
$$V_{out}-V_{X} \ge V_{in}-V_{X}-V_{th}$$
i.e.
$$V_{out}\ge V_{in}-V_{th}$$

Both carry the same DC current.

$M_{1}$ has the larger $V_{GS}$. To carry the
same current as $M_{2}$ with similar size it needs
smaller $V_{DS}$. Hence in normal operation:

* $M_{1}$ triode
* $M_{2}$ saturation

Put $k_{1}=\mu_{n}C_{ox}(W/L)_{1}$,
$k_{2}=\mu_{n}C_{ox}(W/L)_{2}$,
$V_{od}=V_{in}-V_{th}$.

$$I_{D1}=k_{1}\left[V_{od}V_{X}-\frac{V_{X}^{2}}{2}\right]$$
triode
$$I_{D2}=\frac{k_{2}}{2}(V_{od}-V_{X})^{2}$$
saturation.

$I_{D1}=I_{D2}$ gives:

$$k_{1}V_{od}V_{X}-\frac{k_{1}}{2}V_{X}^{2}
 =\frac{k_{2}}{2}(V_{od}-V_{X})^{2}$$

$$(k_{1}+k_{2})V_{X}^{2}-2(k_{1}+k_{2})V_{od}V_{X}
 +k_{2}V_{od}^{2}=0$$

$$V_{X}^{2}-2V_{od}V_{X}+\frac{k_{2}}{k_{1}+k_{2}}V_{od}^{2}=0$$

Physical root $V_{X}<V_{od}$:

$$V_{X}=V_{od}\left[1-\sqrt{\frac{k_{1}}{k_{1}+k_{2}}}\right]$$

$$V_{od2}=V_{GS2}-V_{th}=V_{od}-V_{X}=V_{od}\sqrt{\frac{k_{1}}{k_{1}+k_{2}}}$$

Then

$$I_{D}=\frac{k_{2}}{2}V_{od2}^{2}
 =\frac12\frac{k_{1}k_{2}}{k_{1}+k_{2}}V_{od}^{2}$$

i.e. a single saturated NMOS with

$$k_{eff}=\frac{k_{1}k_{2}}{k_{1}+k_{2}}$$

$$\frac{1}{(W/L)_{eff}}=\frac{1}{(W/L)_{1}}+\frac{1}{(W/L)_{2}}$$

If $W_{1}=W_{2}=W$,
$$L_{eff}=L_{1}+L_{2}$$

Indeed splitting a long channel device into two
in series with common gate does not change the DC
channel physics. $V_{X}$ is the channel potential
at the split.

For identical devices $(W/L)_{1}=(W/L)_{2}=(W/L)$:

$$V_{X} = \left(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)V_{od}\approx 0.29V_{od}$$

$$V_{od2}=V_{od}/\sqrt2$$

$$(W/L)_{eff}=(W/L)/2$$

$$I_{D}=\frac14\mu_{n}C_{ox}\frac{W}{L}(V_{in}-V_{th})^{2}$$

Check region: $V_{X}<V_{od}$ so $M_{1}$ triode indeed.
$M_{2}$ saturated if $V_{out}\ge V_{od}=V_{in}-V_{th}$,
exactly like a single device with $V_{GS}=V_{in}$.

Hence seen from the drain, the composite saturates at

$$V_{out}\ge V_{in}-V_{th}$$

and in saturation behaves as one long transistor.
The same is true in deep triode: for small $V_{out}$,
both in triode act as series resistors $1/k_{1}V_{od}+
1/k_{2}V_{od}=1/k_{eff}V_{od}$.

DC transfer with $R_{D}$:

off for $V_{in}<V_{th}$: $V_{out}=V_{DD}$.

on, saturated:

$$V_{out}=V_{DD}-R_{D}\frac12 k_{eff}(V_{in}-V_{th})^{2}$$

until $V_{out}=V_{in}-V_{th}$.

Small signal. $M_{1}$ triode:

$$g_{m1}=k_{1}V_{X}, \quad g_{ds1}=k_{1}(V_{od}-V_{X})=k_{1}V_{od2}$$

Note
$$g_{m1}+g_{ds1}=k_{1}V_{od}$$

$M_{2}$ saturation:

$$g_{m2}=k_{2}V_{od2},\quad g_{ds2}=1/r_{o2}=\lambda_{2}I_{D}$$

Let $v_{x}$ be the small signal at $X$.
$v_{gs1}=v_{in}$, $v_{ds1}=v_{x}$,
$v_{gs2}=v_{in}-v_{x}$, $v_{ds2}=v_{out}-v_{x}$.

$i_{d1}=i_{d2}$:

$$g_{m1}v_{in}+g_{ds1}v_{x}=g_{m2}(v_{in}-v_{x})+g_{ds2}(v_{out}-v_{x})$$

$$v_{x}=\frac{(g_{m2}-g_{m1})v_{in}+g_{ds2}v_{out}}{g_{ds1}+g_{m2}+g_{ds2}}$$

At output, $v_{out}/R_{D}+i_{d2}=0$:

$$g_{m2}(v_{in}-v_{x})+g_{ds2}(v_{out}-v_{x})+v_{out}/R_{D}=0$$

Solving,

$$A_{v}=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=-\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}+g_{m1}g_{ds2}+g_{m2}g_{ds1}}{g_{ds1}g_{ds2}+(g_{ds1}+g_{m2}+g_{ds2})/R_{D}}$$

With $g_{m}\gg g_{ds}$,

$$A_{v}\approx -R_{D}\frac{g_{m2}(g_{m1}+g_{ds1})}{g_{ds1}+g_{m2}+g_{ds2}}$$

But $g_{m1}+g_{ds1}=k_{1}V_{od}$ and
$g_{ds1}+g_{m2}=(k_{1}+k_{2})V_{od2}$,
so numerator/denominator is

$$\frac{k_{2}V_{od2}k_{1}V_{od}}{(k_{1}+k_{2})V_{od2}}
 =\frac{k_{1}k_{2}}{k_{1}+k_{2}}V_{od}=g_{m,eff}$$

where

$$g_{m,eff}=\frac{\partial I_{D}}{\partial V_{in}}
 =\mu_{n}C_{ox}(W/L)_{eff}(V_{in}-V_{th})$$

Hence

$$A_{v} = -g_{m,eff}\,(R_{D}\parallel R_{o,comp})$$

The output resistance looking into $M_{2}$ with
$v_{in}=0$ is from test source:

$$R_{o,comp}=\frac{g_{ds1}+g_{m2}+g_{ds2}}{g_{ds1}g_{ds2}}
 \approx \frac{1}{g_{ds2}}\left(1+\frac{g_{m2}}{g_{ds1}}\right)$$

Since $g_{m2}/g_{ds1}=k_{2}/k_{1}$,

$$R_{o,comp}\approx r_{o2}\frac{k_{1}+k_{2}}{k_{1}}$$

For identical devices $R_{o,comp}\approx 2r_{o2}$.
$M_{1}$ in triode presents low $\approx 1/g_{ds1}$
degeneration, so there is little cascode boosting.

In terms of effective $\lambda$,
$g_{ds,eff}=1/R_{o,comp}\approx \lambda_{2}I_{D}k_{1}/(k_{1}+k_{2})$,
so

$$\lambda_{eff}=\lambda_{2}\frac{k_{1}}{k_{1}+k_{2}}$$

If $\lambda\propto 1/L$, $\lambda_{eff}\propto 1/(L_{1}+L_{2})$,
as for a true long device. Intrinsic gain
$g_{m,eff}R_{o,comp}$ equals that of a $L_{1}+L_{2}$
device, $\sqrt{2}\times$ that of a single $L$ device
at same current for the identical case.

If $\lambda=0$, $R_{o,comp}\to\infty$,

$$A_{v}=-g_{m,eff}R_{D}$$

half the $g_{m}$ of a single device at same $V_{od}$
for the identical case, because current is halved.
It is an inverting CS stage with infinite input $Z$,
output $Z=R_{D}\parallel R_{o,comp}$.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit of Figure 20.

answer.text:
This is a NMOS differential pair with single
ended input and single ended output. $M_{1}$ gate
is the input, $M_{2}$ gate is ac ground,
tails common to $I_{1}$, $M_{1}$ drain to
ac ground, $M_{2}$ drain to $R_{D}$.

Put $v_{b}=0$ ac, $v_{d1}=0$ ac.
Let the common source node be $v_{x}$.
Let $R_{T}$ be the ac impedance of $I_{1}$
to ground, $\infty$ for ideal.

In dc, with $V_{IN,CM}=V_{b}$ and $M_{1},M_{2}$
matched,

$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_{1}/2$$

$$V_{S}=V_{IN,CM}-V_{GS1}$$
$$V_{OUT}=V_{DD}-I_{D2}R_{D}$$

$M_{2}$ stays in saturation if
$V_{OUT}\ge V_{b}-V_{TH}$.

For small signal put $g_{m1},g_{mb1},g_{ds1}$,
$g_{m2},g_{mb2},g_{ds2}$, $r_{o}=1/g_{ds}$,
$$G_{1}=g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1}$$
$$G_{2}=g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2}$$

with bodies ac ground.
Think of $M_{1}$ as a source follower loaded
by the impedance looking into the source
of the $M_{2}$ common-gate device, and $M_{2}$
as a common-gate stage.

Impedance looking into source of CG with
drain load $R_{D}$:

$$R_{in2}=\frac{R_{D}+r_{o2}}{1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}}
 =\frac{1+g_{ds2}R_{D}}{G_{2}}$$

$\approx 1/(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})$.

$M_{1}$ is a source follower loaded with

$$R_{L}=R_{T}\parallel R_{in2}$$

Its gain to the $v_{x}$ node is

$$i_{d1}=g_{m1}V_{in}-G_{1}v_{x}=v_{x}/R_{L}$$

i.e.

$$A_{1}=\frac{v_{x}}{V_{in}}=\frac{g_{m1}}{G_{1}+1/R_{L}}
 =\frac{g_{m1}R_{L}}{1+G_{1}R_{L}} $$

The gain from the $v_{x}$ node to the drain
of the CG, $M_{2}$, is, with
$i_{d2}=-V_{out}/R_{D}$,

$$i_{d2}=-G_{2}v_{x}+g_{ds2}V_{out}=-V_{out}/R_{D}$$

i.e.

$$A_{2}'=\frac{V_{out}}{v_{x}}=
 \frac{G_{2}}{g_{ds2}+1/R_{D}}=
 \frac{G_{2}R_{D}}{1+g_{ds2}R_{D}}$$

$\approx (g_{m2}+g_{mb2})R_{D}$.
The overall gain is $A_{1}A_{2}'$:

$$A_{v}=\frac{g_{m1}}{G_{1}+1/R_{T}+1/R_{in2}}
 \frac{G_{2}}{g_{ds2}+1/R_{D}}$$

$$A_{v}=\frac{g_{m1}G_{2}}
 {(g_{ds2}+1/R_{D})(G_{1}+1/R_{T})+G_{2}/R_{D}}$$

$$A_{v}= \frac{g_{m1}G_{2}R_{D}}
 {G_{2}+(G_{1}+1/R_{T})(1+g_{ds2}R_{D})} $$

For $R_{T}\to\infty$:

$$A_{v}= \frac{g_{m1}R_{D}G_{2}}
 {G_{2}+G_{1}(1+g_{ds2}R_{D})} $$

This is non-inverting. $V_{in}$ up $\to$
$M_{1}$ takes more of $I_{1}$ $\to$ $M_{2}$
takes less $\to$ less drop in $R_{D}$ $\to$
$V_{out}$ up.

If $r_{o}\to\infty$,

$$A_{v}\approx \frac{g_{m1}(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})R_{D}}
 {g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+1/R_{T}}$$

If matched and $R_{T}\to\infty$:

$$A_{v}= \frac{g_{m}R_{D}}{2+g_{ds}R_{D}}
 =g_{m}\left(r_{o}\parallel \frac{R_{D}}{2}\right)$$

In particular to first order, ignoring $r_{o}$:

$$A_{v}\approx +\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}R_{D}$$

matched:

$$A_{v}\approx +g_{m}R_{D}/2 $$

This is the familiar differential pair
single-ended gain. $M_{1}$ follower gain
$\approx 1/2$, CG gain $\approx g_{m}R_{D}$.

Remarkably, for matched devices and ideal
tail, $g_{mb}$ cancels. Body effect does
not affect first-order gain.

Output resistance: look into $M_{2}$ drain
with $V_{in}=0$. Impedance looking back
from $M_{2}$ source is the $M_{1}$ source
impedance in parallel with $R_{T}$:

$$R_{S}= \frac{1}{G_{1}}\parallel R_{T}
 =\frac{1}{G_{1}+1/R_{T}}$$

Impedance looking into CG drain with
source degeneration $R_{S}$ is

$$R_{o,CG}=r_{o2}+[1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}]R_{S}
 =r_{o2}\left[1+\frac{G_{2}}{G_{1}+1/R_{T}}\right]$$

Total:

$$R_{out}=R_{D}\parallel R_{o,CG}$$

$$1/R_{out}=1/R_{D}+
 g_{ds2}\frac{G_{1}+1/R_{T}}{G_{1}+G_{2}+1/R_{T}}$$

For $R_{T}\to\infty$, matched:

$$R_{out}=R_{D}\parallel 2r_{o}\approx R_{D}$$

Input resistance at low frequency is the
MOS gate impedance:

$$R_{in}=\infty$$

So approximately a non-inverting amplifier
of gain $g_{m}R_{D}/2$, infinite input
impedance, output impedance $R_{D}$.

answer.text:
This is a single ended differential pair.
$M_{1}$ is a source-follower loaded by the input impedance
of the $M_{2}$ common-gate device. $M_{2}$ gate is ac ground.

Put $V_{in,DC}=V_{b}$ for balance, $M_{1},M_{2}$ matched.
Then in saturation

$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_{1}/2$$

$$V_{X}=V_{in,DC}-V_{GS}=V_{b}-V_{GS}$$

$$V_{out,DC}=V_{DD}-\frac{I_{1}}{2}R_{D}$$

$M_{2}$ stays in saturation if

$$V_{DS2}\ge V_{GS2}-V_{TH}$$
i.e. $V_{out}\ge V_{b}-V_{TH}$.

For small signal put $g_{m1},g_{mb1},g_{ds1}=1/r_{o1}$
for $M_{1}$, $g_{m2},g_{mb2},g_{ds2}=1/r_{o2}$ for $M_{2}$.
Let tail impedance be $R_{SS}$. Ideal $R_{SS}=\infty$.
Let $v_{x}$ be ac voltage of the common source node.

$$v_{gs1}=v_{in}-v_{x},\; v_{bs1}=-v_{x},\; v_{ds1}=-v_{x}$$
$$v_{gs2}=-v_{x},\; v_{bs2}=-v_{x},\; v_{ds2}=v_{out}-v_{x}$$

$$i_{d1}=g_{m1}v_{gs1}+g_{mb1}v_{bs1}+g_{ds1}v_{ds1}$$
$$=g_{m1}v_{in}-(g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1})v_{x}$$

$$i_{d2}=g_{m2}v_{gs2}+g_{mb2}v_{bs2}+g_{ds2}v_{ds2}$$
$$=g_{ds2}v_{out}-(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2})v_{x}$$

$i_{d1},i_{d2}$ flow from the drains to the sources,
i.e. into node $X$ from the transistors.

KCL $X$:

$$i_{d1}+i_{d2}=v_{x}/R_{SS} \tag{1}$$

i.e.

$$g_{m1}v_{in}+g_{ds2}v_{out}=v_{x}\left[\frac1{R_{SS}}+G_{m1}+G_{m2}\right]$$

where

$$G_{m1}=g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1}$$
$$G_{m2}=g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2}$$

KCL $V_{out}$:

$$v_{out}/R_{D}+i_{d2}=0 \tag{2}$$

i.e.

$$v_{out}\left(\frac1{R_{D}}+g_{ds2}\right)=G_{m2}v_{x}$$

Hence

$$ \frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=
\frac{g_{m1}G_{m2}}{\frac1{R_D}\left[\frac1{R_{SS}}+G_{m1}+G_{m2}\right]
+g_{ds2}\left[\frac1{R_{SS}}+G_{m1}\right]} \tag{3}$$

This is exact.

In particular $R_{SS}\to\infty$:

$$A_v =\frac{g_{m1}G_{m2}}{\frac1{R_D}(G_{m1}+G_{m2})+g_{ds2}G_{m1}}$$

Neglect $g_{ds}$ against $g_m$ and $1/R_D$:

$$A_v\approx g_{m1}\frac{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}R_D$$

Matched devices:

$$A_v\approx \frac{g_m R_D}{2}$$

Body effect cancels to first order. It is non-inverting.

This can be seen intuitively with $\lambda=\gamma=0$.
Then (1) is $g_{m1}(v_{in}-v_x)-g_{m2}v_x=0$, i.e.

$$\frac{v_x}{v_{in}}=\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}$$

and (2) is $v_{out}=-R_D i_{d2}=g_{m2}R_D v_x$, i.e.

$$\frac{v_{out}}{v_x}=g_{m2}R_D$$

so

$$A_v=\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}R_D$$

Indeed look into source of CG $M_2$:

$$R_{in2}=\frac{R_D+r_{o2}}{1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}}\approx\frac1{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}$$

$M_1$ is a source follower loaded by $R_{SS}\parallel R_{in2}$:

$$\frac{v_x}{v_{in}}=\frac{g_{m1}(r_{o1}\parallel R_{SS}\parallel R_{in2})}
{1+g_{m1}(r_{o1}\parallel R_{SS}\parallel R_{in2})}\approx\frac12$$

for $R_{SS}$ large, matched $g_m$ and $R_{in2}\approx1/g_m$.
This $1/2$ times the CG gain $\approx (g_{m2}+g_{mb2})R_D$
gives $\approx g_mR_D/2$.

In words: with ideal tail, ac $i_{s1}+i_{s2}=0$.
$M_1$ V-to-I current is steered into $M_2$ and then
into $R_D$.

Terminal impedances at low frequency:

$R_{in}=\infty$ into $M_1$ gate.

For $R_{out}$, set $v_{in}=0$. Looking into $M_1$ source
with gate and drain grounded:

$$Z_1=\frac1{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1}}$$

This in parallel with $R_{SS}$ is the source degeneration
for $M_2$:

$$R_{S2}=R_{SS}\parallel Z_1$$

Looking into $M_2$ drain with gate grounded:

$$R_{d2}=r_{o2}+[1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}]R_{S2}$$

$$R_{out}=R_D\parallel R_{d2}$$

With $R_{SS}=\infty$, no body, $r_o$ large,
$R_{S2}\approx1/g_{m1}$, $R_{d2}\approx r_{o2}+(1+g_{m2}r_{o2})/g_{m1}$.
If matched, $\approx 2r_{o2}$. Normally

$$R_{out}\approx R_D.$$

answers.question: Analyze the circuit of Figure 20.

answer.text:
The circuit is a single ended differential pair.
$M_{1}$ is a common drain, $M_{2}$ is a common gate.
The common source is biased by $I_{1}$.
$V_{b}$ is a.c. ground.

Put the bodies to the sources, so $g_{mb}=0$.
Let $R_{1}$ be the a.c. impedance of $I_{1}$,
$G_{1}=1/R_{1}$, $G_{D}=1/R_{D}$.

In d.c. with matched devices and $V_{IN,DC}\approx
V_{b}$,

$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_{1}/2$$

$$V_{out,DC}=V_{DD}-I_{D2}R_{D}$$

$M_{2}$ stays in saturation if

$$V_{D2}\ge V_{b}-V_{TH}$$

i.e. $V_{DD}-I_{D2}R_{D}\ge V_{b}-V_{TH}$.

For small signal let $v_{x}$ be the common
source node. $v_{g1}=v_{in}$, $v_{d1}=0$,
$v_{g2}=0$, $v_{d2}=v_{out}$.

$$v_{gs1}=v_{in}-v_{x},\;v_{ds1}=-v_{x}$$
$$v_{gs2}=-v_{x},\;v_{ds2}=v_{out}-v_{x}$$

$$i_{d1}=g_{m1}v_{gs1}+g_{ds1}v_{ds1}$$
$$=g_{m1}(v_{in}-v_{x})-g_{ds1}v_{x}$$

$$i_{d2}=g_{m2}v_{gs2}+g_{ds2}v_{ds2}$$
$$=-g_{m2}v_{x}+g_{ds2}(v_{out}-v_{x})$$

KCL at $V_{out}$:

$$i_{d2}+\frac{v_{out}}{R_{D}}=0 \tag{1}$$

KCL at $v_{x}$, the sum of the source currents
flows in $R_{1}$:

$$i_{d1}+i_{d2}=\frac{v_{x}}{R_{1}} \tag{2}$$

From (1):

$$-g_{m2}v_{x}+g_{ds2}(v_{out}-v_{x})+G_{D}v_{out}=0$$

$$ \frac{v_{out}}{v_{x}} = \frac{g_{m2}+g_{ds2}}{g_{ds2}+G_{D}} $$

$$ = (g_{m2}+g_{ds2})(r_{o2}\parallel R_{D}) \tag{3}$$

This is the common-gate gain with zero source
resistance, from the source node to the drain.
It is $>0$.

Put (1) in (2): $i_{d2}=-v_{out}/R_{D}$,

$$g_{m1}(v_{in}-v_{x})-g_{ds1}v_{x}-\frac{v_{out}}{R_{D}}=\frac{v_{x}}{R_{1}}$$

$$g_{m1}v_{in}=v_{x}(g_{m1}+g_{ds1}+G_{1})+G_{D}v_{out} \tag{4}$$

With $A_{cg}=v_{out}/v_{x}$ from (3),

$$\frac{v_{x}}{v_{in}}=\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}+G_{1}+A_{cg}G_{D}}$$

Hence

$$A_{v}=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=A_{cg}\frac{v_{x}}{v_{in}}$$

$$ A_{v}= \frac{g_{m1}A_{cg}}{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}+G_{1}+A_{cg}G_{D}} $$

i.e.

$$ A_{v}= \frac{g_{m1}(g_{m2}+g_{ds2})}{(g_{m1}+g_{ds1}+G_{1})(g_{ds2}+G_{D})+G_{D}(g_{m2}+g_{ds2})} $$

This is source-follower $M_{1}$ driving
common-gate $M_{2}$.

Indeed, impedance looking into the source of
$M_{2}$ loaded by $R_{D}$ is

$$R_{in2}=\frac{1+g_{ds2}R_{D}}{g_{m2}+g_{ds2}}=\frac{r_{o2}+R_{D}}{1+g_{m2}r_{o2}}$$

$M_{1}$ sees $R_{1}\parallel R_{in2}$.
Its gain to $v_{x}$ is

$$A_{1}=\frac{v_{x}}{v_{in}}=\frac{g_{m1}R_{tot}}{1+g_{m1}R_{tot}}$$

$$R_{tot}=r_{o1}\parallel R_{1}\parallel R_{in2}$$

and $A_{v}=A_{1}A_{cg}$.

Ideal case: $r_{o1},r_{o2}\to\infty$, $R_{1}\to\infty$:

$$A_{cg}\approx g_{m2}R_{D}$$
$$A_{1}\approx \frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}$$

$$A_{v}\approx \frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}R_{D}$$

non-inverting. For matched $g_{m1}=g_{m2}=g_{m}$:

$$A_{v}\approx \frac{g_{m}R_{D}}{2}$$

$v_{x}\approx v_{in}/2$. Increase in $V_{in}$
steers current from $M_{2}$ to $M_{1}$, drop
in $R_{D}$ falls, $V_{out}$ rises.

With $r_{o}$ finite, $R_{1}=\infty$:

$$A_{v}= \frac{g_{m1}r_{o1}R_{D}(g_{m2}r_{o2}+1)}{(g_{m1}r_{o1}+1)(R_{D}+r_{o2})+r_{o1}(g_{m2}r_{o2}+1)}$$

For matched devices, $g_{m}r_{o}\gg 1$:

$$A_{v}\approx g_{m}r_{o}\frac{R_{D}}{R_{D}+2r_{o}}=\frac{g_{m}}{2}(R_{D}\parallel 2r_{o})$$

If $R_{D}\ll r_{o}$, $A_{v}\approx g_{m}R_{D}/2$.
Load asymmetry matters when $r_{o}$ is finite.

Input resistance at the gate is infinite at low
frequency.

Output resistance: look into $M_{2}$ drain
with $v_{in}=0$. $M_{2}$ source sees to ground

$$R_{S}=R_{1}\parallel \frac{1}{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}}$$

$\frac{1}{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}}$ is the impedance
looking into the source of $M_{1}$ with gate
grounded. Then for a common-gate with source
degeneration $R_{S}$:

$$R_{o,drain}=r_{o2}+(1+g_{m2}r_{o2})R_{S}$$

$$R_{out}=R_{D}\parallel R_{o,drain}$$

$$R_{out}=R_{D}\parallel\left[r_{o2}+(1+g_{m2}r_{o2})\left(R_{1}\parallel\frac{1}{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}}\right)\right]$$

With $R_{1}=\infty$, matched:

$$R_{out}=R_{D}\parallel 2r_{o}$$

so $A_{v}=G_{m}R_{out}$ with $G_{m}\approx g_{m}/2$.

answers.question: Explain why the output impedance of the circuit shown in Figure 21 can be inductive.

answer.text:
To find $Z_{out}$ put $V_{in}=0$ and drive
$V_{out}$ by $V_x$. Measure $I_x$.

At low frequency $M_{1}$ is a source follower with the
gate grounded through $R_{S}$:

$$ Z_{out0} \approx \frac{1}{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}}\parallel r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2} $$

resistive. Ignore $M_{2}$ which is $r_{o2}$ to ac ground
in parallel. The inductive part comes from $M_{1}$,
$R_{S}$ and its $C_{gs}$.

Neglect $r_{o}$, body, $C_{gd}$ etc. for the mechanism.

Gate KCL:

$$\frac{V_{g}}{R_{S}}+(V_{g}-V_{x})sC_{gs}=0$$

i.e.

$$ V_{g} = V_{x}\frac{sR_{S}C_{gs}}{1+sR_{S}C_{gs}} \tag{1}$$

$C_{gs}$ couples the output to the gate. $R_{S}$ to
ac ground makes it a differentiator / high pass.

Source KCL: current $I_{x}$ entering the $V_{x}$ node
goes into $C_{gs}$ and into the transistor.

Intrinsic NMOS: $I_{d}=g_{m}V_{gs}$ into drain,
i.e. out of source. Let $V_{gs}=V_{g}-V_{x}$.

Current leaving $V_{x}$ node for $C_{gs}$:
$(V_{x}-V_{g})sC_{gs}$. Current leaving $V_{x}$ node
for the transistor source: $-g_{m}V_{gs}$, since
$g_{m}V_{gs}$ enters the node from the transistor.

Hence, entering:

$$I_{x}-(V_{x}-V_{g})sC_{gs}+g_{m}(V_{g}-V_{x})=0$$

$$ I_{x} = (V_{x}-V_{g})sC_{gs}+g_{m}(V_{x}-V_{g}) \tag{2}$$

Insert (1):

$$ \frac{I_{x}}{V_{x}} = g_{m}+sC_{gs}
 -(sC_{gs}+g_{m})\frac{sR_{S}C_{gs}}{1+sR_{S}C_{gs}} $$

$$ Y = g_{m}+\frac{sC_{gs}(1-g_{m}R_{S})}{1+sR_{S}C_{gs}} \tag{3}$$

At $s\to 0$, $Y\to g_{m}$, $Z\to 1/g_{m}$.

Put $s=j\omega$:

$$ Y = g_{m} + \frac{j\omega C_{gs}(1-g_{m}R_{S})}
{1+j\omega R_{S}C_{gs}} $$

The second term has

$$\Im\{Y\} = \frac{\omega C_{gs}(1-g_{m}R_{S})}
{1+(\omega R_{S}C_{gs})^{2}} $$

If

$$g_{m}R_{S}>1$$

$\Im\{Y\}<0$. Negative susceptance is inductive.
Indeed for $|\omega R_{S}C_{gs}|\ll 1$,

$$Y\approx g_{m}-j\omega C_{gs}(g_{m}R_{S}-1)$$

$$Z=\frac{1}{Y}\approx \frac{1}{g_{m}}
+ j\omega \frac{R_{S}C_{gs}}{g_{m}} $$

i.e. $R\approx 1/g_{m}$ in series with

$$L\approx \frac{R_{S}C_{gs}}{g_{m}}$$

In parallel with $r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$ and the
output capacitances.

Physically, for $\omega \ll 1/R_{S}C_{gs}$,
from (1):

$$V_{g}\approx R_{S}C_{gs}\,sV_{x}$$

i.e. $V_{g}\approx R_{S}C_{gs}\,dV_{x}/dt$,
$90^{\circ}$ leading $V_{x}$.

Current drawn from $V_{x}$ into the source is
from (2) $\approx g_{m}(V_{x}-V_{g})$.
The $g_{m}V_{x}$ part is in phase: $1/g_{m}$.
The $-g_{m}V_{g}$ part is $-g_{m}R_{S}C_{gs}\,dV_{x}/dt$,
i.e. in quadrature lagging.

Current lags voltage: inductive.

In time domain: step $V_{x}=\Delta V$.
$C_{gs}$ cannot change voltage instantaneously,
$\Delta V_{g}=\Delta V$ initially, then $V_{g}$
decays to 0 with $R_{S}C_{gs}$. So $V_{gs}=0$
initially, $\to -\Delta V$ finally.

The extra transistor source current $g_{m}V_{gs}$
is 0 initially, $\to -g_{m}\Delta V$ finally.
KCL then requires $I_{x}\approx \Delta V/R_{S}$
initially to feed $R_{S}$ via $C_{gs}$, growing
to $\approx g_{m}\Delta V$ finally. If $g_{m}>1/R_{S}$,
current builds up after the voltage step, like
$V=L\,dI/dt$.

answers.question: Explain why the output impedance of the circuit shown in Figure 21 can be inductive.

answer.text:
This is a source follower. For $Z_{out}$ put
$V_{in}=0$.

At low frequency neglect caps. Looking into the source
with the gate grounded through $R_{S}$,

$$ Z_{out0} \approx \frac{1}{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}}
\parallel r_{o1} \parallel r_{o2} $$

resistive, $\approx 1/g_{m1}$.

At high frequency consider $C_{gs1}$.
Simplified small signal, neglecting $r_{o}$, body,
$C_{gd}$, $C_{db}$ and $M_{2}$ caps, apply $V_{x}$
at the source, measure $I_{x}$.

Gate node:

$$ \frac{V_{g}}{R_{S}} + (V_{g}-V_{x})sC_{gs}=0 $$

i.e.

$$ V_{g}=V_{x}\frac{sC_{gs}R_{S}}{1+sC_{gs}R_{S}} $$

Source node:

$$ I_{x} = (V_{x}-V_{g})(g_{m}+sC_{gs}) $$

Hence

$$ \frac{V_{x}}{I_{x}} = \frac{1+sC_{gs}R_{S}}{g_{m}+sC_{gs}} $$

$$ Z_{out} = \frac{1}{g_{m}}\frac{1+s/\omega_{z}}{1+s/\omega_{p}} $$

with

$$ \omega_{z} = \frac{1}{R_{S}C_{gs}},\quad \omega_{p}= \frac{g_{m}}{C_{gs}} $$

At $s\to 0$, $Z_{out}\to 1/g_{m}$. At $s\to\infty$,
$Z_{out}\to R_{S}$.

In particular at low $s$,

$$ Z_{out}\approx \frac{1}{g_{m}}\left[1+sC_{gs}(R_{S}-1/g_{m})\right] $$
$$ \approx \frac{1}{g_{m}}+sL_{eq} $$

where

$$ L_{eq}= \frac{C_{gs}}{g_{m}}\left(R_{S}-\frac{1}{g_{m}}\right) $$

That is a resistor in series with an inductor if
$R_{S}>1/g_{m}$. More generally if $\omega_{z}<\omega_{p}$,
$|Z_{out}|$ rises with frequency between zero and pole.
Rising $|Z|$ with positive phase is inductive.

Physically: $C_{gs}$ bootstraps the gate to the source.

- At low $f$, $C_{gs}$ is open, $V_{g}\approx 0$.
$V_{gs}\approx -V_{x}$, M1 supplies $g_{m}V_{x}$,
low impedance $1/g_{m}$.

- At high $f$, $C_{gs}$ shorts gate to source.
Fast change in $V_{x}$ cannot change $V_{Cgs}$
instantaneously, so $V_{g}$ follows $V_{x}$,
$V_{gs}\to 0$. The transistor then supplies
almost no small signal current. The test current
must go through $C_{gs}$ and $R_{S}$ to ground,
$Z_{out}\to R_{S}$.

In between, a rise in $V_{x}$ pushes current
through $C_{gs}$ into $R_{S}$, generating

$$ V_{g} \approx R_{S}C_{gs}\frac{dV_{x}}{dt} $$

in quadrature with $V_{x}$. This reduces $|V_{gs}|$
for a given $|V_{x}|$, i.e. reduces the transistor
current for a given output voltage. Impedance therefore
grows with frequency.

In other words the $V_{gs}$ needed to change the
transistor source current cannot be established
instantaneously because the gate follows the source
via the $R_{S}$-$C_{gs}$ low-pass. Voltage must lead
current, $V\approx IR+L\,dI/dt$, like an inductor.

$R_{S}$ is essential. If $R_{S}=0$, $V_{g}=0$ at all
frequencies, $Z_{out}=1/(g_{m}+sC_{gs})$, capacitive.
Large $R_{S}$ makes bootstrapping start early,
at $1/R_{S}C_{gs}$, and overcome capacitive feedthrough,
giving net $L_{eq}>0$.

answers.question: Explain why the output impedance of the circuit shown in Figure 21 can be inductive.

answer.text:
The circuit is a source follower loaded by an
impedance. $M_{2}$ is ac ground. For $Z_{out}$
set $V_{in}=0$, apply $V_{x}$ to the output and
measure $I_{x}$.

At low frequency $C_{gs1}$ is open, the gate is
ac ground through $R_{S}$ and

$$V_{gs} = -V_{x}$$

so the small signal drain current changes promptly
with $V_{x}$ and

$$Z_{out}\approx \frac{1}{g_{m}+g_{mb}}\parallel r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$$

resistive.

At high frequency $C_{gs}$ couples source to gate.
The gate is not ac ground if $R_{S}\ne 0$.
Let $V_{g}$ be the gate voltage. Gate draws no current:

$$\frac{V_{g}}{R_{S}}+(V_{g}-V_{x})sC_{gs}\approx 0$$

i.e.

$$V_{g}=V_{x}\frac{sC_{gs}R_{S}}{1+sC_{gs}R_{S}} $$

In particular for $\omega C_{gs}R_{S}\ll 1$,

$$V_{g} \approx V_{x}\,sC_{gs}R_{S} .$$

The current in $C_{gs}$, essentially $C_{gs}dV_{x}/dt$,
must flow in $R_{S}$ and develops a gate voltage
proportional to the derivative of $V_{x}$, $90^{\circ}$
leading $V_{x}$.

The transistor current responding to

$$V_{gs}=V_{g}-V_{x}$$

is therefore no longer in phase with $V_{x}$.
Neglecting $r_{o}$ for simplicity, KCL at the source:

$$I_{x} = (V_{x}-V_{g})(g_{m}+sC_{gs})$$

$$Y_{x}=\frac{I_{x}}{V_{x}} =\frac{g_{m}+sC_{gs}}{1+sC_{gs}R_{S}}$$

i.e.

$$Z_{x}= \frac{1+sC_{gs}R_{S}}{g_{m}+sC_{gs}}+ r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$$

For $sC_{gs}\ll g_{m}$, i.e. well below $f_{T}$,

$$Z_{x}\approx \frac{1}{g_{m}}+s\frac{C_{gs}R_{S}}{g_{m}} .$$

That is $1/g_{m}$ in series with an inductor

$$L\approx \frac{R_{S}C_{gs}}{g_{m}} .$$

$|Z_{x}|$ grows with $\omega$ and $I_{x}$ lags $V_{x}$.

In time domain: let $V_{x}$ step by $\Delta V$.
$V_{Cgs}$ cannot jump, so $V_{g}$ jumps by $\Delta V$
too. $V_{gs}$ is momentarily unchanged, the transistor
does not change its current. Only as $V_{g}$ decays
to ac ground with $\tau=R_{S}C_{gs}$ does $V_{gs}\to -\Delta V$
and the transistor current change to $g_{m}\Delta V$ develop:

$$V_{g}\approx \Delta V e^{-t/R_{S}C_{gs}}$$
$$-\Delta I_{D}\approx g_{m}\Delta V\,(1-e^{-t/R_{S}C_{gs}})$$

Current in response to a voltage step starts small
and builds up gradually. That is inductor behaviour,
$V=L\,dI/dt$. The delay is provided by $R_{S}$ charging
$C_{gs}$.

Hence a finite gate drive impedance plus $C_{gs}$
feedback makes the impedance looking into the source
inductive over a range of frequency.

No major errors or omissions.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 22.

answer.text:
The $X\to V_{out}\to X$ loop is
voltage sampled current mixed.

* $M_{1}$ : forward common source.
Drain load $R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}$, input $V_{X}$,
output $V_{out}$.

* $M_{2}$ : feedback device.
It senses $V_{out}$ on its gate with essentially
infinite impedance, i.e. voltage, shunt sampling.
Its drain current is returned to the input node
$X$ in parallel, i.e. current, shunt mixing.

It is nominally a shunt-shunt, i.e. transimpedance,
$I_{in}\to V_{out}$ amplifier.

Put $g_{m1},r_{o1}$ for $M_{1}$ and $g_{m2},r_{o2}$
for $M_{2}$. Body effect $=0$. $I_{in}$ ideal
for a.c. Let for low frequency

$$R_{D1}'=R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}$$

At $V_{out}$, $M_{2}$ gate draws no current:

$$(v_{out}/R_{D1})+g_{m1}v_{x}+v_{out}/r_{o1}=0 \tag{1}$$

i.e.

$$v_{out}/R_{D1}'+g_{m1}v_{x}=0$$

At $X$, $M_{1}$ gate draws no current. $M_{2}$
drain current flowing from $X$ to ground is
$g_{m2}v_{out}+v_{x}/r_{o2}$:

$$-i_{in}+g_{m2}v_{out}+v_{x}/r_{o2}=0 \tag{2}$$

Hence

$$v_{x}= -\frac{v_{out}}{g_{m1}R_{D1}'}$$

$$i_{in}=v_{out}\left[g_{m2}-\frac{1}{g_{m1}R_{D1}'r_{o2}}\right] \tag{3}$$

### Polarity

Let $I_{in}\uparrow$. $V_{X}\uparrow$,
$M_{1}$ : $V_{out}\downarrow$. $V_{GS2}\downarrow$,
$I_{D2}\downarrow$. But $I_{D2}$ is the current
subtracted from $I_{in}$ at $X$. A rise in $I_{in}$
causes a fall in feedback current. Feedback aids
the change. It is positive.

Intuitively $M_{2}$ loaded by the $I_{in}$ current
source is itself an inverter:

$V_{out}\downarrow \to I_{D2}\downarrow \to$
with $I_{in}$ fixed $V_{X}\uparrow$.

Two inversions $X\to V_{out}\to X$ give a
non-inverting loop.

### Loop gain

Break at the high impedance $M_{1}$ gate.
Drive $M_{1}$ gate with $v_{t}$, leave the
$M_{2}$ drain side open, $I_{in}$ a.c. open,
compute returned $v_{r}$.

$$v_{out}=-g_{m1}R_{D1}'v_{t}$$

At open $X'$ node: $g_{m2}v_{out}+v_{r}/r_{o2}=0$,
i.e.

$$v_{r}=-g_{m2}r_{o2}v_{out}$$

Hence return ratio

$$L=\frac{v_{r}}{v_{t}}=+g_{m1}R_{D1}'\,g_{m2}r_{o2} \tag{4}$$

$>0$ : positive feedback. Normally $g_{m}r_{o}\gg1$,
$g_{m1}R_{D1}'$ of order a few, so $L\gg 1$.

With finite source resistance $R_{S}$ in parallel
with $I_{in}$ and load $R_{L}$ at output,

$$L=g_{m1}(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}\parallel R_{L})\,
  g_{m2}(r_{o2}\parallel R_{S})$$

### Closed loop transimpedance

From (3),

$$R_{M}=\frac{v_{out}}{i_{in}}=
\frac{1}{g_{m2}-1/g_{m1}R_{D1}'r_{o2}}$$

Write $L$ from (4). Then

$$R_{M}= -\frac{g_{m1}R_{D1}'r_{o2}}{1-L}
 =\frac{1}{g_{m2}}\frac{L}{L-1} \tag{5}$$

i.e. of the form $A_{0}/(1-L)$ for positive
feedback, with feedthrough with loading

$$A_{0}=-g_{m1}R_{D1}'r_{o2}$$

For $L\to0$, $R_{M}\to A_{0}$, the ordinary
CS gain with $r_{o2}$ as input load:
$v_{x}=i_{in}r_{o2}$, $v_{out}=-g_{m1}R_{D1}'v_{x}$.

For $L<1$, denominator $<1$, $|R_{M}|>|A_{0}|$:
positive feedback enhances gain, preserving
negative sign.

For $L\gg1$,

$$R_{M}\approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}}$$

positive small. This is the small signal gain
about the metastable bias, not a usable
stable gain.

### Input and output impedance

$$Z_{in}=\frac{v_{x}}{i_{in}}=
-\frac{R_{M}}{g_{m1}R_{D1}'}=\frac{r_{o2}}{1-L} \tag{6}$$

Indeed $L=0\to r_{o2}$. $L\to1^{-}\to +\infty$:
bootstrapping. $L>1\to$ negative,
$\approx -1/g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}'$.

For $Z_{out}$, set $i_{in}=0$, apply $v_{test}$
at output. From (2) with $i_{in}=0$:
$g_{m2}v_{test}+v_{x}/r_{o2}=0$,
$v_{x}=-g_{m2}r_{o2}v_{test}$. KCL at output:

$$i_{test}=v_{test}/R_{D1}'+g_{m1}v_{x}
 =v_{test}\left[1/R_{D1}'-g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}\right]$$

$$Z_{out}=\frac{1}{1/R_{D1}'-g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}}
 =\frac{R_{D1}'}{1-L} \tag{7}$$

$L=0\to R_{D1}'$. $L\to1^{-}\to +\infty$.
$L>1\to$ negative, $\approx -1/g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}$.

This is Blackman with positive feedback:
shunt impedances are multiplied by $1/(1-L)$.

With $\lambda=0$, $r_{o}\to\infty$, $L\to\infty$,
$R_{M}=1/g_{m2}$, $Z_{in}=-1/g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}$,
$Z_{out}\to0$.

### Poles and stability

Add ground caps $C_{X}$ at $X$, $C_{out}$ at
output, neglecting $C_{gd}$ bridging for
first order. (1)-(2) become

$$v_{out}(1/R_{D1}'+sC_{out})+g_{m1}v_{x}=0$$
$$-i_{in}+v_{x}(1/r_{o2}+sC_{X})+g_{m2}v_{out}=0$$

Characteristic:

$$(1/R_{D1}'+sC_{out})(1/r_{o2}+sC_{X})-g_{m1}g_{m2}=0$$

$$(1+sC_{out}R_{D1}')(1+sC_{X}r_{o2})-L=0$$

$$s^{2}C_{out}C_{X}R_{D1}'r_{o2}
 +s(C_{out}R_{D1}'+C_{X}r_{o2})+1-L=0 \tag{8}$$

$s^{2}$ and $s$ coefficients $>0$. Stability
needs $1-L>0$, i.e.

$$L<1\;\; \rm{stable}$$

$$L>1\;\; \rm{one\;LHP,\;one\;RHP\;pole:\;latch}$$

Discriminant $=(a-b)^{2}+4abL>0$ with
$a=C_{out}R_{D1}'$, $b=C_{X}r_{o2}$, so low
frequency poles are real. As $L\to1^{-}$,
product $\to0$: one pole $\to0$, bandwidth
shrinks while gain grows. For $L>1$ the RHP
pole gives regenerative $\exp(+t/\tau)$,
$\tau\approx (C_{out}R_{D1}'+C_{X}r_{o2})/L$.

In practice with intrinsic gains, $L\gg1$.
The both-transistors-on bias with

$$I_{in}=I_{D2},\;(V_{DD}-V_{out})/R_{D1}=I_{D1}$$

is metastable. Any perturbation regenerates
to a rail where one device is off or in
deep triode with $L<1$. The circuit is
bistable / Schmitt with current input.

Qualitatively, $M_{1}+R_{D1}$ and
$M_{2}+I_{in}$ are two inverters in a loop.
Their voltage transfer intersection gives
two stable and one metastable point, with
hysteresis in $V_{out}$ vs $I_{in}$. Negative
$Z_{in},Z_{out}$ for $L>1$ are the small signal
manifestation of the snap.

To use as linear TIA the loop must be
tamed to $L<1$ by small $R_{D1}$, small
effective load at $X$, i.e. explicit shunt
resistors, triode operation, so positive
feedback only $Q$-enhances gain and
impedances. As drawn with ideal loads it
is essentially a current comparator latch.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 22.

answer.text:
This is a shunt-shunt amplifier with active
feedback. It uses positive feedback.

$M_{1}$ is a common-source stage:

* gate : $X$, input current node
* source : ac ground
* drain : $V_{out}$, load $R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}$

$M_{2}$ senses $V_{out}$ at its gate and
feeds a current back to $X$ at its drain:

* gate : $V_{out}$
* source : ac ground
* drain : $X$

Assume both in saturation, small signal $g_{m1},r_{o1}$,
$g_{m2},r_{o2}$, bodies grounded. Ignore $C$'s first.
Put

$$R_{D}' = R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}$$

### 1. Topology and sign

Output voltage sampling: $M_{2}$ gate to $V_{out}$.
Input current mixing: $M_{2}$ drain in parallel
with $I_{in}$ at $X$. Hence voltage-sampling,
current-mixing, i.e. shunt-shunt, transimpedance.

Trace the sign around the loop:

$V_{x} \uparrow \;\to\; $ via $M_{1}$ inverting
$V_{out}\downarrow \;\to\; $ $V_{gs2}\downarrow\;\to\; $
$I_{d2}$ drawn out of $X$ $\downarrow$.

Less current drawn out of $X$ is equivalent to
more current pushed into $X$. With $I_{in}$ ac fixed,
$V_{x}$ is pushed further $\uparrow$.

That is regenerative: positive feedback.

### 2. Small signal equations

$M_{2}$ model between $X$ and ground:

current from $X$ to ground $= g_{m2}V_{out} + V_{x}/r_{o2}$

$M_{1}$ gate draws no current, so KCL at $X$:

$$ I_{in} = g_{m2}V_{out} + g_{ds2}V_{x} \tag{1}$$

KCL at output, $M_{2}$ gate draws no current:

$$ 0 = g_{m1}V_{x} + (G_{D1}+g_{ds1})V_{out} \tag{2}$$

where $G_{D1}=1/R_{D1}$. Hence

$$V_{out} = -g_{m1}R_{D}'\,V_{x} \tag{3}$$

This is the forward voltage gain with $M_{2}$ gate loading
$=\infty$.

Insert in (1):

$$I_{in}=V_{x}\,[g_{ds2}-g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D}']$$

$$ \frac{V_{x}}{I_{in}} = \frac{1}{g_{ds2}-g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D}'} \tag{4}$$

Transimpedance:

$$ R_{T}= \frac{V_{out}}{I_{in}} = \frac{-g_{m1}R_{D}'}{g_{ds2}-g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D}'} \tag{5}$$

i.e.

$$R_{T}= \frac{-g_{m1}R_{D}'r_{o2}}{1-g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D}'r_{o2}}$$

### 3. Loop gain in two-port language

Consider $M_{2}$ as feedback 2-port in parallel with
forward 2-port. Port1 $=X$, Port2 $=V_{out}$.

Feedback $M_{2}$: $I_{1}=g_{ds2}V_{1}+g_{m2}V_{2}$,
$I_{2}=0$. So $Y_{11F}=g_{ds2}$, $Y_{12F}=g_{m2}$,
$Y_{21F}=Y_{22F}=0$.

Forward $M_{1}+R_{D1}$: $I_{1A}=0$,
$I_{2A}=g_{m1}V_{1}+(g_{ds1}+G_{D1})V_{2}$.
So $Y_{21A}=g_{m1}$, $Y_{22A}=1/R_{D}'$.

With loading but unilateral:

$Y_{11}'=g_{ds2}$, $Y_{22}'=1/R_{D}'$.

Open-loop with loading, feedback $g_{m2}=0$:

$$A_{ol}= \frac{V_{2}}{I_{in}}\Big|_{Y_{12F}=0}
= -\frac{Y_{21A}}{Y_{11}'Y_{22}'}
= -g_{m1}R_{D}'r_{o2}$$

Indeed input current develops $V_{x}=I_{in}r_{o2}$,
amplified by $-g_{m1}R_{D}'$.

Closed loop from Sec.2 can be written:

$$R_{T} = \frac{A_{ol}}{1+T}$$

with

$$T = -\frac{Y_{21A}Y_{12F}}{Y_{11}'Y_{22}'} 
= -g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D}'r_{o2}$$

$T$ is the conventional return loop gain.
$T<0$ denotes positive feedback. Define magnitude

$$L = g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D}'r_{o2} >0,\quad T=-L$$

Then

$$R_{T}= \frac{A_{ol}}{1-L},\quad A_{ol}=-g_{m1}R_{D}'r_{o2}$$

Positive feedback enhances $|R_{T}|$ by $1/(1-L)$.

Note sign change: for $L<1$, $1-L>0$, $R_{T}<0$,
inverting like $A_{ol}$. For $L>1$, $1-L<0$,
linearized $R_{T}>0\approx 1/g_{m2}$.
The $L\gg 1$ limit $R_{T}\to 1/g_{m2}$ is around
an unstable bias point.

### 4. Input and output resistance

From (4):

$$R_{in}= \frac{V_{x}}{I_{in}} = \frac{r_{o2}}{1-L}$$

To get $R_{out}$, open $I_{in}$, apply $V_{test}$ at
output. Then $0=g_{ds2}V_{x}+g_{m2}V_{test}$,
$I_{test}=V_{test}/R_{D}'+g_{m1}V_{x}$, giving

$$R_{out}= \frac{1}{1/R_{D}'-g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}}
= \frac{R_{D}'}{1-L}$$

Negative feedback reduces $R_{in},R_{out}$.
Positive feedback increases them by the same
$1/(1-L)$ factor. For $L\to 1^{-}$, both $\to +\infty$.
For $L>1$, both go negative in the linearized model.

### 5. Stability - poles

Add ground caps $C_{x},C_{out}$. Characteristic:

$$\det\begin{bmatrix}g_{ds2}+sC_{x} & g_{m2}\\
g_{m1} & 1/R_{D}'+sC_{out}\end{bmatrix}=0$$

$$(g_{ds2}+sC_{x})(1/R_{D}'+sC_{out})-g_{m1}g_{m2}=0$$

$$s^{2}C_{x}C_{out}+s(C_{x}/R_{D}'+C_{out}g_{ds2})
+g_{ds2}/R_{D}'-g_{m1}g_{m2}=0$$

For LHP poles need constant term $>0$:

$$g_{ds2}/R_{D}'>g_{m1}g_{m2}$$

i.e.

$$L = g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D}'r_{o2} < 1$$

This is $1+T>0$. Sum of poles $=-(g_{ds2}/C_{x}+1/R_{D}'C_{out})$
is independent of feedback, product $=p_{10}p_{20}(1-L)$.
As $L$ increases $0\to 1$, dominant pole moves toward
origin, bandwidth shrinks, gain grows. At $L=1$,
pole at origin. At $L>1$, product $<0$, one pole RHP:
latch-up.

In practice $g_{m}r_{o}\gg 1$, so $L<1$ requires
very small $R_{D}'$, i.e. low $M_{1}$ gain, and/or
extra conductance at $X$. With source resistance $R_{s}$
in parallel with $I_{in}$ and load $R_{L}$ at output:

$$L = g_{m1}g_{m2}\,(r_{o2}\parallel R_{s})\,(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}\parallel R_{L})$$

Small $R_{s},R_{L}$ help stabilize.

Example: $g_{m1}=g_{m2}=1$mS, $r_{o1}=r_{o2}=10$k.
Need $R_{D}'<100\,\Omega$ for $L<1$.
With $R_{D1}\approx 50\,\Omega$, $L\approx0.5$,
$A_{ol}\approx-0.5$k, $R_{T}\approx-1.0$k,
$R_{in}\approx 20$k vs 10k, $R_{out}\approx100\,\Omega$
vs $50\,\Omega$. With $90\,\Omega$, $L\approx0.9$,
enhancement $\approx 10\times$.

Ignoring $r_{o}$ gives $L\to\infty$, i.e. predicts
instability and negative $R_{in}=-1/g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}$.
$r_{o2}$ cannot be ignored.

$C_{gd1}+C_{gd2}$ bridge $X$ and $V_{out}$ directly,
Miller-multiplied by the $X\to V_{out}$ inverting gain,
further limiting bandwidth.

In short: stable positive-feedback TIA gives
inverting, gain- and impedance-boosted operation
at the expense of reduced bandwidth, increased
sensitivity $\sim 1/(1-L)$, and tight stability margin.
For $L>1$ the circuit becomes bistable - a latch,
negative-resistance, or Schmitt element.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 22.

answer.text:
This is shunt-shunt feedback with two inversions
in the loop. It is positive.

$M_{1}$ is the forward common-source:

$$ X \to V_{out} : A_{1} = -g_{m1}(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}) $$

$M_{2}$ senses $V_{out}$ at its gate and returns
a current to node $X$ at its drain. With $I_{in}$ ac
open its gain to $X$ is

$$ V_{out}\to X : A_{2}= -g_{m2}r_{o2} $$

Two minus signs give in-phase return. Positive feedback.

Put $G_{1}=1/R_{D1}+1/r_{o1}$, $G_{2}=1/r_{o2}$.
Low frequency, saturation, no body effect:

At $V_{out}$, KCL, $V_{DD}$ ac ground:

$$ \frac{V_{out}}{R_{D1}}+(g_{m1}V_{x}+g_{ds1}V_{out})=0 \tag{1}$$

i.e.

$$ G_{1}V_{out}+g_{m1}V_{x}=0 $$

At $X$, $M_{1}$ gate draws no current:

$$ I_{in}=g_{m2}V_{out}+g_{ds2}V_{x} \tag{2}$$

i.e.

$$ g_{m2}V_{out}+G_{2}V_{x}=I_{in} $$

Hence in matrix form

$$\begin{bmatrix} G_{1} & g_{m1} \\ g_{m2} & G_{2} \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} V_{out} \\ V_{x} \end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ I_{in} \end{bmatrix}$$

Determinant:

$$ D = G_{1}G_{2}-g_{m1}g_{m2} $$

$$ \frac{V_{out}}{I_{in}} = \frac{-g_{m1}}{D} $$
$$ \frac{V_{x}}{I_{in}} = \frac{G_{1}}{D} $$

i.e.

$$ R_{T}= \frac{V_{out}}{I_{in}}=
\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m1}g_{m2}-G_{1}G_{2}} \tag{3}$$
$$ R_{in}= \frac{V_{x}}{I_{in}}=
\frac{1}{G_{2}-g_{m1}g_{m2}/G_{1}} \tag{4}$$

Break the loop at the gate of $M_{1}$, which draws
no current so loading is unchanged. Inject $V_{test}$:

$$V_{out} = -g_{m1}(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1})V_{test}$$

With $I_{in}$ open, KCL at $X$:

$$0=g_{m2}V_{out}+G_{2}V_{r}$$

$$V_{r} = -\frac{g_{m2}}{G_{2}}V_{out}=-g_{m2}r_{o2}V_{out}$$

Return to test ratio:

$$ \frac{V_{r}}{V_{test}} =
g_{m1}(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1})\,g_{m2}r_{o2} \equiv L_{0}>0 $$

This is the positive-feedback loop gain:

$$ L_{0}= \frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{G_{1}G_{2}} $$

Intuition: $\Delta V_{x} \uparrow \to \Delta V_{out}
= -A_{1}\Delta V_{x}\downarrow \to \Delta I_{D2}
= g_{m2}\Delta V_{out}\downarrow$.
Less current is pulled out of $X$, so with $I_{in}$
fixed net current into $X$ rises, pushing $V_{x}$
further up. The regenerated voltage is

$$\Delta V_{x}' = r_{o2}(-\Delta I_{D2})
= g_{m1}(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1})g_{m2}r_{o2}\Delta V_{x}
= L_{0}\Delta V_{x}$$

in phase with the original.

Write $D=G_{1}G_{2}(1-L_{0})$. Then (3)-(4) become

$$ R_{T} = \frac{-g_{m1}(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1})r_{o2}}
{1-L_{0}} $$

$$ R_{in} = \frac{r_{o2}}{1-L_{0}} $$

With $I_{in}=0$ open, driving the output with
$V_{test}$, $0=g_{m2}V_{test}+G_{2}V_{x}$,
$I_{test}=G_{1}V_{test}+g_{m1}V_{x}$,

$$ G_{out}=G_{1}(1-L_{0}) $$

$$ R_{out} = \frac{R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}}{1-L_{0}} $$

Without feedback action, i.e. $g_{m2}\to 0$,
$R_{T0}=-g_{m1}(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1})r_{o2}$,
$R_{in0}=r_{o2}$, $R_{out0}=R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}$.
Positive feedback multiplies all by $1/(1-L_{0})$:

$$ A_{CL} = \frac{A_{OL}}{1-L_{0}} $$

Negative shunt-shunt divides by $1+L$; positive
multiplies by $1/(1-L)$.

Stability: add $C_{x}$ at $X$, $C_{L}$ at output:

$$(G_{1}+sC_{L})(G_{2}+sC_{x})-g_{m1}g_{m2}=0$$

$$C_{L}C_{x}s^{2}+(G_{1}C_{x}+G_{2}C_{L})s
+G_{1}G_{2}-g_{m1}g_{m2}=0$$

For LHP poles need

$$G_{1}G_{2}-g_{m1}g_{m2}>0$$

i.e.

$$ L_{0}<1 $$

Then $R_{in}>0$, $R_{out}>0$, $R_{T}<0$.
As $L_{0}\to 1$, resistances and $|R_{T}| \to \infty$.

If $L_{0}>1$, $G_{1}G_{2}-g_{m1}g_{m2}<0$,
product of poles $<0$, one RHP pole. $R_{in}$,
$R_{out}$ become negative. The bias with both
in saturation is metastable. In practice the
circuit latches. Small signal gain about that
metastable point is positive, $\approx 1/g_{m2}$
for large $L_{0}$.

In particular with $\lambda=0$, $G_{2}=0$,
$L_{0}=\infty$, always unstable. Finite $r_{o2}$
is essential to get $L_{0}<1$, requiring

$$g_{m1}(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1})\,g_{m2}r_{o2}<1$$

i.e. very low forward gain. Finite source or
load resistance at $X$ or $V_{out}$ replaces
$G_{2},G_{1}$ by $G_{2}+1/R_{S}$, $G_{1}+1/R_{L}$
and lowers $L_{0}$.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit of Figure 23.

answer.text:
The circuit is a current to voltage converter.

$M_{1}$ is a common-gate stage with $R_{D1}$ load.
$M_{2}$ is a common-source stage with $R_{D2}$ load.
$R_{F}$ goes from output voltage to input current.

Let small signal ground be $V_{DD}$ and $V_{b}$.
Let

* $A$ : input node $=$ source of $M_{1}$, voltage $v_{A}$
* $X$ : drain of $M_{1}$ $=$ gate of $M_{2}$, voltage $v_{X}$
* output, voltage $v_{out}$

$M_{1}$ : $v_{gs1}=-v_{A}$, $v_{bs1}=-v_{A}$,
$v_{ds1}=v_{X}-v_{A}$
$$i_{d1}=g_{m1}v_{gs1}+g_{mb1}v_{bs1}+g_{ds1}v_{ds1}$$
$$i_{d1}=-(g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1})v_{A}+g_{ds1}v_{X}$$
$M_{2}$ : source grounded, no body effect
$$i_{d2}=g_{m2}v_{X}+g_{ds2}v_{out}$$
$r_{o1}=1/g_{ds1}$, $r_{o2}=1/g_{ds2}$.
$$i_{RF}=\frac{v_{out}-v_{A}}{R_{F}}$$
defined from output to input.

KCL $X$:
$$-\frac{v_{X}}{R_{D1}}-i_{d1}=0$$
i.e.
$$i_{d1}= -\frac{v_{X}}{R_{D1}}$$

Hence
$$-\frac{v_{X}}{R_{D1}}=-(g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1})v_{A}+g_{ds1}v_{X}$$

$$v_{X}=A_{1}v_{A}$$

$$A_{1}=\frac{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1}}{g_{ds1}+1/R_{D1}}
=(g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1})(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1})>0$$

This is the CG gain, non-inverting.

### Feedback type

$R_{F}$ connects in parallel with output: it senses
output voltage. Short $v_{out}$, forward signal to
feedback is killed: voltage, shunt sampling.

$R_{F}$ connects in parallel with input: it steals
current from the input node. It mixes in parallel:
current, shunt mixing.

This is shunt-shunt, voltage-sampling current-mixing,
transimpedance amplifier.

Polarity: $I_{in}\uparrow \rightarrow v_{A}\uparrow
\rightarrow V_{GS1}\downarrow \rightarrow I_{D1}\downarrow
\rightarrow v_{X}\uparrow \rightarrow V_{GS2}\uparrow
\rightarrow I_{D2}\uparrow \rightarrow v_{out}\downarrow$.

$I_{in}$ up gives $v_{out}$ down. The $R_{F}$
current fed into the input node decreases, opposing
the increase in $I_{in}$. Negative feedback.

In steady state with large gain, $v_{A}\approx 0$
and $i_{RF}\approx -I_{in}$ :
$$\frac{0-v_{out}}{R_{F}}\approx I_{in}$$
$$ \frac{v_{out}}{I_{in}}\approx -R_{F} $$
ideal shunt-shunt.

### Open loop with loading

Put $R_{F}$ in $y$-form. For loading:

* short output for input loading: $R_{F}$ from $A$ to gnd.
* short input for output loading: $R_{F}$ from output to gnd.

Forward amplifier input resistance looking into source
of $M_{1}$ with $R_{D1}$ at drain:

$$R_{in1}=\frac{R_{D1}+r_{o1}}{1+(g_{m1}+g_{mb1})r_{o1}}$$

$$\approx \frac{1}{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}}\;\;{\rm if}\;r_{o1}\gg R_{D1}$$

With $R_{F}$ loading:
$$R_{in,OL}=R_{in1}\parallel R_{F}$$

Input current to $v_{A}$:
$$v_{A}=I_{in}R_{in,OL}$$

$v_{A}$ to $v_{X}$: $A_{1}$ above.

$v_{X}$ to $v_{out}$: CS with load $R_{D2}\parallel r_{o2}\parallel R_{F}$:
$$A_{2,OL}=-g_{m2}(R_{D2}\parallel r_{o2}\parallel R_{F})$$

Hence open-loop transimpedance:
$$A_{OL}=\frac{v_{out}}{I_{in}}\Big|_{open}=R_{in,OL}A_{1}A_{2,OL}$$
$$A_{OL}=-(R_{in1}\parallel R_{F})A_{1}g_{m2}(R_{D2}\parallel r_{o2}\parallel R_{F})$$
$<0$.

Feedback factor: feedback current from output to
input. Current from input into $R_{F}$ toward output:
$$I_{F}=\frac{v_{A}-v_{out}}{R_{F}}\approx -\frac{v_{out}}{R_{F}}$$
$$\beta=\frac{I_{F}}{v_{out}}=-\frac{1}{R_{F}}$$

With $I_{i}=I_{in}-I_{F}$, $v_{out}=A_{OL}I_{i}$:
$$v_{out}=A_{OL}(I_{in}-\beta v_{out})$$
$$\frac{v_{out}}{I_{in}}=\frac{A_{OL}}{1+A_{OL}\beta}$$

Loop gain:
$$T=A_{OL}\beta = -\frac{A_{OL}}{R_{F}} = \frac{|A_{OL}|}{R_{F}}>0$$
$$T=\frac{(R_{in1}\parallel R_{F})A_{1}g_{m2}(R_{D2}\parallel r_{o2}\parallel R_{F})}{R_{F}}$$

But in general:
$$R_{in1}A_{1}=R_{D1}$$
exactly. Indeed
$$R_{in1}=\frac{R_{D1}+r_{o1}}{1+(g_{m1}+g_{mb1})r_{o1}}$$
$$A_{1}=(g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+1/r_{o1})(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1})$$
product $=R_{D1}$.

Let $R_{out,OL}=R_{D2}\parallel r_{o2}\parallel R_{F}$.
Then $(R_{in1}\parallel R_{F})A_{1}=R_{D1}R_{F}/(R_{in1}+R_{F})$,
$$T=\frac{R_{D1}g_{m2}R_{out,OL}}{R_{in1}+R_{F}}$$

If $R_{F}\gg R_{in1},R_{out,OL}\approx R_{D2}\parallel r_{o2}$:
$$T\approx \frac{R_{D1}}{R_{F}}g_{m2}(R_{D2}\parallel r_{o2})$$
If $r_{o}\gg R_{D}$:
$$T\approx \frac{g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}}{R_{F}}$$

Large when forward gain $\gg R_{F}$.

### Closed-loop gain

$$A_{CL}=\frac{A_{OL}}{1+T}=-R_{F}\frac{T}{1+T}$$

since $A_{OL}=-TR_{F}$.

For $T\gg 1$:
$$A_{CL}\approx -R_{F}\left(1-\frac{1}{T}\right)$$

Feedforward through $R_{F}$ is the $1$ in $1-g_{m2}A_{1}R_{F}$,
negligible when $g_{m2}A_{1}R_{F}\gg 1$.

Direct nodal analysis gives the same:
with $M=(1-g_{m2}A_{1}R_{F})R_{out,OL}'/(R_{F}+R_{out,OL}')$
where $R_{out,OL}'=R_{D2}\parallel r_{o2}$,
$$ \frac{v_{out}}{I_{in}}=\frac{MR_{F}}{1-M+g_{m1,eff}R_{F}} $$
which $\to -R_{F}$ for large $M$.

### Input resistance

Input voltage $v_{A}$ over $I_{in}$.

From $A_{1}/R_{D1}=1/R_{in1}$:
Denominator $1/R_{F}+A_{1}/R_{D1}=1/R_{in,OL}$,
and $1+A_{CL}/R_{F}=1/(1+T)$,
$$R_{in}=\frac{v_{A}}{I_{in}}=\frac{R_{in,OL}}{1+T}$$

$$R_{in}=\frac{R_{in1}\parallel R_{F}}{1+T}$$

$\to 0$ for large $T$. Approx:
$$R_{in}\approx \frac{R_{F}}{A_{1}g_{m2}R_{out,OL}}\frac{T}{1+T}$$
For large $T$, $\lambda=0$, no body:
$$R_{in}\approx \frac{R_{F}}{g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{m2}R_{D2}}$$

### Output resistance

Set $I_{in}=0$, apply $V_{x}$ at output.
Then $(V_{x}-v_{A})/R_{F}=v_{A}/R_{in1}$,
$v_{A}=V_{x}R_{in,OL}/R_{F}$.
$$I_{x}=V_{x}\left(\frac{1}{R_{D2}}+g_{ds2}+\frac1{R_{F}}\right)
+v_{A}(g_{m2}A_{1}-1/R_{F})$$
$$\frac{I_{x}}{V_{x}}=\frac1{R_{out,OL}}+\frac{R_{in,OL}}{R_{F}}(g_{m2}A_{1}-1/R_{F})$$

i.e.
$$R_{out}=\frac{R_{out,OL}}{1+T-\dfrac{R_{in,OL}R_{out,OL}}{R_{F}^{2}}}$$

Second term in denominator is feedthrough,
usually negligible:
$$R_{out}\approx \frac{R_{out,OL}}{1+T}=\frac{R_{D2}\parallel r_{o2}\parallel R_{F}}{1+T}$$

Shunt sampling lowers output impedance by $1+T$.

In summary, two-stage inverting forward path
$A_{1}>0$, $A_{2}<0$ with $R_{F}$ shunt-shunt
feedback gives large loop gain $T\approx g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}/R_{F}$,
closed-loop $V_{out}/I_{in}\approx -R_{F}$,
low $R_{in}$ and low $R_{out}$, both divided by $1+T$.
$R_{F}$ also provides DC feedback stabilizing the bias.

$$v_{gs1}=-V_{A}\;,\;v_{ds1}=V_{X}-V_{A}$$

$$i_{d1}=g_{m1}v_{gs1}+g_{ds1}v_{ds1}$$
into drain = out of source.

Current $(V_{A}-V_{out})/R_{F}$ from input

$$-I_{in}+\frac{V_{A}-V_{out}}{R_{F}}-i_{s1}=0$$

where

since $1-R_{X}g_{ds1}=R_{X}/R_{D1}$.

$$g_{m1,eff}=A_{1}/R_{D1}
=\frac{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}}{1+R_{D1}g_{ds1}}
=\frac{1+g_{m1}r_{o1}}{r_{o1}+R_{D1}}$$
$1/R_{in,CG}$. Then
$$V_{A}(1/R_{F}+g_{m1,eff})-V_{out}/R_{F}=I_{in} \tag{1'}$$

+V_{out}(1/R_{D2}'+1/R_{F})=0 \tag{3'}$$

$g_{m1}R_{D1}\to A_{1}$,
$R_{D2}\to R_{D2}'$.

output for $R_{out}$ gives a common
denominator.

$$D_{0}'=1+g_{m1,eff}R_{F}+g_{m1,eff}R_{D2}'
+A_{1}g_{m2}R_{D2}'$$
$$=1+g_{m1,eff}(R_{F}+R_{D2}')+A_{1}g_{m2}R_{D2}'$$

$$R_{T}=\frac{V_{out}}{I_{in}}
=\frac{R_{D2}'\,(1-A_{1}g_{m2}R_{F})}{D_{0}'} $$

$$D_{0}=1+g_{m1}R_{F}+g_{m1}R_{D2}
+g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}$$

\frac{R_{D2}(1-g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{F})}{D_{0}} $$

$$R_{in}=\frac{R_{F}+R_{D2}}{D_{0}}$$

$$R_{out}=\frac{R_{D2}(1+g_{m1}R_{F})}{D_{0}}$$

This is exact including $R_{F}$ loading
and feedthrough.

input and output, $R_{p}'=R_{D2}'\parallel R_{F}$,

$$D_{0}'\approx A_{1}g_{m2}R_{D2}'$$

{A_{1}g_{m2}}=\frac{1}{1/R_{D2}'+g_{m1,eff}(1+A_{1}'?)/...}$$

$\approx R_{D2}\parallel R_{F}/g_{m2}R_{D1}$.

This is a 2-stage shunt-shunt, i.e.
voltage sampling current mixing, negative feedback

$$i_{RF}=\frac{V_{out}-V_{in}}{R_{F}}$$
