Polarity: with $I_{in}=0$ opened, let $V_{in}\uparrow$.

CG: $V_{gs1}=-V_{in}\downarrow$, $I_{d1}\downarrow$,
$V_{X}=V_{DD}-I_{d1}R_{D1}\uparrow$.

CS: $V_{gs2}=V_{X}\uparrow$, $V_{out}\downarrow$.

Then $i_{RF}=(V_{out}-V_{in})/R_{F}\downarrow$.
More current must be supplied by the test source to
hold $V_{in}$ up. Input impedance is lowered.
This is negative shunt feedback.

In the limit of large loop gain $V_{in}$ is a
virtual ground and all of $I_{in}$ is forced
in $R_{F}$:

$$I_{in}\approx -\frac{V_{out}-V_{in}}{R_{F}}\approx -\frac{V_{out}}{R_{F}}$$

i.e.

$$R_{M ideal}=\frac{V_{out}}{I_{in}}\approx -R_{F}$$

### Small signal loaded open loop

Put $g_{ds}=1/r_{o}$. Neglect body for now, then
replace $g_{m1}\to g_{m1}+g_{mb1}$.

For shunt-shunt the $R_{F}$ loads input with
$R_{F}$ to gnd for $V_{out}=0$ and loads output
with $R_{F}$ to gnd for $V_{in}=0$. Feedback
$Y_{12}=-1/R_{F}$.

Forward loaded amplifier:

Input resistance of CG stage with drain load $R_{D1}$:

KCL at $X$:

$$\frac{V_{X}}{R_{D1}}+\frac{V_{X}-V_{in}}{r_{o1}}
+g_{m1}(-V_{in})=0$$

$$V_{X}=V_{in}\frac{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}}{G_{D1}+g_{ds1}}
=V_{in}A_{1}$$

$$A_{1}=\frac{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}}{G_{D1}+g_{ds1}}$$

$G_{D1}=1/R_{D1}$. With $r_{o1}\to\infty$,
$A_{1}\approx g_{m1}R_{D1}>0$.

Input conductance seen looking into source:

$$G_{in,open}=\frac{(g_{m1}+g_{ds1})G_{D1}}{G_{D1}+g_{ds1}}$$

i.e. $R_{in1}=1/G_{in,open}=(R_{D1}+r_{o1})/(1+g_{m1}r_{o1})
\approx 1/g_{m1}$.

With input shunt $R_{F}$:

$$V_{in}=I_{in}\,(R_{F}\parallel R_{in1})$$

CS stage voltage gain with output shunt $R_{F}$:

$$A_{v2}=\frac{V_{out}}{V_{X}}=-g_{m2}(R_{D2}\parallel R_{F}
\parallel r_{o2})$$

Hence loaded open-loop transimpedance:

$$A_{open}=\frac{V_{out}}{I_{in}}\Big|_{Y_{12}=0}
=(R_{F}\parallel R_{in1})A_{1}A_{v2}$$

$A_{open}<0$, large magnitude.

Feedback factor magnitude $|\beta|=1/R_{F}$.
Loop gain:

$$T=-\frac{A_{open}}{R_{F}}=
\frac{(R_{F}\parallel R_{in1})A_{1}g_{m2}
(R_{D2}\parallel R_{F}\parallel r_{o2})}{R_{F}}>0$$

With $r_{o}\to\infty$, $R_{F}\gg R_{in1}$:

$$|A_{open}|\approx R_{D1}g_{m2}(R_{D2}\parallel R_{F})$$

$$T\approx g_{m2}R_{D1}\frac{R_{D2}\parallel R_{F}}{R_{F}}$$

If $R_{F}\gg R_{D2}$, $T\approx g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}/R_{F}$.

### Closed loop transimpedance

Solving full nodal equations:

input: $-I_{in}+(V_{in}-V_{out})/R_{F}
-(V_{X}-V_{in})/r_{o1}+g_{m1}V_{in}=0$

$X$: $V_{X}/R_{D1}+(V_{X}-V_{in})/r_{o1}-g_{m1}V_{in}=0$

output: $V_{out}/R_{D2}+V_{out}/r_{o2}+g_{m2}V_{X}
+(V_{out}-V_{in})/R_{F}=0$

Let $G_{out}=G_{D2}+g_{ds2}+1/R_{F}$.
Then $V_{in}(-1/R_{F}+g_{m2}A_{1})+V_{out}G_{out}=0$ and

$$I_{in}=V_{in}(1/R_{F}+G_{in,open})-V_{out}/R_{F}$$

$$R_{M}=\frac{V_{out}}{I_{in}}=
\frac{1/R_{F}-g_{m2}A_{1}}
{G_{out}(1/R_{F}+G_{in,open})-1/R_{F}^{2}+g_{m2}A_{1}/R_{F}}$$

With $r_{o1},r_{o2}\to\infty$:

$$R_{M}=\frac{1-g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{F}}
{g_{m1}+(1+g_{m1}R_{F})/R_{D2}+g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}}$$

If $g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{F}\gg 1$:

$$R_{M}\approx -R_{F}\frac{g_{m2}R_{D1}}
{1+g_{m2}R_{D1}+R_{F}/R_{D2}}\approx -R_{F}$$

provided $g_{m2}R_{D1}\gg 1+R_{F}/R_{D2}$.
This is $A_{open}/(1+T)$ form.

### Terminal impedances

Shunt mixing lowers $R_{in}$, shunt sampling lowers
$R_{out}$ by $\approx 1+T$.

Open input: $R_{in,open}=R_{F}\parallel R_{in1}$.
Closed:

$$R_{in,closed}\approx \frac{R_{in,open}}{1+T}$$

Exact low frequency:

$$R_{in}=\frac{V_{in}}{I_{in}}
=\frac{G_{out}}{G_{out}(1/R_{F}+G_{in,open})-1/R_{F}^{2}+g_{m2}A_{1}/R_{F}}$$

With $r_{o}\to\infty$:

$$R_{in}=\frac{1+R_{F}/R_{D2}}
{(1+g_{m1}R_{F})/R_{D2}+g_{m1}+g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}}
\approx \frac{R_{F}}{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}}$$

for large $T$, $\ll 1/g_{m1}$.

Output: zero $I_{in}$, apply $V_{test}$ at output.
Let $D=1+R_{F}G_{in,open}$, $V_{in}=V_{out}/D$:

$$R_{out}=\frac{1}{G_{D2}+g_{ds2}+1/R_{F}+(g_{m2}A_{1}-1/R_{F})/D}$$

With $r_{o}\to\infty$, $g_{m1}R_{F}\gg 1$:

$$R_{out}\approx \frac{1}{1/R_{D2}+(1+g_{m2}R_{D1})/R_{F}}
\approx \frac{R_{F}}{1+g_{m2}R_{D1}}$$

$\ll R_{D2}$ for large loop gain.

With body effect on $M_{1}$ whose body is grounded,
$g_{m1}\to g_{m1}+g_{mb1}$ in $A_{1}$ and $G_{in,open}$.
$M_{2}$ has no body effect.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 24.

answer.text:
The circuit is a current input voltage output amplifier.

* $M_{1}$ : gate ac ground, source = input node $X$,
drain = output node. Common gate forward stage.
* $M_{2}$ : source ac ground $V_{DD}$, gate = $V_{out}$,
drain = $X$. Common source feedback stage.
* $I_{1}$ : load of $M_{1}$.
* $I_{B}$ : dc bias sink at $X$.

Put $V_{b}$ ac ground. Neglect body effect, or replace
$gm_{1}$ by $gm_{1}+gmb_{1}$. Let $ro_{1}=1/gds_{1}$,
$ro_{2}=1/gds_{2}$. Let $R_{1}$ be the impedance of $I_{1}$,
$R_{B}$ the impedance of $I_{B}$. Ideal is $R_{1},R_{B}\to\infty$.

DC, with $I_{in}=0$:

KCL $V_{out}$ : $I_{D1}=I_{1}$
KCL $X$ : $I_{D1}-I_{D2}-I_{B}=0$

with $I_{D2}<0$ for PMOS. I.e.

$$ |I_{D2}| = I_{B}-I_{1} >0 $$

$$ V_{X}=V_{b}-V_{GS1},\quad V_{out}=V_{DD}-|V_{SG2}| $$

Saturation requires

$$V_{out}-V_{X}\ge V_{ov1},\quad V_{DD}-V_{X}\ge V_{ov2} $$

Small signal. Define $vx$, $vout$.

For either device, current entering drain:

$$I_{d}=gm\,vgs+gds\,vds$$

$$M_{1}: vgs_{1}=-vx,\; vds_{1}=vout-vx$$
$$I_{d1}=-gm_{1}vx+gds_{1}(vout-vx) \tag{1}$$

$$M_{2}: vgs_{2}=vout,\; vds_{2}=vx$$
$$I_{d2}=gm_{2}vout+gds_{2}vx \tag{2}$$

Current from $M_{1}$ into $X$ is $+I_{d1}$,
current from $M_{2}$ into $X$ is $-I_{d2}$.

KCL $X$:

$$ i_{in}+I_{d1}-I_{d2}-\frac{vx}{R_{B}}=0 \tag{3}$$

KCL $out$, open output:

$$ -\frac{vout}{R_{1}}-I_{d1}=0 \tag{4}$$

i.e. $I_{d1}=-vout/R_{1}$.

This is voltage sampling at the output, current mixing
at the input: shunt-shunt, transimpedance feedback.

Loop sense: $vx\uparrow \to$ $M_{1}$ $V_{GS}\downarrow$
$\to$ $I_{D1}\downarrow$ $\to$ $vout\uparrow$,
non-inverting CG. $vout\uparrow \to$ $M_{2}$ $|V_{SG}|\downarrow$
$\to$ current supplied to $X$ $\downarrow$ $\to$ $vx\downarrow$,
inverting CS. The loop inverts: negative feedback.

From (1)(4):

$$-(gm_{1}+gds_{1})vx+gds_{1}vout = -\frac{vout}{R_{1}}$$

Let $R_{D1}=ro_{1}\parallel R_{1}$,

$$(gm_{1}+gds_{1})vx = vout\left(gds_{1}+\frac1{R_{1}}\right)
 =\frac{vout}{R_{D1}} $$

$$ \frac{vout}{vx}=(gm_{1}+gds_{1})R_{D1}\approx gm_{1}R_{D1} \tag{5}$$

the CG gain with load $R_{D1}$.

From (3), $i_{in}=-I_{d1}+I_{d2}+vx/R_{B}$:

$$i_{in}= \frac{vout}{R_{1}}+gm_{2}vout+vx\left(gds_{2}+\frac1{R_{B}}\right)$$

Using (5):

$$i_{in}=vout\left[\frac1{R_{1}}+gm_{2}
 +\frac{gds_{2}+1/R_{B}}{(gm_{1}+gds_{1})R_{D1}}\right]$$

Hence closed loop transimpedance:

$$ Z_{T}=\frac{vout}{i_{in}}
 =\frac{1}{gm_{2}+1/R_{1}+ \dfrac{gds_{2}+1/R_{B}}{(gm_{1}+gds_{1})R_{D1}}} \tag{6}$$

For $R_{1},R_{B}\to\infty$:

$$ Z_{T}=\frac{1}{gm_{2}+ \dfrac{gds_{2}gds_{1}}{gm_{1}+gds_{1}}}
 \approx \frac1{gm_{2}} $$

Positive because forward is non-inverting. Ideally
$I_{d1}\approx 0$ and $i_{in}\approx I_{d2}\approx gm_{2}vout$.

Input impedance $Z_{in}=vx/i_{in}$. From (5)(6):

$$ Z_{in}= \frac{Z_{T}}{(gm_{1}+gds_{1})R_{D1}} \tag{7}$$

For ideal sources:

$$Z_{in}=Z_{T}\frac{gds_{1}}{gm_{1}+gds_{1}}
 \approx \frac{1}{gm_{2}}\frac{1}{gm_{1}ro_{1}}$$

Very low, $\to 0$ for $\lambda\to 0$. Virtual ground at $X$.

Output impedance: deactivate $i_{in}$, apply $v_{test}$
at output, measure $i_{test}$ into node.

$$i_{test}=\frac{v_{test}}{R_{1}}+I_{d1}$$
$$I_{d1}=I_{d2}+\frac{vx}{R_{B}}$$

This gives

$$vx=v_{test}\frac{gds_{1}-gm_{2}}{gm_{1}+gds_{1}+gds_{2}+1/R_{B}}$$

and

$$Y_{out}=\frac1{R_{1}}+gm_{2}
 +(gds_{1}-gm_{2})\frac{gds_{2}+1/R_{B}}{gm_{1}+gds_{1}+gds_{2}+1/R_{B}}$$

i.e.

$$ R_{out}= \frac{gm_{1}+gds_{1}+gds_{2}+1/R_{B}}
 {(1/R_{1}+gm_{2})(gm_{1}+gds_{1})+(gds_{2}+1/R_{B})(1/R_{1}+gds_{1})} \tag{8}$$

For $R_{1},R_{B}\to\infty$:

$$R_{out}= \frac{gm_{1}+gds_{1}+gds_{2}}
 {gm_{2}(gm_{1}+gds_{1})+gds_{1}gds_{2}}\approx\frac1{gm_{2}}$$

In general to first order:

$$R_{out}\approx Z_{T}\approx \frac1{gm_{2}}\parallel R_{1}$$

Loop gain: break at $M_{2}$ gate, ideal break,
set $i_{in}=0$, drive $v_{t}$, return $v_{r}$ at output.

$$I_{d1}=-\frac{v_{r}}{R_{1}},\;
vx=\frac{v_{r}}{(gm_{1}+gds_{1})R_{D1}}$$
$$-\frac{v_{r}}{R_{1}}=gm_{2}v_{t}+vx(gds_{2}+1/R_{B})$$

$$\frac{v_{r}}{v_{t}}=
 -\frac{gm_{2}}{1/R_{1}+(gds_{2}+1/R_{B})/(gm_{1}+gds_{1})R_{D1}}$$

Loop gain $L=-v_{r}/v_{t}$:

$$ L =\frac{gm_{2}}{1/R_{1}+(gds_{2}+1/R_{B})/(gm_{1}+gds_{1})R_{D1}} \tag{9}$$

For ideal sources $L=(gm_{1}+gds_{1})gm_{2}/gds_{1}gds_{2}
\approx gm_{1}ro_{1}gm_{2}ro_{2}\gg 1$.
For finite $R_{1}$, $L\approx gm_{2}R_{1}\gg 1$.

Thus with $\lambda=0$:

$$V_{out}/I_{in}\approx 1/gm_{2},\; R_{in}\approx 0,\;
R_{out}\approx 1/gm_{2}$$

a low input impedance TIA linearized by large
shunt-shunt loop gain.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 24.

answer.text:
This is a current input, voltage output amplifier.

* $M_{1}$ : gate ac ground, source $=x$
input node, drain $=$ output node. Common-gate
forward stage.

* $M_{2}$ : source ac ground $V_{DD}$,
gate $=$ output, drain $=x$ input.
Common-source feedback stage.

* $I_{1}$ on top, $I_{B}$ on bottom are dc bias
with ac impedance $R_{1},R_{B}$.

Put $v_{x}$ = ac input node, $v_{out}$ = ac output,
$i_{in}$ = ac input. Let

$$M_{1}: g_{m1},g_{mb1},r_{o1} \qquad
  M_{2}: g_{m2},r_{o2}$$

$g_{mb2}=0$, n-well to source.
If body to source for $M_{1}$ put $g_{mb1}=0$.
Put $g_{ds}=1/r_{o}$.

DC, $I_{in}=0$:

$$I_{D1}=I_{1}$$
$$I_{D2}+I_{S1}=I_{B}$$

i.e. $I_{D2}=I_{B}-I_{1}>0$.
$$V_{GS1}=V_{b}-V_{X}\,,\quad V_{SG2}=V_{DD}-V_{out}$$
$$V_{DS1}=V_{out}-V_{X}\ge V_{ov1}$$
$$V_{SD2}=V_{DD}-V_{X}\ge V_{ov2}$$

$M_{2}$ provides dc negative feedback and
stabilizes $V_{X},V_{out}$.

### Feedback type

Sense $v_{out}$ at $M_{2}$ gate, return current
at $M_{2}$ drain to input node. Voltage sampling,
current mixing - shunt-shunt, transimpedance
amplifier.

Polarity: $v_{x}\uparrow$

- $M_{1}$ CG: $v_{gs1}=-v_{x}$, $i_{d1}\downarrow$,
  $v_{out}\uparrow$ . Non-inverting.

- $M_{2}$ CS: $v_{sg2}=-v_{out}$, source to drain
  current $\downarrow$, i.e. less current injected
  into $x$, $v_{x}\downarrow$. Inverting.

$x\to out\to x$ is inverting: negative feedback.

Forward $A=v_{out}/i_{in}>0$ with $M_{2}$ off.
Feedback $\beta = i_{f}/v_{out}\approx g_{m2}>0$.
Closed loop $A_{f}=A/(1+A\beta)\approx 1/\beta$.

### Small signal nodal

Model $M_{1}$ drain to source current:

$$i_{ds1}=(g_{m1}+g_{mb1})v_{gs,eff}+g_{ds1}v_{ds1}$$

$$v_{gs1}=-v_{x}\,,\;v_{bs1}=-v_{x}\,,\;v_{ds1}=v_{out}-v_{x}$$

$$i_{ds1}=-(g_{m1}+g_{mb1})v_{x}+\frac{v_{out}-v_{x}}{r_{o1}}$$

flows from output node into $M_{1}$ and out
of $M_{1}$ into input node.

Model $M_{2}$ source to drain current, source ground:

$$v_{sg2}=-v_{out}\,,\;v_{sd2}=-v_{x}$$
$$i_{sd2}=g_{m2}v_{sg2}+g_{ds2}v_{sd2}
 =-g_{m2}v_{out}-g_{ds2}v_{x}$$

flows from ground through $M_{2}$ into input node.

Output node $v_{out}$:

$$\frac{v_{out}}{R_{1}}+i_{ds1}=0 \tag{1}$$

i.e.

$$v_{out}\left(\frac1{R_{1}}+\frac1{r_{o1}}\right)
 -v_{x}\left[g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+\frac1{r_{o1}}\right]=0$$

Let

$$G_{1}=g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+1/r_{o1}$$
$$R_{D}'=R_{1}\parallel r_{o1}$$

then

$$v_{out}=v_{x}\,G_{1}R_{D}' \tag{1a}$$

CG voltage gain $>0$.

Input node $v_{x}$: $i_{in}$ enters, $R_{B}$
to ground, $-i_{ds1}$ leaving toward $M_{1}$,
$-i_{sd2}$ leaving toward $M_{2}$:

$$\frac{v_{x}}{R_{B}}-i_{in}-i_{ds1}-i_{sd2}=0 \tag{2}$$

i.e.

$$v_{x}\left[\frac1{R_{B}}+G_{1}+\frac1{r_{o2}}\right]
 +v_{out}\left[g_{m2}-\frac1{r_{o1}}\right]=i_{in} \tag{2a}$$

### Closed loop transimpedance

From (1a)-(2a):

$$v_{x}\left[\frac1{R_{B}}+G_{1}+\frac1{r_{o2}}
 +G_{1}R_{D}'\left(g_{m2}-\frac1{r_{o1}}\right)\right]=i_{in}$$

Note $1+R_{D}'(g_{m2}-1/r_{o1})=R_{D}'(1/R_{1}+g_{m2})$.

Define

$$D=\frac1{R_{B}}+\frac1{r_{o2}}+G_{1}R_{D}'
 \left(\frac1{R_{1}}+g_{m2}\right)$$

Then input resistance $R_{in}=v_{x}/i_{in}$:

$$R_{in}=\frac1{D} $$

$$R_{in}=\frac{1}{\frac1{R_{B}}+\frac1{r_{o2}}+G_{1}R_{D}'\left(\frac1{R_{1}}+g_{m2}\right)} \tag{3}$$

and

$$ \frac{v_{out}}{i_{in}} = G_{1}R_{D}'R_{in} $$

$$Z_{T}=\frac{G_{1}R_{D}'}{\frac1{R_{B}}+\frac1{r_{o2}}+G_{1}R_{D}'\left(\frac1{R_{1}}+g_{m2}\right)} \tag{4}$$

This is $Z_{T0}/(1+T)$, $R_{in0}/(1+T)$ with

$$D_{0}=\frac1{R_{B}}+\frac1{r_{o2}}+G_{1}\frac{R_{D}'}{R_{1}}$$
$$T=\frac{G_{1}R_{D}'g_{m2}}{D_{0}}$$

$T$ is the loop gain. Indeed breaking at $M_{2}$
gate, driving $v_{t}$, returning $v_{r}$ at output:

$$\frac{v_{r}}{v_{t}}=-T$$

so $T>0$ means negative feedback.

In particular with $R_{B},r_{o1},r_{o2}\to\infty$:

$$T\approx g_{m2}R_{1}$$
$$Z_{T}\approx \frac{R_{1}}{1+g_{m2}R_{1}}
 =\frac1{g_{m2}+1/R_{1}}=R_{1}\parallel\frac1{g_{m2}}$$
$$R_{in}\approx \frac{1}{(g_{m1}+g_{mb1})(1+g_{m2}R_{1})}$$

In general large $G_{1}R_{D}'$:

$$Z_{T}\approx \frac1{g_{m2}+1/R_{1}}$$

Set by feedback device. For ideal $R_{1}$:

$$Z_{T}\to 1/g_{m2}\,,\;R_{in}\to 0$$

Virtual ground at input. Feedback reduces CG
$1/g_{m1}$ input resistance by $1+T$.

### Output resistance

Put $i_{in}=0$, apply $v_{t}$ at output,
measure $i_{t}$. From (2a) with $i_{in}=0$:

$$v_{x}=-v_{t}\frac{g_{m2}-1/r_{o1}}{1/R_{B}+G_{1}+1/r_{o2}}$$

KCL at output: $i_{t}=v_{t}/R_{1}+i_{ds1}$:

$$Y_{out}=\frac{i_{t}}{v_{t}}=\frac1{R_{1}}+\frac1{r_{o1}}
 +\frac{G_{1}(g_{m2}-1/r_{o1})}{1/R_{B}+G_{1}+1/r_{o2}} \tag{5}$$

$$R_{out}=1/Y_{out}$$

With large $r_{o},R_{B}$:

$$R_{out}\approx \frac1{g_{m2}+1/R_{1}}
 =R_{1}\parallel\frac1{g_{m2}}$$

same as $Z_{T}$. Feedback lowers the high
CG output impedance to $\approx 1/g_{m2}$.

This is a regulated common-gate TIA.
Loop gain $\approx g_{m2}R_{1}$. Two poles
at input and output nodes can give complex
poles/peaking; input pole is pushed to very
high frequency by small $R_{in}$, output pole
$\approx 1/R_{out}C_{out}$ is usually dominant.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in Figure 24.

answer.text:
This is a shunt-shunt feedback TIA.

* $M_{1}$ : NMOS common-gate. Source is input,
drain is output, gate AC ground at $V_{b}$.
Body is substrate GND, so backgate matters.
* $M_{2}$ : PMOS. Source to $V_{DD}$ AC ground,
gate to $V_{out}$, drain to input.
It is a $V_{out}$ to input-current transconductor.
Body to N-well to $V_{DD}$, no backgate.
* $I_{1}$ : pull-up load for $M_{1}$.
* $I_{B}$ : DC sink at input.
* $I_{in}$ : signal current into input.

Let $X$ be input node, $Y$ output node,
$v_{x},v_{out}$ small signal.
Let $R_{1}$ be impedance of $I_{1}$ from $Y$
to AC ground, $R_{b}$ impedance of $I_{B}$
from $X$ to ground. Ideal is infinite.

Put $G_{m1}=g_{m1}+g_{mb1}$,
$G_{1}=G_{m1}+g_{ds1}$,
$g_{ds}=1/r_{o}$.

DC: KCL at $Y$:

$$ I_{D1}=I_{1} $$

$M_{1}$ current is fixed. Hence, neglecting $\lambda$,

$$V_{GS1}=V_{b}-V_{X}= {\rm const}$$

$V_{X}$ is set by $V_{b}$. KCL at $X$:

$$ I_{B}=I_{IN,DC}+I_{1}+I_{SD2} $$

$I_{SD2}$ sets $V_{SG2}=V_{DD}-V_{out}$.
Increase $I_{in}$ decreases $I_{SD2}$, decreases
$V_{SG2}$, increases $V_{out}$. Large signal:

$$V_{out}\approx V_{DD}-|V_{thp}|-
\sqrt{\frac{2(I_{B}-I_{IN}-I_{1})}
{\mu_{p}C_{ox}(W/L)_{2}}}$$

$M_{1}$ stays in saturation if
$V_{out}\ge V_{b}-V_{thn}$. $M_{2}$ easily
stays in saturation.

Small signal, saturation. For NMOS define
$I_{DS}$ drain to source:

$$i_{ds1}=g_{m1}v_{gs1}+g_{mb1}v_{bs1}+g_{ds1}v_{ds1}$$

$$v_{gs1}=-v_{x},\; v_{bs1}=-v_{x},\;
v_{ds1}=v_{out}-v_{x}$$

$$i_{ds1}=-G_{1}v_{x}+g_{ds1}v_{out} \tag{1}$$

Current enters drain, leaves source.

For PMOS define $I_{SD}$ source to drain:

$$i_{sd2}=g_{m2}v_{sg2}+g_{ds2}v_{sd2}$$

$$v_{sg2}=-v_{out},\; v_{sd2}=-v_{x}$$

$$i_{sd2}=-g_{m2}v_{out}-g_{ds2}v_{x} \tag{2}$$

Current enters source, leaves drain to $X$.

KCL at $X$. Currents leaving $X$:
to $R_{b}$: $v_{x}/R_{b}$, to $I_{in}$: $-i_{in}$,
to $M_{1}$ source: $-i_{ds1}$, to $M_{2}$ drain:
$-i_{sd2}$.

$$-i_{in}+\frac{v_{x}}{R_{b}}-i_{ds1}-i_{sd2}=0$$

$$i_{in}=\left[\frac1{R_{b}}+G_{1}+g_{ds2}\right]v_{x}
+(g_{m2}-g_{ds1})v_{out} \tag{3}$$

KCL at $Y$. To $R_{1}$: $v_{out}/R_{1}$,
to $M_{1}$ drain: $+i_{ds1}$, to gate: 0.

$$\frac{v_{out}}{R_{1}}+i_{ds1}=0$$

$$-G_{1}v_{x}+(g_{ds1}+1/R_{1})v_{out}=0 \tag{4}$$

i.e.

$$v_{x}=\frac{g_{ds1}+1/R_{1}}{G_{1}}v_{out}$$

No.

Viewed as digital it has no stable logic state.
Viewed as analog, let each inverter at the
trip point be

$$A(s) = \frac{-g_mR_o}{1+sR_oC_L} = \frac{-a}{1+s\tau}$$

with $a=g_mR_o$, $\tau=R_oC_L$.
The 3-stage loop gives for small signal

$$v_1(1+s\tau)=-av_3$$
$$v_2(1+s\tau)=-av_1$$
$$v_3(1+s\tau)=-av_2$$

i.e.

$$(1+s\tau)^3 + a^3=0$$

$$1+s\tau = -a \,, -a e^{j2\pi/3}\,, -a e^{j4\pi/3}$$

In particular

$$s\tau = -1 -a e^{\pm j2\pi/3}= -1+\frac{a}{2}\mp j a\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$$

The common analog equilibrium is unstable iff

$${\rm Re}\,s >0$$

i.e.

$$a>2$$

This is independent of $\tau=R_oC_L$.

In Barkhausen terms, the raw loop gain is

$$\left(\frac{-a}{1+s\tau}\right)^3$$

$540^{\circ}-3\tan^{-1}\omega\tau = 360^{\circ}$ requires

$$\tan^{-1}\omega_{osc}\tau = 60^{\circ}$$

$$\omega_{osc} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{\tau}= \frac{\sqrt{3}}{R_oC_L}$$

Magnitude at that frequency:

$$|A(j\omega_{osc})|^3
= \left(\frac{a}{\sqrt{1+(\omega_{osc}\tau)^2}}\right)^3
= \left(\frac{a}{2}\right)^3$$

$>1$ iff $a>2$, independent of $C_L$.

Arbitrarily large finite $C_L$ only makes
$\omega_{osc}\propto 1/C_L \to 0$ and the
startup growth rate

$${\rm Re}\,s = \frac{a/2-1}{\tau}\to 0^{+}$$

arbitrarily slow, but the circuit remains
unstable and oscillates.

answers.question: What happens to the phase noise if the three capacitors in Figure 5 are doubled?

answer.text:
Doubling all $C_L$ is time scaling.

With the same inverters the charge/discharge
current $I$ during a transition and the device
noise $ \overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f $ during a
transition are essentially unchanged.

Stage delay
$$ T_D \propto \frac{C_L V_{DD}}{I} $$
so
$$f_0 =\frac{1}{2NT_D} \propto \frac1{C_L} $$
is halved.

The max charge swing
$$q_{max} \approx C_L V_{DD}$$
is doubled.

In Hajimiri-Lee,
$$ {\cal L}(\Delta\omega) \propto 
 \frac{1}{q_{max}^{2}}\,
 \frac{\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f}{(\Delta\omega)^2} $$

The normalized waveform, and hence the ISF
$\Gamma$, is unchanged, just stretched in time.
$\overline{i_n^2}/\Delta f$ is unchanged.

Hence
$$ {\cal L} \propto \frac{1}{C_L^{2}} .$$

In Leeson terms $P_s$ is unchanged,
$f_0$ is halved:
$${\cal L} \propto \left(\frac{f_0}{\Delta f}\right)^2 \frac1{P_s}$$

At a given absolute $\Delta f$ the whole
$1/f^2$ and $1/f^3$ profile is lowered by

$$20\log 2 \approx 6\,{\rm dB},$$

i.e. a factor 4 in power.

{\sqrt{1+(\omega_1/\omega_{p1})^2}\,[1+(\omega_1/\omega_0)^2]} \tag{2}$$

Normal $C_L=0$: $\omega_{p1}=\omega_0$,
(1) gives $\arctan=60^\circ$, $\omega_1=\sqrt3\,\omega_0$,
$|T|=A_0^3/8$. If $A_0>2$, $|T|>1$: unstable,
oscillates.

Now let $\omega_{p1}\ll\omega_0$.
For any $\omega>0$ not extremely small,
$\arctan(\omega/\omega_{p1})\approx 90^\circ$.
Then (1) requires

$$2\arctan\frac{\omega_1}{\omega_0}\approx 90^\circ$$

i.e.

$$\omega_1\approx \omega_0 .$$

Put in (2):

$$|T(j\omega_1)|\approx \frac{A_0^3}{(\omega_1/\omega_{p1})\cdot 2}
 =\frac{A_0^3}{2}\frac{\omega_{p1}}{\omega_0}
 =\frac{A_0^3}{2}\frac{1}{1+C_L/C_0}\to 0$$

as $C_L\to\infty$.

In particular magnitude $<1$ for large $C_L$.
Phase condition can be met, magnitude condition
cannot. No $j\omega$ crossing with gain.

Indeed $(1+s\tau_L)(1+s\tau_0)^2+A_0^3=0$,
$\tau_L/\tau_0=K$, is stable by Routh-Hurwitz if

$$(1+2K)(2+K) > K(1+A_0^3)$$

i.e. $A_0^3 < 2/K+4+2K$.
For $K=1$ this is $A_0<2$, violated, unstable.
For $K\to\infty$ this is $A_0^3<2K$, satisfied.
Stable.

Intuitively this is dominant-pole compensation.
The 3-pole negative-feedback loop is unstable.
Making one pole dominant stabilizes it like
compensating an opamp. The circuit settles to the
linear DC point with all inverters at $V_M$ and
noise decays.

answer.text:
In the 3-stage inverter ring, let all $W$'s
scale by $S$.

The rail to rail swing is still $\approx V_{DD}$.

* load per stage: gate $+$ drain capacitance

$$C \propto W$$

$$C \to S\,C$$

* charge current in transition, square-law or
velocity saturated:

$$I_{D} \propto W$$

$$I \to S\,I$$

Hence the large signal delay per stage

$$T_{D}\approx \frac{C\,V_{DD}}{I}$$

is to first order unchanged:

$$T_{D} \to \frac{S}{S}T_{D}$$

$$f_{0}=\frac{1}{2NT_{D}} \approx {\rm const}$$

Energy per transition is $CV_{DD}^{2}$.

$$P_{DC}=Nf_{0}CV_{DD}^{2} \to S\,P_{DC}$$

With $S=2$, power doubles.

For phase noise, e.g. Hajimiri-Lee,

$$ {\cal L}(\Delta\omega)\propto
\frac{\Gamma_{rms}^{2}}{q_{max}^{2}}
\frac{\overline{i_{n}^{2}}/\Delta f}{(\Delta\omega)^{2}} $$

Normalized waveform, hence $\Gamma_{rms}$, is
unchanged.

Maximum charge swing:

$$q_{max}\approx C V_{DD}\propto W$$

$$q_{max}\to S\,q_{max}$$

MOS thermal noise when the device is on:

$$\frac{\overline{i_{n}^{2}}}{\Delta f}=4kT\gamma g_{m}$$

with, for the same $V_{GS}$ swing,

$$g_{m}\propto W$$

$$\frac{\overline{i_{n}^{2}}}{\Delta f}\to S\,\frac{\overline{i_{n}^{2}}}{\Delta f}$$

Same for $1/f$: $\overline{v_{n1/f}^{2}}\propto 1/WL$,
$\overline{i_{n1/f}^{2}}=g_{m}^{2}\overline{v_{n1/f}^{2}}\propto W$.

Hence

$${\cal L}\propto \frac{S}{S^{2}}=\frac{1}{S}$$

For $S=2$:

$${\cal L}\to \frac{1}{2}{\cal L}$$

i.e. 3-dB lower thermal $1/f^{2}$ and upconverted $1/f^{3}$ phase noise, for the same $f_{0}$ at twice the power.

charge from the supply.

$$ Q_{tot} = 3\, CL\, VDD $$

Average DC supply current:

$$ I_{DD} = \frac{Q_{tot}}{T_{0}} = 3\,CL\,VDD\,f_{0} $$

This is the switched-capacitor $V/I$.
To first order with $f_{0}$ held fixed,
the low frequency incremental conductance
is:

$$\frac{\partial I_{DD}}{\partial VDD} = 3\,CL\,f_{0}$$

Hence the resistance seen looking into
the supply:

$$R_{X} = \frac{1}{3\,CL\,f_{0}}$$

This is the switched-capacitor $1/fC$ resistor.
Dynamic power per stage is $C_{L}V_{DD}^{2}f_{0}$.

For $N=3$ stages in parallel, total average supply
current is

$$I_{avg} = 3\,C_{L}V_{DD}f_{0}$$

For a low-frequency perturbation $\Delta V_{DD}$,
treating $f_{0}$ as given, the change in charge
supplied per cycle is

$$\Delta Q = 3C_{L}\Delta V_{DD}$$

$$\Delta I_{avg} = \frac{\Delta Q}{T_{0}} = 3C_{L}f_{0}\,\Delta V_{DD}$$

Hence the low-frequency impedance looking into
the common supply is resistive:

$$R_{X} = \frac{\Delta V_{DD}}{\Delta I_{avg}} = \frac{1}{3C_{L}f_{0}}$$

For the ring oscillator in Figure 8, consider the small-signal resistance `RX`
seen looking into the supply node.

Use `CL` for the effective load capacitance at each internal oscillator node,
`f0` for the oscillation frequency, and `TD` for the delay of one inverter stage.

From the dynamic charging and discharging of the three load capacitances, one
can write

```text
RX ~= 1 / (3 f0 CL)
```

Somebody then argues that, because the circuit is oscillating, the path from
`VDD` to ground through the transistors is off for much of the cycle, so the
average resistance should be much higher than the MOS on-resistance or inverse
transconductance scale.

Do you agree with this argument?

answer.text:
No. The $1/(3f_0C_L)$ is already the
switched-$C$ equivalent, and it is on the order
of the on-resistance.

Per period $T_0=1/f_0$ each node charges once
from the supply:

$$ Q_{sup} = 3 \times C_L V_{DD} $$

$$ I_{avg} = \frac{Q_{sup}}{T_0}=3 f_0 C_L V_{DD} $$

Hence DC:

$$\frac{V_{DD}}{I_{avg}} = \frac{1}{3f_0 C_L}$$

Small signal $dV_{DD}/dI_{avg}$ is the same
to $O(1)$. $f_0$ itself increases with $V_{DD}$,
so it is even smaller.

For $N=3$,

$$f_0 =\frac{1}{2N T_D} = \frac{1}{6 T_D}$$

so

$$R_X \approx \frac{1}{3f_0 C_L} = \frac{2T_D}{C_L}$$

But $T_D$ is the $R_{on}C_L$ scale:

$$T_D \approx R_{eq} C_L $$

Elmore-like, where $R_{eq}$ is the effective
resistance of the MOS during its switching
trajectory, i.e. on-resistance, $1/g_m$ scale.
Indeed

$$R_X \approx 2 \frac{T_D}{C_L} \approx 2R_{eq}$$

It cannot be $\gg R_{on},1/g_m$. The $f_0$ in
the denominator is $\propto 1/R_{on}C_L$.

The fallacy is averaging $R(t)$.
$\langle R(t)\rangle$ is indeed huge because
$R_{off}\approx \infty$ most of the time.
What sets $V/I$ is $\langle I(t)\rangle$,
i.e. average conductance, charge delivered
per cycle.

In CMOS the supply current is not a VDD-to-gnd
DC current. It is displacement current VDD to $C_L$
when the PMOS is on, zero when it is off.
Off-time contributes zero current, not large $V/I$.
Short on-time with large on-current $\approx V_{DD}/R_{on}$
gives average current $\approx$ duty-cycle$/R_{on}$.

Roughly each PMOS conducts $\sim T_D/T_0\sim 1/6$
of the time. 3 stages:

$$\langle G\rangle \sim 3\times \frac16 \times \frac1{R_{on}}
 \sim \frac1{2R_{on}}$$

$$1/\langle G\rangle \sim 2R_{on}$$

$\langle 1/G\rangle \gg 1/\langle G\rangle$.

$$ R_X \sim 2 \frac{T_D}{C_L} \sim 2R_{eff} \sim \frac{V_{DD}}{I_D} \sim \frac1{g_m} $$

forcing $1/f_0C_L \sim R_{on}$.

Averaging $R(t)$ is the fallacy. The relevant
average is average current, i.e. average conductance.

answer.text:
In the StrongARM of Fig.9 let

* $X,Y$ be the drains of the n-latch $M_{3},M_{4}$,
* $P,Q$ be the sources of the n-latch / drains of
the input pair $M_{1},M_{2}$.

Precharge $CK=0$ puts $P,Q,X,Y$ to $V_{DD}$.
$M_{5},M_{6}$ are OFF.

On $CK=1$, $M_{7}$ goes ON, $S_{1-4}$ go OFF.
$M_{1,2}$ discharge $P,Q$ from $V_{DD}$.
As $P,Q$ fall $M_{3},M_{4}$ turn ON and start to
discharge $X,Y$ from $V_{DD}$.

$M_{5},M_{6}$ stay OFF until $X,Y$ common mode has
fallen by $\approx |V_{THP}|$. Up to that moment
the circuit is a dynamic amplifier with n-latch
positive feedback. The differential voltage
$\Delta V_{XY}$ developed at that moment divided by
$\Delta V_{in}$ is the voltage gain prior to
p-latch regeneration.

Put in small signal, $M_{5,6}$ OFF:

$ M_{3}: i_{d3}=g_{m3}(v_{y}-v_{p}) $
$ M_{4}: i_{d4}=g_{m3}(v_{x}-v_{q}) $

$$C_{X}\frac{d}{dt}v_{x} = -i_{d3} $$
$$C_{X}\frac{d}{dt}v_{y} = -i_{d4} $$
$$C_{P}\frac{d}{dt}v_{p} = -i_{d1}+i_{d3} $$
$$C_{P}\frac{d}{dt}v_{q} = -i_{d2}+i_{d4} $$

For $\Delta X=v_{x}-v_{y}$, $\Delta P=v_{p}-v_{q}$,
$v_{id}=v_{in1}-v_{in2}$, $g_{ds}\approx 0$:

$$C_{X}\frac{d\Delta X}{dt}= g_{m3}(\Delta X+\Delta P)$$
$$C_{P}\frac{d\Delta P}{dt}= -g_{m1}v_{id}-g_{m3}(\Delta X+\Delta P)$$

i.e. with $Y=\Delta X+\Delta P$,

$$\frac{dY}{dt}= g_{m3}\left(\frac1{C_{X}}-\frac1{C_{P}}\right)Y
-\frac{g_{m1}}{C_{P}}v_{id}$$

The n-pair pole is

$$a = g_{m3}\left(\frac1{C_{X}}-\frac1{C_{P}}\right)$$

Larger $C_{P},C_{Q}$ :

* makes the common-mode discharge $I_{0}/(C_{X}+C_{P})$
slower, so the time to fall $|V_{THP}|$ and turn
$M_{5,6}$ ON,

$$t_{1}\approx |V_{THP}|\,(C_{X}+C_{P})/I_{0}$$

is longer, i.e. longer integration / amplification
time;

* makes $1/C_{P}$ smaller, i.e. $a$ more positive.
Physically $P,Q$ become a better ac ground for the
sources of $M_{3},M_{4}$, increasing their effective
$g_{m}$ and the n-latch positive feedback.

Both effects increase the differential signal built
up before p-regeneration starts:

$$\Delta X(t_{1})/v_{id}$$

grows with $C_{P}=C_{Q}$.

In first order you trade speed/power for pre-regeneration
gain.

answer.text:
In Fig.9 the $CK=0$ phase precharges

$$P,Q,X,Y \to V_{DD}$$

$M_{7}$ off, $S_{1}-S_{4}$ on, $M_{3}-M_{6}$ off.

Let $CK$ go high. $S_{1}-S_{4}$ off, $M_{7}$ on.
Let $I_{CM}=I_{SS}/2$ be the common mode
drain current of $M_{1},M_{2}$ and

$$I_{D1}-I_{D2} = g_{m1}\Delta V_{in}$$

$P$ and $Q$ must discharge from $V_{DD}$.

$M_{3}$ has $G=Y\approx V_{DD}$, $S=P$.
It is off until

$$V_{GS3}=V_{Y}-V_{P}>V_{thn}$$

i.e. $P$ has fallen by $\approx V_{thn}$. Same for $M_{4}$.
During this time $t<t_{1}$, $I_{D3}=I_{D4}=0$ :

$$C_{P}\frac{dV_{P}}{dt}=-I_{D1}, \quad C_{X}\frac{dV_{X}}{dt}=0$$

So

$$t_{1}\approx \frac{C_{PQ}V_{thn}}{I_{CM}} $$

X,Y stay at $V_{DD}$ but P,Q develop a differential:

$$C_{PQ}\frac{d(V_{P}-V_{Q})}{dt}=-(I_{D1}-I_{D2})$$

At $t=t_{1}$ :

$$(V_{P}-V_{Q})_{1} \approx -\frac{g_{m1}\Delta V_{in}}{I_{CM}}V_{thn}$$

After $t_{1}$, $M_{3},M_{4}$ turn on and $X,Y$
start to discharge:

$$\begin{aligned}
C_{P}\frac{dV_{P,CM}}{dt} &= I_{D3,CM}-I_{CM}\\
C_{X}\frac{dV_{X,CM}}{dt} &= -I_{D3,CM}
\end{aligned}$$

$M_{3}$ cascodes $M_{1}$. To first order $P$ must
track $Y$ to keep $V_{GS3}$ to support current.
$P$ and $X$ fall together at

$$\frac{dV}{dt}\approx -\frac{I_{CM}}{C_{PQ}+C_{XY}}$$

Regeneration by $M_{5},M_{6}$ does not start
until $X$ or $Y$ has fallen by $|V_{thp}|$ below
$V_{DD}$, i.e.

$$\Delta t \approx \frac{(C_{PQ}+C_{XY})|V_{thp}|}{I_{CM}}$$

Total amplification time before the PMOS
latch turns on:

$$t_{amp}=t_{1}+\Delta t\approx
\frac{C_{PQ}V_{thn}+ (C_{PQ}+C_{XY})|V_{thp}|}{I_{CM}}$$

It is proportional to $C_{PQ}$.

During $t_{amp}$ the pair $M_{1}-M_{2}$ is
integrating its differential current onto
the output caps. Roughly, with $M_{5,6}$ off,

$$C_{XY}\frac{d(V_{X}-V_{Y})}{dt}\approx -(I_{D3}-I_{D4})\approx -(I_{D1}-I_{D2})$$

i.e. an integrator of gain $g_{m1}/C_{XY}$ :

$$|V_{X}-V_{Y}|(t) \approx \frac{g_{m1}\Delta V_{in}}{C_{XY}}t$$

Evaluated at $t=t_{amp}$, the differential
built up just before regeneration, the
"initial" voltage gain, is

$$A_{v0}= \frac{|V_{X}-V_{Y}|_{t_{amp}}}{\Delta V_{in}}
\approx \frac{g_{m1}t_{amp}}{C_{XY}}$$

$$\approx \frac{g_{m1}}{I_{CM}}\left[|V_{thp}|
+\frac{C_{PQ}}{C_{XY}}(V_{thn}+|V_{thp}|)\right]$$

Larger $C_{PQ}$ requires more charge from
$M_{1,2}$ to get the same $V_{thn},|V_{thp}|$
drop. The common-mode discharge is slower,
$t_{amp}$ is longer, the $g_{m}\Delta V_{in}$
has more time to integrate.

Hence increasing capacitance at $P,Q$
increases the pre-regeneration voltage
gain, at the expense of delay in both
evaluate and reset phases.

answers.question: In the circuit of Figure 10, does the speed improve or degrade if we increase the widths of the clocked transistors?

answer.text:
The two 4-high stacks are tri-state inverters.

* Left: in $=Z$, out $=X$, on for $CK=1$
* Right: in $=X$, out $=Y$, on for $\overline{CK}=1$

with $Z=\overline{Y}$ from $\rm Inv_{3}$.
It is a dynamic toggle. For $CK=1$, $X=\overline Z$ is
driven while $Y$ is floating. For $CK=0$, $Y=\overline X$
is driven while $X$ is floating. $f_{max}$ is set by
the $Z\to X$ delay in the half cycle $CK=1$ and the
$X\to Y\to Z$ delay in the half cycle $CK=0$.

During transparency the clock device is on, in series
with the data device. E.g. for the $Z\to X$ pull down:

$$ V_{DD}\!-\!GND : Z\to M_{1} \to CK{\rm -NMOS} \to X $$

The current that (dis)charges $X$ is set by the
series combination of the data FET, whose $W$ is
fixed, and the clock FET.

The load at the dynamic node is

* drain diffusion of the clock NMOS and clock PMOS
  itself,
* input gate cap of the next data FETs,
* wire cap.

i.e. $C_{X,Y} = C_{0}+C_{d,clk}W_{clk}$.

The Elmore delay is roughly

$$ \tau \approx (R_{data}+R_{clk})(C_{0}+C_{d}W_{clk}) $$

$$ R_{clk} \propto 1/W_{clk} $$

Widening the clock FET lowers $R_{clk}$ but directly
widens $C_{X,Y}$. The charging current soon becomes
limited by $R_{data}$. Beyond $W_{clk}\approx W_{data}$
you add self-loading with essentially no more current:

$$ \frac{\partial \tau}{\partial W_{clk}}
\approx R_{data}C_{d} - \frac{kC_{0}}{W_{clk}^{2}} >0 $$

so $\tau_{Z\to X}$ and $\tau_{X\to Y}$ grow.

In addition, $X$ and $Y$ are dynamic. At turn-off
the clock FET dumps channel charge and $C_{ov}$ clock
feedthrough onto the node that is about to float and
drive the next stage for a full half cycle. Larger
$W_{clk}$ means larger droop/jump on the held $X,Y$,
smaller overdrive for the following data FET/$Inv_{3}$,
slower transition.

Hence larger clocked devices slow the (dis)charge of
$X,Y$ and lower $f_{max}$.

answers.question:
For the divide-by-two topology in Figure 11, does the speed improve or degrade
if we increase the widths of the clocked transistors, i.e. the transistors whose
gates are driven by `CK` or `CKbar`?

answer.text:
In Fig.11 the middle devices are the signal devices.
The top PMOS and bottom NMOS are in series with them
and are on alternately.

* $CK=1$: left tristate on, right tristate off.
$B = \bar A$, $C$ is floating.
* $CK=0$: left tristate off, right tristate on.
$C = \bar B$, $B$ is floating.

$A=\bar C$ through the static inverter. $B$ and $C$
are stored dynamically on the drain capacitance of
the OFF tristate.

When on, the clock device is just a series resistor.
Once its $R_{on}$ is $<< R_{on}$ of the signal device,
making it wider does not make the stage appreciably
stronger.

When off, it hurts. Consider the left stage.

$CK=1$, $A=0$, $B=1$. $M_{sig,n}$ is off, $M_{ck,n}$
is on. The internal node $S_x$ between them is at 0V.

Go to $CK=0$. Left stage is off, $B$ floats at $V_{DD}$.
The loop then makes $A$ go to 1. $M_{sig,n}$ turns on
while $M_{ck,n}$ is off. $B$ is shorted to $S_x$:

```
B ~ VDD , C_B   <-->   S_x ~ 0 , C_Sx
```

Charge sharing:

$$\Delta V_B \approx V_{DD}\frac{C_{Sx}}{C_{Sx}+C_B}$$

$C_B$ is the drain of the signal devices + fanout,
independent of $W_{ck}$. $C_{Sx}$ is the source of
the signal device + drain of the clock device,
$\propto W_{ck}$.

Larger $W_{ck}$ means larger droop of the held 1.
Similarly larger $W_{ck,p}$ means larger rise of
a held 0 via the $S_y$ node between $M_{ck,p}$
and $M_{sig,p}$.

$B$ is the gate drive of the stage that is currently
on. A degraded high means its NMOS gets less $V_{GS}$
and its PMOS is not fully off. Its pull-down becomes
weaker and slower, with crowbar current. A degraded
low does the converse.

Hence the enabled-stage delay gets longer, the
half-cycle must be longer, $f_{max}$ falls.

In addition $C_{clk} \propto W_{ck}$ loads the
clock, slowing its edges.

There is no contention to overcome as in a static
latch. Optimum is essentially minimum $W_{ck}$. Increasing
it degrades speed.

For the divide-by-two topology in Figure 11, does the speed improve or degrade
if we increase the widths of the clocked transistors, i.e. the transistors whose
gates are driven by `CK` or `CKbar`?

answer.text:
This is a $C^{2}$MOS master-slave loop.

* left gated inverter: $V_{DD}$-P$_{\overline{CK}}$-P$_{in}$-N$_{in}$-N$_{CK}$-GND
* right gated inverter: $V_{DD}$-P$_{CK}$-P$_{in}$-N$_{in}$-N$_{\overline{CK}}$-GND

plus the static inverter. When $CK=1$ the left is
an inverter and the right is floating, when $CK=0$
the opposite.

Consider one gated inverter in evaluation, e.g. left
with $CK=1$. It has to charge/discharge the capacitance
at its output:

* its own drain diffusion of $P_{in},N_{in}$
* the gate capacitance of $P_{in},N_{in}$ of the next stage
* wiring

with current supplied through a switch in series:

$$V_{DD} - R_{on,Pck} - R_{on,Pin} - C_{L} $$
$$C_{L} - R_{on,Nin} - R_{on,Nck} - GND $$

The propagation delay in evaluation is roughly

$$t_{eval} \approx (R_{sig}+R_{ck})C_{L} + R_{ck}C_{int}$$

where $C_{int}$ is the capacitance of the series node
between the clock device and the signal device.

The $CK,\overline{CK}$ devices are not connected to the
critical output node. Their drains see only the internal
series nodes, isolated by the cascode $P_{in},N_{in}$
devices. To first order they do not load $C_{L}$.

Widening them therefore :

* does not increase the load seen by the previous stage,
* does not increase $C_{L}$,
* decreases $R_{ck}\propto 1/W_{ck}$.

The evaluation current and $dV/dt$ on $C_{L}$ go up,
$t_{eval}$ goes down. Each half-cycle needs one
evaluation, so

$$f_{max}\propto 1/t_{eval}$$

goes up.

In contrast to e.g. a CML latch, where the clock pair
drains are on the output, here extra clock-device
capacitance is hidden from the output.

The improvement saturates when $R_{ck}\ll R_{sig}$.
Price is larger clock load, power, and internal-node
capacitance.

rises and the delay falls.

Crucially the $CK$ device drain does {\it not}

It connects to the source of the cascode signal
device, a node already precharged to $V_{DD}$ or

$$t_{d} \approx (R_{CK}+R_{SIG})C_{out}$$

$C_{out} = C_{db,SIG}+C_{g,next}+C_{wire}$
is independent of $W_{CK}$.

Extra $W_{CK}$ puts extra diffusion $C$ only on
the non-switching internal $V_{DD}/GND$-side node.
No extra self loading on $M/R_{out}$, no extra

decreases monotonically to $R_{SIG}C_{out}$.

on the clock driver.

answers.question: Analyze the arrangement in Figure 12(a).

answer.text:
The circuit is a master-slave toggle flip-flop.

Put

* $A=$ output of right-most inverter = left of $CK$ switch
* $B=$ right of $CK$ switch = input of $Inv_{1}$
* $C=$ output of $Inv_{1}=$ left of $\overline{CK}$ switch
* $D=$ right of $\overline{CK}$ switch = input of next inverter
* $E=$ output of next inverter = input of right-most inverter

Idealize the switches as closed for $CK=1$ and
$\overline{CK}=1$ respectively, i.e. complementary.

$$C=\bar B, \quad E=\bar D, \quad A=\bar E = D$$

$M$: $CK$ switch + $Inv_{1}$ + capacitance at $B$
is an inverting dynamic latch.
$S$: $\overline{CK}$ switch + 2 inverters + capacitance
at $D$ is a non-inverting dynamic latch.

$B$ and $D$ store on gate capacitance when driven
open. The cascade $M\to S$ inverts once, and
output $A$ is fed back to $M$ input. This is
a $D$-flip-flop with $Q_{next}=\bar Q$.

Assume break-before-make, i.e. the two switches
are never on together.

$CK=1$: SW1 ON, SW2 OFF.
Master transparent, slave holding.

* $B = A$
* $C = \bar A$, driven but disconnected
* $D$ floating, holding old value $D_{old}$
* $E=\bar D_{old}$, $A = D_{old}$ driven

In steady state $A=D_{old}$, so master samples
slave: $B=D_{old}$.

$CK=0$: SW1 OFF, SW2 ON.
Master holding, slave transparent.

* $B$ floating, holding $B_{old}=A_{old}$ sampled
in previous phase
* $C=\bar B_{old}$ still driven by $Inv_{1}$
* $D = C =\bar B_{old}$ through SW2
* $A = D =\bar B_{old}$

The loop is open at SW1.

Hence on the $1\to 0$ transition of $CK$:

$$B_{new\,held}=A_{old}$$
$$A_{new}=D_{new}=\bar B_{old}=\bar A_{old}$$

Example: $A=1$.

$CK=1$: $B=1,\;C=0$. $D=1$, $A=1$ held by slave.
$CK\downarrow 0$: $B$ holds $1$, $C=0$, $D=0$,
after SW2+2 inv delay $A=0$.
$CK=1$: $B=0$, $C=1$. $D=0$, $A=0$ held.
$CK\downarrow 0$: $B$ holds $0$, $C=1$, $D=1$,
$A=1$.

Master is transparent on high, slave transparent
on low. The whole is negative-edge-triggered.
Output changes only on falling edge, after

$$t_{CK\downarrow\to A}\approx t_{SW}+t_{Inv2}+t_{Inv3}$$

It toggles once per $CK$ period:

$$f_A = f_{CK}/2$$

$A$ is $Q$, $E$ is $\bar Q$. Change occurs only
on one $CK$ edge, so distance between output
transitions is $T_{CK}$. Duty $\approx 50\%$
independent of $CK$ duty, provided min pulse
widths are met.

This requires:

High phase long enough to set $C$:
$$T_{high,min} > t_{SW1}+t_{Inv1}$$

Low phase long enough to set $D$ and $A$:
$$T_{low,min} > t_{SW2}+t_{Inv2}+t_{Inv3}$$

This sets $f_{max}$.

It is dynamic. $B$ must hold during $CK=0$,
$D$ must hold during $CK=1$. Off leakage,
junction leakage, subthreshold, noise discharge
the floating capacitance. Hence

$$f_{min} \gg I_{leak}/C\,\Delta V$$

typically minimum kHz-MHz. Clock cannot be stopped.

Race: if SW1 and SW2 are ON together the loop
is $Inv_{1}-Inv_{2}-Inv_{3}$ closed, i.e. 3-inverter
ring oscillator. In practice short overlap corrupts
state:

* at fall: $A$ starts to change to $\bar B$ while
$B$ still connected to $A$, $B$ is corrupted.
SW1 must open before $A$ changes, i.e. overlap
$< t_{SW2}+t_{Inv2}+t_{Inv3}$.
* at rise: $B$ changes to new $A$, $C$ changes,
while $D$ still connected to $C$, $D$ is corrupted.
SW2 must open before $C$ changes, i.e. overlap
$< t_{SW1}+t_{Inv1}$.

Hence true non-overlapping two phase clocks are
required. A simple inverter-generated $\overline{CK}$
gives $\sim$ one inverter of overlap and is marginal
at high speed.

Subject to $f_{min}<f<f_{max}$ and non-overlap,
(a) is a self-starting dynamic $\div 2$.

answer.text:
This is a single phase master-slave dynamic
$D$-flip-flop connected as $D=\bar Q$.

Put

* $SW_{1}$ : $CK$, $SW_{2}$ : $\overline{CK}$
* $A$ : input of $Inv_{1}$, i.e. right of $SW_{1}$
* $B$ : output of $Inv_{1}$, i.e. left of $SW_{2}$
* $C$ : input of $Inv_{2}$, i.e. right of $SW_{2}$
* $D$ : output of $Inv_{2}$ = input of $Inv_{3}$
* $Q_{b}$ : output of $Inv_{3}$

$Q_{b}$ is fed back to the left of $SW_{1}$.
So $D$-input of the flop is $Q_{b}$.

$SW_{1}+Inv_{1}$ is a dynamic latch.
$SW_{2}+Inv_{2}$ is a dynamic latch.

When the series switch is ON the latch is transparent,
the $C_{g}$ of the following inverter is driven.
When the series switch is OFF the information is
left as charge on:

$C_{A}$ : gate cap of $Inv_{1}$ + switch parasitics
$C_{C}$ : gate cap of $Inv_{2}$ + switch parasitics

There is no DC feedback path. This is the dynamic
storage.

$Inv_{3}$ is the $\bar Q$ output driver. $D$ is the
$Q$ output. There are 3 inversions round the loop,
so $D\to Q_{b}$ is inverting.

Idealize switches and inverters. Let $CK$ and
$\overline{CK}$ be non-overlapping, never 1 together.

$CK=1$ : $SW_{1}$ ON, $SW_{2}$ OFF.
Master transparent, slave hold.

$$A = Q_{b}$$
$$B = \bar A = \bar Q_{b}$$
$C$ floating, held at previous value $C_{p}$:
$$D = \bar C_{p}$$
$$Q_{b}= \bar D = C_{p}$$

i.e. output holds old slave value while master
acquires $\bar Q_{b}$ at $B$.

Both OFF dead time: $A$ and $C$ hold.

$CK=0$ : $SW_{1}$ OFF, $SW_{2}$ ON.
Master hold, slave transparent.

$A$ floating, held at $Q_{b,old}=C_{p}$ sampled
in previous phase:
$$B = \bar A = \bar C_{p}$$
$$C = B = \bar C_{p}$$
$$D = \bar C = C_{p}$$
$$Q_{b}= \bar D = \bar C_{p}$$

i.e. the new $B$ is transferred to slave.

On the next $CK=1$, $SW_{1}$ ON, $SW_{2}$ OFF:
$$A = Q_{b,new}= \bar C_{p}$$
$$B = C_{p}$$
$C$ held at $\bar C_{p}$, so $Q_{b}$ stays at
$\bar C_{p}$.

In short:

* $CK$ high: $Q_{b}=C_{p}$, master follows.
* $CK$ high to low: slave follows master.
* $CK$ low to high: no change.

This is a falling-edge triggered $D$-FF.

Since $D=Q_{b}$ :

Let $Q_{b}[n]$ be value after $n$th falling edge.
$C_{p}$ before $(n+1)$th falling edge is $Q_{b}[n]$.

After the edge:

$$Q_{b}[n+1] = \bar C_{p} = \overline{Q_{b}[n]}$$

It toggles every $CK$ cycle. This is $T=1$.
$$f_{Q}=f_{Q_{b}}=f_{CK}/2$$

$Q$ at output of $Inv_{2}$ and $Q_{b}$ at output
of $Inv_{3}$ are complementary 50% duty half-rate
clocks, apart from $t_{clk-Q}$ delay:

$$t_{clk-Q}=t_{SW2}+t_{Inv2}(+t_{Inv3}\;\text{for}\;Q_{b})$$

After power up first 1-2 edges flush undefined
initial charge and it locks into divide-by-2.

This works only if:

1. Break-before-make clocking. $SW_{1}$ and $SW_{2}$
must never be ON together.

If both ON, $Q_{b}\to SW_{1}\to Inv_{1}\to SW_{2}
\to Inv_{2}\to Inv_{3}\to Q_{b}$ is a closed
combinatorial loop of 3 inverters, i.e. a ring
oscillator with period $\approx 2(t_{p1}+t_{p2}+t_{p3})$.
Even brief overlap gives race-through from $D$ to $Q$ in
the same phase, corrupting the master-slave isolation.
In practice $CK,\overline{CK}$ must be generated
non-overlapping.

This sets the race requirement: $SW_{1}$ must open
before $SW_{2}$ closes at fall, and $SW_{2}$ must
open before $SW_{1}$ closes at rise.

2. Maximum frequency: evaluation time.

During high, $B$ must settle:
$$T_{high} > t_{SW1}+t_{Inv1}+t_{setup,slave}$$

During low, $C,D,Q_{b}$ must settle:
$$T_{low} > t_{SW2}+t_{Inv2}+t_{Inv3}$$

for next sampling. Approx $f_{max}\sim1/(T_{high,min}+
T_{low,min})$.

3. Minimum frequency: leakage.

In hold, $A$ floats for $\approx T_{low}$,
$C$ floats for $\approx T_{high}$. Charge leaks
via subthreshold, junction, gate leakage:

$$\Delta V \approx I_{leak}T_{hold}/C_{store}$$

Must stay within inverter noise margin. Storage
cap is only a gate cap, very noise, clock-feedthrough
and charge-injection sensitive. Hence the divider
fails at DC and low speed. It has a bandpass
frequency characteristic.

In transistor form switches are usually TGs needing
true and complement clocks. Single nMOS passes
weak $1$, degrading high noise margin of dynamic
node.

Advantage: no contention, small area, fast, low
power, ideal for high speed $/2$ prescaler.
Disadvantage: dynamic, ratio-less but leaky,
needs careful non-overlap clocks, cannot be
stopped.

wired as a toggle, made with dynamic latches.

* $A=$ output of last inverter = overall output $OUT$
  = left of $CK$ switch
* $B=$ right of $CK$ switch = input of $Inv_1$
* $C=$ output of $Inv_1=$ left of $\overline{CK}$ switch
* $D=$ right of $\overline{CK}$ switch = input of $Inv_2$
* $E=$ output of $Inv_2$ = input of $Inv_3$
* $OUT=$ output of $Inv_3$

$SW_1$ is ON for $CK=1$, OFF for $CK=0$.
$SW_2$ is ON for $CK=0$, OFF for $CK=1$.
Ideally break-before-make.

That is:

* Master dynamic latch: $SW_1$ + $Inv_1$.
  Storage is the parasitic capacitance at $B$.
* Slave dynamic latch: $SW_2$ + $Inv_2$.
  Storage is the parasitic capacitance at $D$.
* Extra output inverter $Inv_3$.
* Feedback $OUT$ to $SW_1$ input.

A dynamic latch = switch in series with inverter.
When switch is ON latch is transparent, when switch
is OFF the previous voltage is held floating on the
gate capacitance.

Here the two latches are in opposite phase, so
there is never a transparent path $A\to OUT$.
It is an edge-triggered D-FF.

Counting inversions $B\to C\to D\to E\to OUT$:

$$ B \xrightarrow{Inv_1} \bar B \xrightarrow{Inv_2}
 \overline{\bar B} \xrightarrow{Inv_3} \bar B $$

i.e. $D$-to-$Q$ is inverting. With $D=Q$ connected,
$$Q_{next} = \bar Q$$
a $T=1$ flip-flop.

In detail:

$CK=1$: $SW_1$ ON, $SW_2$ OFF.

$$B = A = OUT_{old}$$
$$C = \bar B = \overline{OUT_{old}}$$
$D$ holds its old value, $OUT = D_{held}$.

Master samples $OUT$, slave holds.

$CK=0$: $SW_1$ OFF, $SW_2$ ON.

$B$ floats and holds the value acquired during $CK=1$,
$Inv_1$ continues to drive:

$$C = \bar B$$
$$D = C$$
$$E = \bar D,\quad OUT = \bar E = D$$

i.e.
$$OUT = D = C = \bar B$$

Slave samples master, master holds.

Put together over a full cycle. Let $OUT_n$ be the
value held during $CK=1$:

$CK=1$: $B_n=OUT_n$, $C_n=\overline{OUT_n}$,
$OUT_n = D_{n-1/2}$ held.

Fall to $CK=0$:
$B$ holds $OUT_n$, $D=\overline{OUT_n}$,
$$OUT_{n+1/2}= \overline{OUT_n}$$

Rise to $CK=1$ next cycle:
$B=OUT_{n+1/2}=\overline{OUT_n}$,
$C=OUT_n$, $SW_2$ OFF, $D$ holds $\overline{OUT_n}$,
$$OUT_{n+1}=D=\overline{OUT_n}=OUT_{n+1/2}$$

So:

* nothing changes on the rising edge,
* output toggles on the falling edge.

After one or two starting cycles independent of the
initial floating voltages, the circuit settles into:

$$OUT[k+1] = \overline{OUT[k]} \text{ on each H-to-L of CK}$$

This is a negative-edge-triggered divide-by-2.
$f_{OUT}=f_{CK}/2$, period $2T_{CK}$. Since toggling
is on successive falling edges spaced by $T_{CK}$,
duty becomes 50%.

$CK$-to-$Q$ delay on the falling edge is

$$t_{CK\to Q} \approx t_{SW}+t_{Inv2}+t_{Inv3}.$$

For correct operation the half cycles must allow
propagation:

* $T_{HIGH} > t_{SW}+t_{Inv1}$ : $B\to C$ must settle
  before $SW_2$ closes,
* $T_{LOW} > t_{SW}+t_{Inv2}+t_{Inv3}$ : $C\to D\to OUT$
  must settle before $SW_1$ closes.

This sets $f_{max}$. With TGs and 2-transistor
inverters this is only $\sim 10$ transistors, hence
fast, low power, used as high speed prescaler.

It is fully dynamic. When $SW_1$ is OFF, $B$ floats;
$A=OUT=\bar B$, i.e. there is voltage across the OFF
switch. When $SW_2$ is OFF, $D$ floats; $C=\bar D$.
Leakage through the OFF switch, subthreshold and
junction leakage of the floating capacitance,
coupling and clock feedthrough via the switch
overlap capacitance, supply noise, will destroy
the state if the phase is held too long.

In particular:

* long $CK=0$: master node $B$ leaks,
* long $CK=1$: slave node $D$ leaks.

Hence a minimum clock frequency / maximum hold time

$$\Delta V \approx I_{leak} T_{hold}/C < \text{noise margin}$$

The clock cannot be stopped. Turn-on also
shorts a driver to the opposite-valued floating
capacitor: e.g. just before rise $B=\overline{OUT}$,
$SW_1$ closing shorts them; $Inv_3$ must overwrite $B$.
Just before fall $C=\bar D$, $SW_2$ closing shorts
them; $Inv_1$ must overwrite $D$. This is normal
charge-sharing overwriting, no DC fight, but needs
active drivers.

Also the two switches must never be ON together for
long. Both ON closes a loop of 3 inverters in unity
feedback - a ring oscillator. With transmission gates
the complementary control guarantees essentially
one ON, one OFF, apart from brief race-through
during the clock transition. Fast clock edges and
inverter delay make the race harmless.

In short: ideal toggle D-FF $\div 2$, but volatile.
That is why (b) adds - in red - a weak feedback
inverter $C\to B$ anti-parallel to $Inv_1$. It makes
the master a static cross-coupled latch, holding $B$
indefinitely for $CK=0$ idle. The slave in (b) is
still dynamic.

* CK on, CKB off: $B=A$, $C=\bar A$, $D$ floating
* CK off, CKB on: $B$ floating, $D=C$, $A=D$ through

loads $C$ and its drain loads $A$. $Inv_{1}$
now sees larger fanout capacitance, the output
buffer sees larger load capacitance. Delay of

the divider loop, goes up.

2. Wrong-phase latching - ratioed write.
$A$-CK switch-$B$ - $Inv_{1}$ - $C$ - red - $A$
has 2 inversions.

When the CK switch is ON, the loop is closed.
That is when the master should be transparent.
Instead you have positive feedback holding the
old $A$. The output inverter must overpower
the red inverter to write a new $B,C$.

Write becomes ratioed: slower edge, crowbar
current, more power, larger setup / clk-to-Q.

When the CK switch is OFF, the loop is open
and $B$ is still floating. The leakage failure
at low $f_{clk}$ is not cured, $D$ is still
dynamic either.

in transparency. Loop delay increases, maximum
divide frequency drops, power goes up.

answer.text:
In (a) you have a dynamic toggle flip-flop.

* `CK=1`: master switch on, slave switch off.
Master samples, slave holds on the gate cap
at the input of the slave.
* `CK=0`: master switch off, slave switch on.
Master holds on the gate cap at the input
of $Inv_1$, call it $A$, slave samples.

$A$ and $B$, the input of the slave, are floating
for half a period. That is what limits $f_{min}$:
leakage kills the state.

A staticizer for the master is a weak inverter
from the output of $Inv_{1}$, $M$, back to
its input $A$, i.e. to the node **after** the
$CK$ switch:

* switch open: $Inv_1$ + weak inverter is a
closed latch, restores leakage.
* switch closed: input driver overpowers the
weak inverter and writes the latch.

That costs you:

* $C_{g}+C_{d}$ of the weak inverter on $A$ and $M$,
* contention during write,

i.e. larger write/setup delay, larger Clk-Q
delay around the toggle loop, lower $f_{max}$,
crowbar power, for $f_{min}\to 0$.

The red inverter as drawn is **not** that.
It goes from $M$ to $D$, the node **before**
the $CK$ switch.

1. No hold: When the master must hold, $CK=0$,
the switch is open. The floating node $A$ is
still floating. The red puts no DC path on $A$.
It does not cure leakage. $f_{min}$ is not improved.

2. Load: It hangs directly on $M$, the output of
$Inv_1$, and on $D$, the output of the divider.
$Inv_1$ delay up, slave load up, loop delay up.
Clk-to-Q and setup of the toggle get larger.
$f_{max}$ goes down.

3. Loss of isolation: It is an always-on path
across the sampling switch. With input left,
output right, $M = \overline D$ through the red
in parallel with $D\to$switch$\to Inv_1\to M$.

* $CK=1$, transparent: parallel drive, no fight.
* $CK=0$, hold: switch open, slave closed.
Red still forces $M=\overline D$ while $Inv_1$
tries to hold $M = \overline{A_{old}}$.
But slave transparent forces $D = M$.
You get $D \to$red$\to M\to$slave 2 inv$\to D$,
a 3-inversion loop, contended by $Inv_1$.
In essence the master can never hold, the circuit
tends to contend/ring instead of divide.

In either direction it fights the wanted state
in one phase, draws contention current, slows
the transition, can flip the node. To survive
you must make it very weak, in which case it is
pure capacitive load + power for no static benefit.

Moved one node to the right, to $A$, weak, it
would be a conventional keeper: lower $f_{max}$
for static operation.

answers.question:
In Figure 12(b), somebody answers:

> The red inverter acts as a keeper, forming a cross-coupled latch with `Inv1`.
> This removes the minimum clock frequency requirement due to leakage.

But the input of the red inverter is not tied to the output of `Inv1`.

Do you agree with this answer? What is the actual role of the red inverter?

answer.text:
No. It is not a keeper and it does not make
anything static.

Call:

* `A` = divider output = left side of `CK` switch
* `B` = right side of `CK` switch = input of `Inv1`,
  master dynamic node
* `C` = output of `Inv1` = left side of `CKB` switch
* `D` = right side of `CKB` switch = input of slave,
  slave dynamic node

`CK=1`: master transparent, slave hold.
`B=A`, `C=~A`, `D` floats.
`CK=0`: master hold, slave transparent.
`B` floats, `C=~B`, `D=C`, `A=D` after 2 inversions.

A keeper for the master would have to be anti-parallel
to `Inv1`:

```
C -> red input, red output -> B
```

so that when the `CK` switch opens, `Inv1` and red
hold `B/C`.

That is not what is drawn. The red inverter is drawn
pointing forward, in parallel with the master:

```
red input = A , red output = C
```

Its output is shorted to the output of `Inv1`.
Its input is the divider output, before the `CK`
switch, not `C`.

So there is no cross-coupled pair. In particular
red touches neither dynamic node `B` nor `D`.
It cannot replenish their leakage. `B` still floats
with `CK=0`, `D` still floats with `CK=1`. The
minimum frequency due to leakage remains.

What it does:

`CK=1`, switch closed: `B=A`. Then

```
Inv1: C = ~B = ~A
red : C = ~A
```

The two inverters drive `C` in parallel with the same
value. Redundant drive.

`CK=0`, master hold, slave transparent: `B` holds
old `A0`, `C` should stay `~A0`. But the slave
becomes transparent and toggles:

```
D = C = ~A0 ,  A = D = ~A0
```

Now

```
Inv1 drives C = ~B = ~A0  = correct
red  drives C = ~A = ~~A0 = A0 = opposite
```

Red drives the wrong value. Similarly, during `CK=0`
red + the two slave inverters close:

```
C -> CKB switch -> slave inv -> slave inv -> A -> red -> C
```

i.e. 3 inversions in a loop, a 3-stage ring, fighting
`Inv1` which also drives `C`.

In other words red is on the wrong side of both
switches:

* as a master keeper it should drive `B`, it drives `C`
  from `A`;
* as a slave keeper it should drive `D`, it drives `C`
  before the `CKB` switch. It drives `D` only when the
  switch is already closed and `D` needs no help, and
  is disconnected from `D` when the switch opens and
  `D` floats.

For the divider to still divide, red must be made
weak so `Inv1` overpowers it during `CK=0`. Then it
is just ratioed contention: static current for half
the cycle, slower toggling, degraded noise margin,
no static storage. If strong, it flips `C`, which
flips `D` and `A`, which flips `C` again - malfunction/
oscillation.

To make it static you need `C->B` around the master
and `A->D` around the slave, connected to the isolated
nodes after the switches.

> The red inverter acts as a keeper, forming a cross-coupled latch with `Inv1`.
> This removes the minimum clock frequency requirement due to leakage.

But the input of the red inverter is not tied to the output of `Inv1`.

Do you agree with this answer? What is the actual role of the red inverter?

answer.text:
No. It is not a keeper and it does not make
the circuit static.

Define

* `A` = left of `CK` switch = divider output `Q`
* `B` = right of `CK` switch = `Inv1` input
* `X` = `Inv1` output = left of `CKb` switch
* `S` = right of `CKb` switch = slave input

In (a) the DFF is dynamic:

* `CK=1`: SW1 closed, SW2 open. `B=A`, `X=~A`.
  `S` floats.
* `CK=0`: SW1 open, SW2 closed. `B` floats,
  `S=X`, `Q` follows.

`B` floats on `CK=0`, `S` floats on `CK=1`.
That is the minimum-frequency limit.

A cross-coupled keeper for the master would be
a weak inverter head-to-tail with `Inv1`:

```
Inv1 input B <-> keeper output
Inv1 output X <-> keeper input
```

i.e. across `Inv1` alone, pointing opposite to `Inv1`.

That is not what is drawn. The red inverter has

* red output tied to `X`, i.e. to `Inv1` output
* red input tied to `A`, i.e. to divider `Q`,
  on the left of the switch, not to `B` and not to `X`.

So the two inverters point the same way, left to right,
and their outputs are shorted:

```
A --SW1-- B --Inv1-- X
A --red-----------> X
```

There is no bistable pair. Outputs tied together,
inputs different and separated by the switch, is not
positive feedback.

In particular it does not hold the floating nodes:

* `B` still floats when SW1 is open.
* `S` still floats when SW2 is open.
* `X` is not a dynamic node in the original circuit;
  it is driven by `Inv1` as long as `B` is valid.

Minimum frequency due to leakage on `B` and `S` remains.

What the red does is force `X = ~A = ~Q` at all times.

On `CK=1`, track: `B=A`, so `Inv1` drives `X=~A`
and red drives `X=~A`. Parallel drive, redundant.

On `CK=0`, hold: SW1 open, SW2 closed.
`B` holds old `Q`, `Inv1` wants `X = ~B` = sampled value.
Red wants `X = ~A` = live output.

After the slave toggles `Q` to `~Qold`,

```
Inv1 wants X = ~Bold = ~Qold = Qnew = A
red wants   X = ~A = ~Qnew = Qold
```

They fight. Red does not hold the sampled bit; it
follows the output, which is supposed to change,
so it corrupts the hold.

If red is weak, `Inv1` wins and divider still
functionally works as dynamic, but with static
fighting current for the rest of `CK=0` and no
leakage improvement. `B` leaking still kills `X`
eventually and `S` leaking still kills `Q`.

If red is strong enough to hold `X` against `Inv1`,
`X=~A` always. Then on `CK=0`, SW2 closed:

```
A -> red -> X -> slave inv -> slave inv -> A
```

is a 3-inverter ring. The circuit oscillates
while `/CK` is closed instead of dividing once.

In short: wrong direction, wrong node. It is a
feed-forward short to `Inv1` output that fights
`Inv1` in hold and can close an odd-inversion
oscillator with the slave.

```
keeper input  to C = output of Inv1
keeper output to B = input of Inv1
```

```
red left  to A, far left of CK switch
red right to C, output of Inv1
```

```
input  = A, NOT C
output = C
```

Its input is separated from the input of `Inv1`
by the `CK` switch.

not anti-parallel to `Inv1`. There is no
cross-coupled pair.

hold `B` when `CK` is OFF, nor `D` when

Normal path: `A -> CK -> Inv1 -> C`
Red path:    `A -> red -> C`

* `CK=0`: `CK` OFF, `CKbar` ON. `B` holds

But `A` has now toggled to `~A_old` through
the slave, so red drives `C = ~A = A_old`.

After the toggle they drive opposite values:

```
Inv1 : C = new value
red  : C = old value
```

i.e. contention on `C`, static current.

answers.question: How do we optimize the circuit of Figure 13 for the NF if Rin must remain equal to 50 Ohm?

answer.text:
Figure 13 is a self-biased CMOS inverter with
shunt-shunt feedback.

Put

$$g_m = g_{m1}+g_{m2} \quad , \quad r_o = r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$$

Small signal the output node sees to ground $r_o$
and a $g_mV_X$ current source from output to ground.
$R_F$ is between input $V_X$ and output $V_Y$.

$$ \frac{V_Y-V_X}{R_F}+\frac{V_Y}{r_o}+g_mV_X=0 $$

i.e.

$$\frac{V_Y}{V_X} = \frac{1/R_F-g_m}{1/R_F+1/r_o} \approx -g_m(R_F\parallel r_o)$$

Input admittance is $(1-A_v)/R_F$, i.e.

$$ R_{in}= \frac{R_F+r_o}{1+g_m r_o} $$

With source $R_S$, $V_X/V_S = R_{in}/(R_{in}+R_S)$.
For match $R_{in}=R_S=50\,\Omega$.

Let the source be $V_S$ with $R_S$. Noise sources:

* $R_S$: $4kTR_S$
* $R_F$: $4kT/R_F$ in parallel with $R_F$
* $M_{1},M_{2}$: $4kT\gamma_n g_{m1}$, $4kT\gamma_p g_{m2}$
  from output to ac ground.

Put $G_S=1/R_S$, $G_F=1/R_F$, $G_o=1/r_o$.
For signal:

$$V_Y = V_S G_S(G_F-g_m)/D$$

$$D= G_S(G_F+G_o)+G_F(G_o+g_m)$$

For $R_F$ noise current $i$ between input and output:

$$V_Y = i\,(G_S+g_m)/D$$

For MOS noise current $i_M$ from output to ground:

$$V_Y = -i_M\,(G_S+G_F)/D$$

Hence $D$ cancels in the noise factor.
Output noise due to $R_S$ alone is proportional to
$G_S(G_F-g_m)^2$.

$$\frac{\overline{V_{o,R_F}^2}}{\overline{V_{o,R_S}^2}}=
\frac{G_F(G_S+g_m)^2}{G_S(G_F-g_m)^2}$$

$$\frac{\overline{V_{o,M}^2}}{\overline{V_{o,R_S}^2}}=
\frac{(\gamma_1g_{m1}+\gamma_2g_{m2})(G_S+G_F)^2}
{G_S(G_F-g_m)^2}$$

For $g_m \gg G_S,G_F$,

$$F \approx 1+\frac{R_S}{R_F}+
\frac{\gamma_{eff}}{g_mR_S}\left(1+\frac{R_S}{R_F}\right)^2$$

where $\gamma_{eff}g_m=\gamma_1g_{m1}+\gamma_2g_{m2}$.
This is the familiar result:

* $R_F$ contributes $R_S/R_F$,
* MOSFETs contribute $\approx \gamma_{eff}/g_mR_S$.

Both want large $R_F$ and large $g_m$.

They are linked by the match:

$$R_S = \frac{R_F+r_o}{1+g_mr_o}$$

$$R_F = R_S(1+g_mr_o)-r_o$$

For $g_mr_o\gg 1$,

$$R_{in}\approx \frac1{g_m}+\frac{R_F}{g_mr_o}=R_S$$

$$R_F \approx r_o(g_mR_S-1)$$

So $R_F$ cannot be increased alone. To keep
$R_{in}=R_S$, $R_F$ must track the loop gain.
In first order:

$$R_{in}\approx R_F/|A_v|$$

Increasing $R_F$ to make its noise small requires
increasing $|A_v|\approx g_m(R_F\parallel r_o)$,
i.e. increasing $g_m$.

Then:

$$y=\frac{R_S}{R_F}= \frac{1}{1+g_mr_o(1-1/g_mR_S)}$$

$$F\approx 1+y+\frac{\gamma_{eff}}{g_mR_S}(1+y)^2$$

$F$ decreases monotonically with:

* $x=g_mR_S$ : MOS noise,
* $A_0=g_mr_o$ : allows large $R_F$ for same $g_m$,
  reduces $R_F$ noise.

There is no finite optimum. For fixed $R_{in}$,
larger is better.

In practice:

Increase $g_{m1}+g_{m2}$ by larger $W$,
larger $I_D$, i.e. more power, keep inverter
trip $\approx V_{DD}/2$, i.e. scale $M_1,M_2$
together, and increase $R_F$ to re-establish
$R_{in}=50\,\Omega$. Gain $\approx g_m(R_F\parallel r_o)$
also grows, helping following stages.

Limit is power, and input capacitance
$C_{gs1}+C_{gs2}+$Miller $C_{gd}$ which
spoils wideband $S_{11}$ and bandwidth,
and finite $g_mr_o$. For given current,
maximize $g_m/I_D$, i.e. large $W/L$, small $V_{ov}$,
and use $L$ larger than minimum to raise $r_o$,
$A_0=g_mr_o$ and lower short-channel $\gamma$,
as far as bandwidth allows.

answers.question: How do we optimize the circuit of Figure 13 for the NF if Rin must remain equal to 50 Ohm?

answer.text:
For the self biased inverter, put

$$g_{m}=g_{m1}+g_{m2}\;\;,\;\;r_{o}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$$

$$ \overline{i_{n}^{2}} =4kT(\gamma_{1}g_{m1}+\gamma_{2}g_{m2}) \approx 4kT\gamma g_{m} $$

Neglect $C_{1}$. With $R_{s}=0$ for the impedance
calculation,

input : $I_{x}=(V_{x}-V_{y})/R_{F}$
output : $g_{m}V_{x}+V_{y}/r_{o}+ (V_{y}-V_{x})/R_{F}=0$

i.e.

$$ R_{in}=\frac{V_{x}}{I_{x}}=\frac{r_{o}+R_{F}}{1+g_{m}r_{o}}
 \approx \frac{1}{g_{m}}\left(1+\frac{R_{F}}{r_{o}}\right) $$

for $g_{m}r_{o}\gg 1$.

With source $R_{s}$ the closed loop gain is

$$A_{v}=\frac{V_{y}}{V_{s}}=-\frac{r_{o}(g_{m}R_{F}-1)}
{r_{o}+R_{F}+R_{s}(1+g_{m}r_{o})} $$

Imposing match

$$R_{in}=R_{s}$$

$$r_{o}+R_{F}=R_{s}(1+g_{m}r_{o}) \tag{1}$$

$$R_{F}=R_{s}(1+g_{m}r_{o})-r_{o}\approx R_{s}g_{m}r_{o}$$

$$A_{v}\approx -\frac{g_{m}r_{o}}{2}$$

i.e. half the open loop gain. $R_{F}>0$ requires
$g_{m}R_{s}\gtrsim 1$.

Noise: $4kTR_{s}$ from the source, $4kTR_{F}$ from
the feedback, $\overline{i_{n}^{2}}$ from the
channel.

Put a voltage $v_{n}$ in series with $R_{F}$,
$V_{s}=0$. Then

$$\frac{V_{y}}{v_{n}}=\frac{g_{m}+1/R_{s}}{D}$$

Put a current $i_{n}$ from output to ground,
$V_{s}=0$. Then

$$\frac{V_{y}}{i_{n}}=-\frac{1+R_{F}/R_{s}}{D}$$

where

$$D=g_{m}+1/R_{s}+\frac{1}{r_{o}}\left(1+\frac{R_{F}}{R_{s}}\right)$$

and

$$A_{v}= -\frac{g_{m}R_{F}-1}{R_{s}D}$$

Hence, referred to the source noise at the output,

$$F = 1+\frac{\overline{v_{o,R_{F}}^{2}}+\overline{v_{o,ch}^{2}}}
{\overline{v_{o,R_{s}}^{2}}}$$

$$F =1+ \frac{R_{s}R_{F}(g_{m}+1/R_{s})^{2}}{(g_{m}R_{F}-1)^{2}}
+ \frac{R_{s}(1+R_{F}/R_{s})^{2}(\gamma_{1}g_{m1}+\gamma_{2}g_{m2})}
{(g_{m}R_{F}-1)^{2}} \tag{2}$$

Under (1), $D=2(g_{m}+1/r_{o})$, and for large
loop gain,

$$ \left|\frac{V_{y}}{v_{n}}\right|\approx \frac12\;,\;
\left|\frac{V_{y}}{i_{n}}\right|\approx \frac{r_{o}}{2}\;,\;
|A_{v}|\approx \frac{g_{m}r_{o}}{2} $$

so (2) becomes approximately

$$F\approx 1+\frac{R_{F}}{(g_{m}r_{o})^{2}R_{s}}
+\frac{\gamma_{1}g_{m1}+\gamma_{2}g_{m2}}{g_{m}^{2}R_{s}}$$

i.e. with (1)

$$F \approx 1 + \frac{R_{s}}{R_{F}}+\frac{\gamma_{eff}}{g_{m}R_{s}} $$

$$\gamma_{eff}=\frac{\gamma_{1}g_{m1}+\gamma_{2}g_{m2}}{g_{m}}$$

The $R_{s}/R_{F}$ is the $R_{F}$ noise, the
$\gamma/g_{m}R_{s}$ is the MOS noise.

Both decrease with increasing $g_{m}$ and $R_{F}$.
But $R_{F}$ cannot be increased alone, it would
violate (1). For fixed $R_{in}=R_{s}=50\,\Omega$,

$$R_{F}\approx R_{s}g_{m}r_{o}$$

So we must increase the loop gain $g_{m}r_{o}$
and increase $R_{F}$ proportionally to stay
matched.

In practice:

* increase $g_{m}=g_{m1}+g_{m2}$ by increasing
$W_{1},W_{2}$ and $I_{DD}$, i.e. small $V_{ov}$.
This directly lowers $\gamma/g_{m}R_{s}$. The
inverter re-uses current to get $\approx 2\times$
$g_{m}$ for the same power.

* keep $r_{o}$ large, i.e. not minimum $L$,
to get large intrinsic gain $g_{m}r_{o}$. This
allows large $R_{F}$ for the same $50\,\Omega$,
lowering $R_{s}/R_{F}\approx 1/g_{m}r_{o}$.
Longer $L$ also keeps $\gamma$ closer to 2/3.

* size $P/N$ to self-bias near $V_{DD}/2$ for
maximum gain and swing.

Then set from (1) $R_{F}$ for $R_{in}=50\,\Omega$.

The limit is power, headroom, and bandwidth.
Large $W$ increases $C_{in}\approx C_{gs1}+C_{gs2}
+(1+A_{v})(C_{gd1}+C_{gd2})$, lowering the input
pole, and large $I_{DD}$ eventually lowers
$r_{o}$ and $g_{m}r_{o}$.

answers.question: How do we optimize the circuit of Figure 13 for the NF if Rin must remain equal to 50 Ohm?

answer.text:
This is a shunt-shunt inverter LNA.

Put

$$g_m =g_{m1}+g_{m2}\;\;,\;\;r_o=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$$
$$A_o =g_m r_o $$

the open loop gain of the inverter.
$R_F$ closes the loop from drain to gate.

Small signal with test source at input:

$$\frac{v_{out}-v_x}{R_F}+g_m v_x+\frac{v_{out}}{r_o}=0$$

$$\frac{v_x-v_{out}}{R_F}=i_x$$

i.e.

$$v_{out}=-v_x\frac{g_mR_F-1}{1+R_F/r_o}$$

$$R_{in}=\frac{v_x}{i_x}=\frac{R_F}{1-A_v}$$

$$ R_{in} = \frac{R_F+r_o}{1+g_m r_o} \approx \frac{R_F}{1+A_o} $$

for $A_o\gg1$. Matching to the source:

$$R_{in}=R_S=50\,\Omega$$

requires

$$R_F = R_S(1+g_mr_o)-r_o \approx R_S A_o \tag{1}$$

i.e. $R_F$ is fixed by $g_mr_o$. Matching does
not fix $g_m$ as in a common gate stage.

Noise at low frequency: $R_F$ and $M_{1,2}$ channel.

Put source $V_S$ with $R_S$, $G_S=1/R_S$,
$G_F=1/R_F$, $G_o=1/r_o$.

$$\begin{aligned}
v_x(G_S+G_F)-v_{out}G_F &= I_1\\
v_x(g_m-G_F)+v_{out}(G_F+G_o)&=I_2
\end{aligned}$$

$$\Delta = G_S(G_F+G_o)+G_F(G_o+g_m)$$

Signal $V_S$: $I_1=V_SG_S$, $I_2=0$:

$$A_{vS}=\frac{v_{out}}{V_S}= -\frac{G_S(g_m-G_F)}{\Delta}$$

Noise of $R_F$: $4kT/R_F$ current $i_{nF}$ from
output to input: $I_1=i_{nF}$, $I_2=-i_{nF}$:

$$Z_F=\frac{v_{out}}{i_{nF}}=-\frac{G_S+g_m}{\Delta}$$

Channel noise of $M_1,M_2$ to ground at output:
$I_1=0$, $I_2=-i_{nM}$,
$\overline{i_{nM}^2}=4kT(\gamma_1g_{m1}+\gamma_2g_{m2})$:

$$Z_M=\frac{v_{out}}{i_{nM}}=-\frac{G_S+G_F}{\Delta}$$

Output noise due to $R_S$ is $|A_{vS}|^2 4kTR_S$.
Hence

$$F=1+\frac{|Z_F|^2G_F+|Z_M|^2(\gamma_1g_{m1}+\gamma_2g_{m2})/4kT}{|A_{vS}|^2R_S}$$

$$\frac{Z_F}{A_{vS}}=\frac{G_S+g_m}{G_S(g_m-G_F)},
\;\frac{Z_M}{A_{vS}}=\frac{G_S+G_F}{G_S(g_m-G_F)}$$

so

$$F=1+\frac{G_F}{G_S}\left[\frac{G_S+g_m}{g_m-G_F}\right]^2
+\frac{\gamma_1g_{m1}+\gamma_2g_{m2}}{G_S}\left[\frac{G_S+G_F}{g_m-G_F}\right]^2$$

For $g_m\gg G_S,G_F$:

$$ F\approx 1+\frac{R_S}{R_F}+ \frac{\gamma_{eff}}{g_mR_S}\left(1+\frac{R_S}{R_F}\right)^2 \tag{2}$$

where

$$\gamma_{eff}g_m=\gamma_1g_{m1}+\gamma_2g_{m2}$$

First excess term is $R_F$, second is MOS.

Both decrease with large $R_F$ and large $g_m$.
Large $R_F$ has small noise current $4kT/R_F$.
Large $g_m$ gives large gain for the same MOS
noise current, i.e. small input referred noise.

But (1) couples them for $R_{in}=R_S$.
Approximately for $A_o\gg1$:

$$\frac{R_S}{R_F}\approx \frac{1}{A_o}=\frac{1}{g_mr_o}$$

Then (2)

$$F \approx 1+\frac{1}{g_mr_o}+\frac{\gamma_{eff}}{g_mR_S}$$

$$ \approx 1+\frac{1}{A_o}\left(1+\gamma_{eff}\frac{r_o}{R_S}\right) $$

F is monotonically decreasing in loop gain
$g_mr_o$ and in $g_mR_S$.

In other words: increase $R_F$ to make it
quiet, and simultaneously increase 
$g_m=g_{m1}+g_{m2}$ to keep

$$R_{in}\approx \frac{R_F}{1+g_mr_o}=R_S$$

constant. The MOS input-referred noise $\propto
(\gamma_1g_{m1}+\gamma_2g_{m2})/g_m^2\approx
\gamma_{eff}/g_m$ then also falls.

Unlike CG, $g_mR_S$ can be $\gg1$ while still
matched, so $F$ can be $\ll 1+\gamma$.

In practice:

* burn more $I_D$ and use large $W/L$, i.e.
small $V_{ov}$, even subthreshold, to maximize
$g_{m1}+g_{m2}$ per current. Both devices reuse
the same current.
* size $W_p/W_n$ to put DC input=output $\approx V_{DD}/2$
so both stay in saturation with maximum $r_o$.
* choose $L$ minimum for $f_T$, long enough for
reasonable $r_o$ and $\gamma$.
* then set $R_F$ from (1) for 50 $\Omega$.

Limit is power, self loading $C_{gs1}+C_{gs2}+
(1+A_o)C_{gd}$, input bandwidth $\approx 1/R_S C_{in}$,
output pole and feedback stability.

answer.text:
The forward path from $P$ to $V_{out}$ can be modeled
as an ideal voltage source in series with the output
resistance. Fig. 14(b).

Let $V_{1}$ be the small signal voltage at $P$.
The first stage $M_{1},R_{D1}$ drives the
differential pair $M_{2}-M_{3}$. Let

$$ -A V_{1} $$

be the open circuit output voltage. In series with
it is the output resistance $\approx R_{D2}$.
$R_{F}$ connects the output node to the input
node. The input of the amplifier draws no current.

Let $I_{1}$ flow from input to output through
$R_{F},R_{D2}$.

At the output node

$$ V_{out} -(-AV_{1}) = I_{1}R_{D2} $$

$$ V_{1}-V_{out} = I_{1}R_{F} $$

Hence

$$ V_{1}+AV_{1}-I_{1}R_{D2}=I_{1}R_{F} $$

$$ V_{1}(1+A)=I_{1}(R_{F}+R_{D2}) \tag{1} $$

KCL at the input, amplifier input open:

$$ I_{t}=I_{1} $$

for a test current $I_{t}$ injected into $P$.
The low frequency resistance seen looking
into $P$ is therefore

$$ R_{in}= \frac{V_{1}}{I_{t}}=\frac{R_{F}+R_{D2}}{1+A} $$

This is the $R_{in}$ marked in Fig.(a).
Seen by $I_{in}$ there is also $C_{in}$ to ground:

$$ Z_{in}(s)=R_{in}\parallel \frac{1}{sC_{in}}
 =\frac{R_{in}}{1+sR_{in}C_{in}} $$

Remains $A$.

First stage: $M_{1}$ is common source, source
grounded, drain load $R_{D1}$, driving gate
of $M_{2}$:

$$ A_{1}=\frac{V_{X}}{V_{1}}=-g_{m1}(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}) $$

Second stage: $M_{2}-M_{3}$ is a PMOS pair
with tail $I_{SS}$, $M_{2}$ drain a.c. ground,
$M_{3}$ drain loaded by $R_{D2}$, $M_{3}$
gate a.c. ground.

Let $V_{s}$ be the common source node.
For ideal tail, a.c. $i_{sd2}+i_{sd3}=0$:

$$ g_{m2}(V_{s}-V_{X})+g_{m3}V_{s}=0 $$

neglecting $g_{o}$, body effect,

$$ V_{s}= \frac{g_{m2}}{g_{m2}+g_{m3}}V_{X} $$

The $M_{3}$ drain current $i_{sd3}=g_{m3}V_{s}$
flows in $R_{D2}$:

$$ V_{out}=i_{sd3}R_{D2}
 = \frac{g_{m2}g_{m3}}{g_{m2}+g_{m3}}R_{D2}\,V_{X} $$

i.e.

$$ A_{2}=\frac{V_{out}}{V_{X}}
 =\frac{g_{m2}g_{m3}}{g_{m2}+g_{m3}}R_{D2} $$

Matched, $=g_{m2,3}R_{D2}/2$, positive.
Including $r_{o}$, $R_{out}$ at $M_{3}$ drain is
$R_{D2}\parallel 2r_{o3}$.

Overall forward gain:

$$ \frac{V_{out}}{V_{1}} = A_{1}A_{2} = -A $$

$$ A = g_{m1}(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1})
   \frac{g_{m2}g_{m3}}{g_{m2}+g_{m3}}
   (R_{D2}\parallel R_{out}) $$

$\approx g_{m1}R_{D1}\,g_{m2,3}R_{D2}/2$.

Then in particular

$$ R_{in}\approx \frac{R_{F}+R_{D2}}
 {1+g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{m2,3}R_{D2}/2}\approx \frac{R_{F}}{A} $$
for $A\gg1$.

answer.text:
The forward path is $P\to V_{out}$ with shunt
resistor $R_{F}$ from output to input.

$M_{1}$ is a C-S with $R_{D1}$.

$$ X = -g_{m1}(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1})P $$

$M_{2}-M_{3}$ is a pMOS pair tailed by $I_{SS}$.
Gate of $M_{2}$ is $X$, gate of $M_{3}$ is ac ground,
drain of $M_{2}$ is ac ground, drain of $M_{3}$
is loaded by $R_{D2}$ to ground.
Let $g_{m2}=g_{m3}=g_{m}$.

For differential mode with infinite tail impedance,
put $v_{g2}=v_{X}$, $v_{g3}=0$, $v_{s}$ the common
source. Neglecting $r_{o}$,

$$ g_{m}(v_{s}-v_{X})+g_{m}v_{s}=0 $$

i.e.

$$ v_{s}=\frac{v_{X}}{2} $$

The small signal current in $M_{3}$ is

$$ i_{d3}=g_{m}v_{s}=g_{m}\frac{v_{X}}{2} $$

flowing in $R_{D2}$. Hence

$$ v_{out}=i_{d3}R_{D2}=+\frac{g_{m}R_{D2}}{2}v_{X} $$

It is non-inverting. With $r_{o}$,

$$ A_{2}= \frac{g_{m}}{2}\,(R_{D2}\parallel 2r_{o}) $$

and $R_{out}=R_{D2}\parallel 2r_{o}$.
To first order put $r_{o}\to\infty$.

Hence the core voltage gain $P\to V_{out}$ is
inverting,

$$ \frac{V_{out}}{V_{1}}\Big|_{open} = -A $$

$$ A = |A_{1}A_{2}| \approx (g_{m1}R_{D1})\frac{g_{m2}R_{D2}}{2}>0 $$

Model the core as a Thevenin source $-AV_{1}$
in series with $R_{out}\approx R_{D2}$,
Fig.14(b). Let $V_{1}$ be the voltage at $P$,
$V_{out}$ the voltage at the right of $R_{F}$.

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{input node: } & I_{in} = \frac{V_{1}-V_{out}}{R_{F}}\\
\text{output node: } & \frac{V_{1}-V_{out}}{R_{F}}=
\frac{V_{out}-(-AV_{1})}{R_{D2}}
\end{aligned}$$

i.e.

$$\frac{V_{1}-V_{out}}{R_{F}}=\frac{V_{out}+AV_{1}}{R_{D2}}$$

$$R_{D2}V_{1}-R_{D2}V_{out}=R_{F}V_{out}+AR_{F}V_{1}$$

$$V_{out}=V_{1}\frac{R_{D2}-AR_{F}}{R_{F}+R_{D2}}$$

Then

$$I_{in}=\frac{V_{1}-V_{out}}{R_{F}}
 =\frac{V_{1}}{R_{F}}\left[1-\frac{R_{D2}-AR_{F}}
 {R_{F}+R_{D2}}\right]
 =V_{1}\frac{1+A}{R_{F}+R_{D2}}$$

Hence looking into $P$,

$$ R_{in}=\frac{V_{1}}{I_{in}}=\frac{R_{F}+R_{D2}}{1+A} $$

With the above $A$,

$$ R_{in}\approx \frac{R_{F}+R_{D2}}
{1+\tfrac12 g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}} $$

For $A\gg 1$, $R_{F}\gg R_{D2}$,

$$R_{in}\approx \frac{R_{F}}{A}
 =\frac{2R_{F}}{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}R_{D2}} $$

The source also sees $C_{in}$ to ground, i.e.

$$Z_{in}(s)=R_{in}\parallel \frac1{sC_{in}}$$

The circuit is a 2-stage voltage amplifier with
shunt-shunt feedback through $R_{F}$.

Neglect channel length modulation and body effect and
let $I_{SS}$ be ideal. $V_{b}$ is ac ground.

M1 is a common source stage. $X$ drives the
PMOS pair M2-M3. The sources of M2-M3 are common
to ac ground, the drain of M2 is ac ground,
the drain of M3 drives $R_{D2}$ to ground.

Let $V_{1}$ be the small signal voltage at $P$.
The forward amplifier can be modeled as in
Fig.14(b) by a VCVS $-AV_{1}$ in series
with the output resistance $R_{D2}$.

$$ V_{X}=-g_{m1}R_{D1}V_{1} $$

Second stage: let $v_{s}$ be the common
source node of M2-M3, $g_{m2}=g_{m3}=g_{m2,3}$.
$v_{g2}=V_{X}$, $v_{g3}=0$, $v_{d2}=0$,
$v_{d3}=V_{out}$.

With the tail open:
$$ i_{d2}+i_{d3}=0 $$

$$g_{m2}(V_{X}-v_{s})+g_{m3}(0-v_{s})\approx 0$$

i.e.
$$ v_{s}\approx \frac{V_{X}}{2} $$

The small signal current of M3 flowing in
$R_{D2}$ is
$$ g_{m3}v_{s}=g_{m3}\frac{V_{X}}{2} $$

Hence
$$ V_{out}=R_{D2}g_{m3}\frac{V_{X}}{2} $$

$$ A_{v2}=\frac{V_{out}}{V_{X}}=+\frac{g_{m3}R_{D2}}{2} $$

The total forward voltage gain is
$$ \frac{V_{out}}{V_{1}} = -g_{m1}R_{D1}\,
\frac{g_{m3}R_{D2}}{2} = -A $$
$$ A=\frac{g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{m3}R_{D2}}{2}>0 $$

Now use (b). Let $V_{out}$ be the right end
of $R_{F}$, i.e. the top of $R_{D2}$.
KCL at the output, no external load except $R_{F}$:
$$ \frac{V_{out}-V_{1}}{R_{F}}+\frac{V_{out}-(-AV_{1})}{R_{D2}}=0 $$

$$ V_{out}\left(\frac1{R_{F}}+\frac1{R_{D2}}\right)
 =V_{1}\left(\frac1{R_{F}}-\frac{A}{R_{D2}}\right) $$

$$ V_{out}=V_{1}\frac{R_{D2}-AR_{F}}{R_{D2}+R_{F}} $$

The forward amplifier draws no input current.
A test current $I_{t}$ injected at the input
flows only in $R_{F}$:
$$ I_{t}= \frac{V_{1}-V_{out}}{R_{F}} $$

$$ V_{1}-V_{out}=V_{1}\left[1-\frac{R_{D2}-AR_{F}}
{R_{D2}+R_{F}}\right]=V_{1}\frac{R_{F}(1+A)}{R_{D2}+R_{F}} $$

Hence the resistance looking into $P$:
$$ R_{in}=\frac{V_{1}}{I_{t}}=\frac{R_{F}+R_{D2}}{1+A} $$

i.e.
$$ R_{in}=\frac{R_{F}+R_{D2}}{1+g_{m1}R_{D1}g_{m3}R_{D2}/2} $$

For $A\gg 1$, $R_{in}\approx (R_{F}+R_{D2})/A$.

answers.question: If the LDO regulator in Figure 15 generates thermal noise with spectrum Sth, how do we compute the VCO output phase noise?

answer.text:
In a free running oscillator a low frequency
perturbation of the supply cannot be treated
by ac analysis. It frequency modulates
the oscillator.

Let the noise of the LDO at its output be

$$v_{n,LDO}(t) \;\; \leftrightarrow\;\; S_{th}(f)\;\; {\rm V^2/Hz}$$

one-sided.

Slow variations of $V_{out}$ in Fig.15 change
the average of $X$ and $Y$ and hence

* the average varactor capacitance $C_{v}(V_X-V_{cont})$,
* the drain junction and overlap capacitance of $M_{1,2}$,
* hence the tank resonance,

$$f_{0} = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{L_{1}C_{tot}}}$$

i.e. AM-PM conversion. To first order:

$$\Delta f(t) = K_{VDD}\, v_{n,LDO}(t)$$

where the supply pushing

$$K_{VDD} =\frac{\partial f_0}{\partial V_{out}} \;\; {\rm Hz/V}$$

is the static tuning sensitivity to the supply.
In simulation / measurement:

$$K_{VDD}\approx \frac{f_{0}(V_{out}+\Delta V)-f_{0}(V_{out}-\Delta V)}{2\Delta V}$$

with small $\Delta V$, i.e.

$$K_{VDD} \approx -\frac{f_{0}}{2C_{tot}}\frac{\partial C_{tot}}{\partial V_{out}}$$

The VCO output is then

$$V_{out,VCO}(t) \approx V_{0}\cos\left[2\pi f_{0}t+\phi_{n}(t)\right]$$

with

$$\phi_{n}(t) = 2\pi\int^{t} \Delta f(\tau)d\tau
 = 2\pi K_{VDD}\int^{t} v_{n,LDO}(\tau)d\tau$$

Integration in time is $1/j2\pi f$ in frequency:

$$\Phi_{n}(f) = 2\pi K_{VDD}\frac{V_{n,LDO}(f)}{j2\pi f}
 = K_{VDD}\frac{V_{n,LDO}(f)}{jf}$$

Hence frequency-noise PSD

$$S_{f}(f_{m}) = K_{VDD}^{2}\,S_{th}(f_{m})\;\; {\rm Hz^{2}/Hz}$$

and phase-noise PSD, for $f_{m}$ offset from
carrier

$$S_{\phi}(f_{m}) = \frac{S_{f}(f_{m})}{f_{m}^{2}}
 = \frac{K_{VDD}^{2}}{f_{m}^{2}}S_{th}(f_{m})\;\;{\rm rad^{2}/Hz}$$

For small index, single-sideband ${\cal L}$ in dBc/Hz:

$${\cal L}(f_{m}) \approx \frac{1}{2}S_{\phi}(f_{m})$$

i.e.

$${\cal L}(f_{m}) = 10\log\left[\frac{K_{VDD}^{2}S_{th}(f_{m})}{2f_{m}^{2}}\right]$$

White $S_{th}$ thus appears as $1/f_{m}^{2}$,
$-20$ dB/dec, phase noise.

The noise on $V_{out}$ frequency-modulates the
oscillator. For offset frequencies $f_{m}\ll f_{0}$
we can use a quasi-static model.

Let the LDO output noise be $v_{n}(t)$, one-sided PSD
in $V^{2}/Hz$

$$ S_{Vout}(f_{m}) = S_{th}(f_{m}) $$

Put a small change $\Delta V_{out}$ on the supply.
The oscillation frequency changes by

$$\Delta f = K_{VDD}\,\Delta V_{out}$$

$$K_{VDD} = \frac{\partial f_{osc}}{\partial V_{out}}\;\; {\rm Hz/V} $$

is the supply pushing. It is FM, exactly like the
control, except with gain $K_{VDD}$ instead of
$K_{VCO}$.

Indeed $X$ and $Y$ in Fig.15 have a dc level $\approx
V_{out}$. E.g. the MOS varactors $M_{v1},M_{v2}$ see

$$V_{G}-V_{cont} \approx V_{out}-V_{cont}+{\rm RF}$$

so $V_{out}$ changes their bias and their average
capacitance, changing

$$f_{0}\approx \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{L_{1}C_{tot}}}$$

$$\frac{\Delta f_{0}}{f_{0}}\approx -\frac{\Delta C_{tot}}{2C_{tot}}$$

$$K_{VDD}\approx -\frac{f_{0}}{2C_{tot}}\frac{\partial C_{tot}}{\partial V_{out}}$$

There are also contributions from $M_{1,2}$ capacitances,
bank switches, swing dependence, etc. In practice
$K_{VDD}$ is extracted by simulation: step $V_{out}$ dc
by e.g. $10\,{\rm mV}$ and measure $\Delta f_{0}$ in PSS,
or modulate $V_{out}$ at small $f_{m}$ and measure FM sideband.
To first order the varactor part is $-K_{VCO}$.

Then with noise:

$$f(t)=f_{0}+K_{VDD}v_{n}(t)$$

Excess phase in radians:

$$\phi_{n}(t)=2\pi\int_{0}^{t}K_{VDD}v_{n}(\tau)d\tau$$

i.e. in Laplace

$$\Phi_{n}(s)=\frac{2\pi K_{VDD}}{s}V_{n}(s)$$

This is the transfer from LDO voltage noise to VCO
phase. Hence PSD of phase, in ${\rm rad^{2}/Hz}$:

$$S_{\phi,LDO}(f_{m})=\left|\frac{K_{VDD}}{f_{m}}\right|^{2}S_{th}(f_{m})$$

For small index the SSB definition $L=S_{\phi}/2$:

$$L_{LDO}(f_{m}) = \frac{K_{VDD}^{2}}{2f_{m}^{2}}S_{th}(f_{m})$$

$$L_{LDO}|_{dBc/Hz}=10\log\frac{K_{VDD}^{2}S_{th}(f_{m})}{2f_{m}^{2}}$$

If $S_{th}\approx \overline{v_{n}^{2}}$ is white in the
band of interest, $L_{LDO}\propto 1/f_{m}^{2}$, -20 dB/dec,
until $S_{th}$ itself rolls off with the LDO bandwidth.
