In Fig. 15 the LDO noise is in series with
the VCO supply $V_{out}$. It FM modulates the VCO.

Let the low frequency noise of the LDO at its output be

$$ \overline{V_{n,LDO}^2} = S_{th}(f)\;\; {\rm V^2/Hz}\;\; {\rm one-sided} $$

$S_{th}$ is essentially white in band, low-pass
filtered by the LDO bandwidth.

A change $\Delta V_{out}$ in the dc value of the
LDO output changes the VCO common-mode, in
particular the average voltage across the varactors
$M_{v1},M_{v2}$, the $C_{db},C_{gd}$ of $M_1,M_2$,
the swing, etc., and hence the oscillation frequency.
Define the quasistatic supply pushing:

$$ K_{VDD} = \frac{\partial f_{osc}}{\partial V_{out}} \;\; {\rm Hz/V} $$

Get it from a $f_{osc}$ vs. $V_{out}$ sweep in PSS.
It is a common-mode FM effect. Differential
operation does not reject it.

For noise frequency $f_m \ll f_0$ we can use
quasistatically:

$$ \Delta f(t) = K_{VDD}\,V_{n,LDO}(t) $$

i.e. the VCO is a voltage-to-frequency converter
for the supply. Frequency to phase is an
integrator:

$$ \phi(t) = 2\pi\int \Delta f(t)dt = 2\pi K_{VDD}\int V_{n,LDO}(t)dt $$

$$ H(s)=\frac{\phi}{V_{n,LDO}}(s)=\frac{K_{VDD}}{s/2\pi} $$

In the frequency domain, for FM:

$$ S_{f}(f) = K_{VDD}^{2}\,S_{th}(f)\;\; {\rm Hz^2/Hz} $$
$$ S_{\phi}(f) = \frac{S_{f}(f)}{f^{2}} = \left(\frac{K_{VDD}}{f}\right)^{2}S_{th}(f)\;\; {\rm rad^2/Hz} $$

one-sided, $f$ = offset from carrier. This is
the double-sideband phase spectrum due to the LDO.

Narrow-band FM, $|\phi|\ll 1$ rad, the single-sideband
to carrier ratio in 1-Hz BW is $S_{\phi}/2$:

$$ {\cal L}_{LDO}(f_m) = \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{K_{VDD}}{f_m}\right)^{2} S_{th}(f_m) $$

linear. In dBc/Hz:

$$ {\cal L}_{LDO}(f_m)=10\log_{10}\left[\frac{K_{VDD}^{2}S_{th}(f_m)}{2f_m^{2}}\right] $$

In-band white $S_{th}$ appears as $1/f_m^{2}$,
-20 dB/dec, phase noise.

answers.question: We add CT to the tail node, as in Figure 16. What happens to the phase noise?

answer.text:
Adding a noiseless $C_T$ does not add noise.
It changes the large signal operation - for the worse.

Naively you would think $C_T$ bypasses the noise
of $I_{SS}$ to ground and helps. In fact the noise
of $I_{SS}$ contributes to differential output
to first order very little:

A current injected at the common-mode tail node $P$
perturbs $X$ and $Y$ equally. The differential
$X-Y$ and hence the differential phase is to
first order undisturbed. The ISF of $P$ for
differential phase is $\approx 0$.

$C_T$ instead lowers the impedance seen at $P$:

$$ Z_T(2\omega_0)\approx \frac{1}{j2\omega_0C_T}\parallel R_{SS} $$

Without $C_T$, $Z_T$ is high. $I_{D1}+I_{D2}\approx
I_{SS}$ is roughly constant. $M_1$-$M_2$ just steer
the current.

With $C_T$ large enough that $|Z_T(2\omega_0)|\ll 1/g_m$,
$P$ is ac ground at $2\omega_0$. During zero-crossings,
when $X\approx Y$, both $M_1$ and $M_2$ are on and can now
draw large simultaneous current from the tank through
$C_T$ to ground. In other words:

* the second harmonic current is allowed to flow.
It loads the tank when both devices are on.
Tank $Q$ is degraded, swing is reduced. Thermal
phase noise floor goes up.

* much more importantly, the oscillator becomes
strongly nonlinear and AM-PM converting. The harmonic
current in the tank has to be accommodated by a
Groszkowski frequency shift away from $\omega_{tank}$.
That shift depends on bias current.

Flicker noise in $I_{SS}$ and in $M_1,M_2$ modulating
bias therefore modulates frequency. In Hajimiri-Lee language,
the waveform loses half-wave symmetry and the effective
ISF acquires a dc value. $1/f$ is upconverted to $1/f^3$.

So the $1/f^3$ corner rises dramatically and the
$1/f^2$ region also degrades. Minimum tail capacitance,
i.e. maximum $|Z_T(2\omega_0)|$, is best.

If you want to filter $I_{SS}$, filter it with a
low-pass that still presents high $Z$ at $2\omega_0$,
e.g. the series-$L$, shunt-$C$ noise filter resonant
at $2\omega_0$. $C_T$ alone to ground does the opposite.

answers.question: We add CT to the tail node, as in Figure 16. What happens to the phase noise?

answer.text:
With an ideal tail, the sum

$$ I_{D1}+I_{D2} = I_{SS} $$

is constant. $P$ is a virtual ground at $f_0$
but not at $2f_0$. $V_P$ bounces at $2f_0$.

In particular consider what happens at the
zero crossing of the differential output.

$X-Y$ crosses zero with $X$ and $Y$ at common-mode,
both $M_1$ and $M_2$ on. To keep $I_{D1}+I_{D2}=I_{SS}$ constant
with two devices sharing current instead of one device
carrying it all, the $V_{GS}$ required is smaller.
Since $V_G$ is fixed by the tank common mode,
$V_P$ must go up.

So without $C_T$ :

* at $X,Y$ peaks, one of $M_1,M_2$ is on,
carrying all of $I_{SS}$, the other off
* at $X,Y$ crossing, both are on, but $V_P$
rises to keep total current $=I_{SS}$, i.e.
to starve them.

This is fortunate. For an $LC$ oscillator

$$ \Gamma(\phi) \approx 0 \;\; \rm at \;peaks $$
$$ \Gamma(\phi) = \Gamma_{max} \;\; \rm at \;zero\;crossings $$

noise injection at the peak only AM-modulates,
noise injection at the crossing PM-modulates the most.

The drain noise current of $M_1,M_2$ is modulated
by their bias current, $\alpha(\phi)$. The effective
ISF for phase is $\Gamma_{eff}= \Gamma(\phi)\alpha(\phi)$.
The $V_P$ bounce helps keep $\alpha$ small when
$\Gamma$ is large. It also keeps the tank unloaded:
looking into the drain of $M_1$ or $M_2$ with the
source driven by a high $Z_{tail}$ is high impedance.

Put a large $C_T$ from $P$ to ground to "filter"
$I_{SS}$ noise. You now ac ground $P$ at $2f_0$.

$V_P$ can no longer bounce. At the zero crossing,
with both gates high at common-mode and source
pinned, $M_1$ and $M_2$ both turn on hard.
$I_{D1}+I_{D2}$ is no longer $I_{SS}$, it shows
a large current spike draining current from the tank
exactly at the zero crossing.

That is:

* maximum transistor thermal noise $\alpha_{max}$
now coincides with maximum sensitivity $\Gamma_{max}$,
hugely increasing $\Gamma_{eff,rms}$ of $M_1,M_2$.

In the frequency domain, at the crossing both
devices present $\approx 1/(g_m+g_{mb})$ from
$X$ and $Y$ to ac ground through $C_T$, loading
the tank and spoiling its $Q$ periodically.

The reduction in $I_{SS}$ noise contribution is
far outweighed by the increase in $M_1,M_2$
contribution. Net $1/f^2$ phase noise goes up by
several dB.

answers.question: We add CT to the tail node, as in Figure 16. What happens to the phase noise?

answer.text:
With a high impedance at $P$, $P$ swings.

$M_1$-$M_2$ steer $I_{SS}$ from side to side.
$V_X = V_{CM}+A\cos\omega_0t$, $V_Y = V_{CM}-A\cos\omega_0t$.
The common source follows the side that is on:

$$ V_P \approx \max(V_X,V_Y)-V_{GS} $$

i.e. $V_P$ goes up when $| \cos\omega_0 t|$ is maximum.
It contains essentially $2\omega_0$.

In particular, when e.g. $X$ is high, $M_2$ is on:

$$ V_P \approx V_X - V_{GS2} $$

$V_P$ rises with $V_X$, keeping $V_{GS2}$ roughly
constant, equal to the $V_{GS}$ for $I_{SS}$.

Now bypass $P$ to ground at $2\omega_0$ with a large
$C_T$. $V_P \approx V_{P,dc} =$ constant.

When $X$ goes high, $+A$, to turn $M_2$ on:

$$ V_{GS2} = V_X-V_P = V_{P,dc}+... + A $$

$V_{GS2}$ now grows by the full oscillation amplitude $A$.
At the same time the drain of $M_2$, $Y$, goes low, $-A$:

$$ V_{DS2} = V_Y - V_P \approx {\rm const} - A $$

Large $V_{GS}$, small $V_{DS}$. $M_2$ is driven deep
into the triode region. Similarly $M_1$ on the other
half cycle.

Without $C_T$, $P$ rising with the gate keeps the
overdrive roughly constant and minimizes the time
in triode. With $C_T$, the pair spends a much larger
fraction of the period in triode.

That is bad for phase noise:

* In triode $M_1, M_2$ present a resistive load
$ \approx 1/(g_{ds})$ across the tank. Tank $Q$ falls,
loss increases, oscillation amplitude falls.
By Leeson $ {\cal L} \propto 1/Q^2 V_{sig}^2$ goes up.

* In triode the channel noise of $M_1, M_2$ and
noise from the tail device feed directly to $X,Y$
through a resistor.

$C_T$ does short high frequency noise of $I_{SS}$
around $2\omega_0$ to ground and prevents it from
mixing down. But the loss of $2\omega_0$ swing at $P$
and the resulting heavy triode loading dominates.
Net: phase noise degrades, by several dB in practice.

That is why noise filtering puts an $L_T$ in series
with $I_{SS}$ so $L_T$ resonates with $C_T$ at
$2\omega_0$: $C_T$ still shorts $I_{SS}$ noise,
but the tail sees high impedance and can still swing.

answers.question: Estimate the oscillation frequency of the circuit in Figure 17.

answer.text:
The circuit is two identical differential $LC$
oscillators in parallel quadrature coupling.

* $X_{1},Y_{1}$ with $L$ to $V_{DD}$ is tank 1
* $X_{2},Y_{2}$ with $L$ to $V_{DD}$ is tank 2

Each has

* a core cross coupled pair, tail $I_{SS}$, $g_{mSS}$,
  gates $X\leftrightarrow Y$,
* a coupling pair, tail $I_{1}$, $g_{m1}$,
  drains $X,Y$, gates driven by the other
  oscillator.

One coupling is straight, one is crossed. Put

$$V_{d1}=V_{X1}-V_{Y1}\;,\qquad V_{d2}=V_{X2}-V_{Y2}$$

and let $Y_{p}(j\omega)$ be the single ended tank
admittance to ac ground,

$$Y_{p}= \frac1{R_{p}}+j\left(\omega C-\frac1{\omega L}\right)$$

$L$ = tank inductor, $R_{p}$ = parallel loss,
$C$ = total capacitance to ground at $X_{1},Y_{1},
X_{2},Y_{2}$: $C_{db}$, $C_{gd}$, $C_{gs}$ of core
and coupling devices, next gate load, $L$ parasitic, etc.

Small signal KCL at $X_{1},Y_{1}$ differential:

$$V_{X1}Y_{p}+g_{mSS}V_{Y1}+i_{c1}=0$$
$$V_{Y1}Y_{p}+g_{mSS}V_{X1}-i_{c1}=0$$

For a differential coupling pair driven differentially
by $V_{d2}$,

$$i_{X1,c}-i_{Y1,c}=g_{m1}V_{d2}$$

i.e. $i_{c1}= \pm (g_{m1}/2)V_{d2}$.

With $V_{Y1}=-V_{X1}$, $V_{d1}=2V_{X1}$ :

$$V_{d1}\left(Y_{p}-g_{mSS}\right)+g_{m1}V_{d2}=0 \tag{1}$$

Similarly for tank 2, with the other coupling
inverted:

$$-g_{m1}V_{d1}+V_{d2}\left(Y_{p}-g_{mSS}\right)=0 \tag{2}$$

Put $A=Y_{p}-g_{mSS}$. Then

$$\begin{vmatrix}A & g_{m1} \\ -g_{m1} & A\end{vmatrix}=0$$

i.e.

$$A^{2}+g_{m1}^{2}=0$$
$$Y_{p}-g_{mSS}= \pm jg_{m1} \tag{3}$$

Then from (1)

$$\frac{V_{d2}}{V_{d1}} = -\frac{A}{g_{m1}} =\mp j$$

i.e. $|V_{d2}|=|V_{d1}|$, $\angle V_{d2}-V_{d1}
= \pm 90^{\circ}$. In-phase and anti-phase
are impossible. The circuit must oscillate
in quadrature.

From (3),

$$Y_{p}=g_{mSS}\pm jg_{m1}$$

i.e.

$$\frac1{R_{p}} = g_{mSS,eff} $$
$$\omega C-\frac1{\omega L}= \pm g_{m1} \tag{4}$$

The core $-G_{m}$ cancels the loss. The coupling
current is in quadrature to the core current
and must be cancelled by detuning the tank
off resonance to provide an opposite susceptance.

Let $\omega_{0}^{2}=1/LC$. From (4)

$$\omega^{2}\mp \frac{g_{m1}}{C}\omega-\omega_{0}^{2}=0$$

For weak coupling $g_{m1}/C \ll \omega_{0}$,

$$\omega_{osc} \approx \omega_{0} \pm \frac{g_{m1}}{2C}$$

The two signs are the two quadrature sequences,
$I$ leads $Q$ below resonance, $I$ lags $Q$
above resonance.

In particular to first order

$$\omega_{osc}\approx \omega_{0}= \frac1{\sqrt{LC}}$$

$$f_{osc}\approx \frac1{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}$$

the $LC$-tank frequency.

$$\omega_{osc}= \omega_{0}\left[\pm\frac{m}{2Q}
 +\sqrt{1+\left(\frac{m}{2Q}\right)^{2}}\right]$$

For normal $Q\gg m$,

$$\omega_{osc}\approx \omega_{0}\left(1\pm\frac{m}{2Q}\right)$$

In large signal switching terms $m\approx I_{1}/I_{SS}$,

answers.question: Estimate the oscillation frequency of the circuit in Figure 17.

answer.text:
The circuit is two identical $LC$ oscillators
coupled to each other.

Let $X_{1},Y_{1}$ be the differential output of the upper
oscillator, $X_{2},Y_{2}$ that of the lower oscillator.
$L$ is the load inductor per side to ac ground.

* $M_{2}-M_{3}$ upper and lower are the normal
cross coupled negative-$g_{m}$ pair, tail $I_{SS}$.
* $M_{1}-M_{4}$ upper and lower are a differential
pair, tail $I_{1}$, whose output is in parallel
with the tank but whose input is the other
oscillator output.

One coupling is straight, one is crossed in the
middle. Put for the differential voltages

$$V_{1}=V_{X1}-V_{Y1}\;,\qquad V_{2}=V_{X2}-V_{Y2} $$

Let per side to ground

$$Y_{1/2}= \frac1{R_{p}}+j\left(\omega C-\frac1{\omega L}\right)$$

$R_{p}$ inductor loss, $C$ total capacitance to
ground at $X,Y$, $L$ load inductor, $\omega_{0}^{2}=1/LC$.

Small signal, differential mode, tails ac ground,
let $g_{SS}$ be the $g_{m}$ of a core device,
$g_{1}$ that of a coupling device.

Upper, $X_{1}$ KCL, e.g. direct coupling:

$$V_{X1}Y_{1/2}+g_{SS}V_{Y1}+g_{1}V_{X2}=0$$

With $V_{Y1}=-V_{X1}= -V_{1}/2$,
$V_{X2}=V_{2}/2$, etc.,

$$(Y_{1/2}-g_{SS})V_{1}+g_{1}V_{2}=0 \tag{1}$$

Lower, crossed coupling:

$$(Y_{1/2}-g_{SS})V_{2}-g_{1}V_{1}=0 \tag{2}$$

i.e. with $Y'=Y_{1/2}-g_{SS}$,

$$\begin{vmatrix}Y' & g_{1}\\ -g_{1} & Y'\end{vmatrix}=0$$

$$Y'^{2}+g_{1}^{2}=0$$

$$Y' = \pm jg_{1}$$

That is

$$\frac1{R_{p}}-g_{SS}+j\left(\omega C-\frac1{\omega L}\right)
 =\pm jg_{1}$$

Real part is the amplitude condition.
Imaginary part is the phase condition:

$$\omega C-\frac1{\omega L}= \pm g_{1} \tag{3}$$

This is the tank susceptance cancelling the
$90^{\circ}$ coupling current. Indeed (1)-(2)
give $V_{2}= \mp jV_{1}$, i.e. quadrature.

(3) is

$$LC\omega^{2}\mp g_{1}L\omega-1=0$$

$$\omega = \pm\frac{g_{1}}{2C}+
\sqrt{\left(\frac{g_{1}}{2C}\right)^{2}+\omega_{0}^{2}}$$

where $\omega_{0}=1/\sqrt{LC}$.

For weak coupling $g_{1}/2C\ll\omega_{0}$,

$$\omega_{osc}\approx \omega_{0}\pm \frac{g_{1}}{2C}$$

two quadrature modes, one leading, one lagging.

Put $g_{SS}\approx 1/R_{p}$ at oscillation
and $Q=R_{p}C\omega_{0}$:

$$\frac{\Delta\omega}{\omega_{0}}\approx
\pm\frac{g_{1}}{g_{SS}}\frac1{2Q}$$

In large-signal hard switching the effective
$G_{m}\propto I/V_{0}$, so $G_{1}/G_{SS}=I_{1}/I_{SS}$ :

$$\omega_{osc}\approx \omega_{0}\left[1\pm
\frac{1}{2Q}\frac{I_{1}}{I_{SS}}\right]$$

In particular to first order:

$$f_{osc}\approx f_{0}= \frac1{2\pi\sqrt{LC_{tot}}}$$

$C_{tot}$ per side: $C_{db}$, $C_{gs}$,
Miller $C_{gd}$, gate load of the other
oscillator, wiring and inductor capacitance.
